en: The Hevajra Tantra, the First King of Rituals. The First Chapter: The Family of Hevajra. Oṃ, homage to the glorious Hevajra! Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling in the wombs of the vajra-ladies, which are the heart of the body, speech, and mind of all the Tathāgatas. (1)

The *Yogaratnamālā*, a Commentary on the *Vajra* [Tantra], composed by the Great Paṇḍita Ācārya Śrī Kṛṣṇapāda. Oṃ! Homage to Hevajra. Having paid homage to the glorious Hevajra, whose nature is supreme bliss, I shall write down the tradition of the lineage of the former masters regarding Hevajra.
This introductory formula beginning with "Thus have I [heard]" is indeed revealed in this way in both the Sūtras and the Tantras;
however, others explain the essential meaning of the Tantra here in a different manner.
And so it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, my Dharma should be compiled thus: 'Thus have I heard. For this reason, the compiler says, "Thus have I heard.
In this regard, some indicate the compilation by means of the word "heard" (*śrutam*).

Otherwise, if it were heard through a lineage of oral tradition (*śrutiparamparā*), the recitation (*saṃgīti*) would lack authority; therefore, in order to exclude these two possibilities, [the Buddha said]: "Thus by me" (*evaṃ mayā*) means "by me indeed," not heard through a lineage;
"thus" (*evam*) means "just as I shall recite";
"at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) means at one particular time, not at all times, nor everywhere.

"Bhagavān" refers to the Vajra-form, the Holder of the Vajra (Vajradhara). He is the Bhagavān because he possesses the qualities (*guṇa*) such as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and so forth. Oṃ! Homage to Śrī Heruka; homage to Hevajra. —ka.
‘Hṛdaya’ is not present in manuscripts ka, ga, gha, cha, ja, ṭa;
‘yoginī’—manuscript gha; ‘yogi’—manuscript cha; ‘bhaga’—manuscript ja; ‘vijahāra’—manuscripts ka, kha.
The nihilist,
having gone to the traditional sequence, will explain it— ga.
It should be recited together— Ka.Gha indicates; Ga [indicates] the tradition heard from the lineage.
Thus, there are these two arrays (vyūha): *aga-kāla* and *aga-i*.
And so it is said in the *Hevajratantra*, in the chapter on the Family of Hevajra (*hevajrakulapaṭala*): "Of complete sovereignty, knowledge, fame, and glory..."

"Form, object, and effort—of these six, 'Bhaga' is the scriptural term" (Sevārthasamgrahaṭīkā, p. ...). Thus he says: "He sported. He sported by means of the sports of the Buddhas. Where did he sport?
In the "concealment of the three secrets," which is the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, that form of the Blessed One Vajradhara, known as the Source of Phenomena (dharmodayā),
is itself the "vulvas" (bhaga) of the Vajra Ladies, Locanā and the others,
because they possess bodies consisting of the stainless and infinite Dharma and Dharmatā.
Therefore, it is a descriptive compound (viśeṣaṇasamāsa) meaning "the bodies, speech, and minds of all Tathāgatas and the bhagas of their Vajra-women.

Regarding the phrase "in those": having perceived the Blessed One’s dwelling in that peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), a place more secret than the most secret, an assembly of a retinue corresponding to this [teaching] will generally arrive; since this was already indicated in the *Pūrvatantra*, it is not elaborated here. This is the explanation according to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*). As for "Thus have I [heard]," etc.:
the letter *e* is said to be the *bhaga*, and the letter *vaṃ* is known as the *vajra*.
"Maya" is said to be movement; that which is heard is considered to be twofold.
And so he will say: "In that way, the Blessed One takes the form of semen; that bliss is known as the beloved woman. Having the nature of the enjoyment of Dharma is the characteristic of Vajradhara."

By this opening statement—"Closed, resembling a kunda flower; open, having the form of bliss"—he indicates the subject matter of the tantra: the nature of emptiness and compassion, the nature of wisdom and skillful means, the nature of the Dharma-body and Enjoyment-body, the nature of the conventional and the ultimate, and the forms of the generation and completion stages.
And so he will say: "Some..."
By the syllable *he*, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is called "vajra," and wisdom (*prajñā*) is also so called;
the tantra whose nature consists of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*)—that which I have proclaimed, listen to it.
(Hevajratantra 1.1.7). Thus, [the phrase] "at one time" and so forth, referring to that which is of such a nature, is easy to understand.
Thus is the traditional explanation; "of the form" (rūpasya) refers to knowledge (jñānasya); "the object" (artha) is heard [in scripture] as "the vulva" (bhaga). — Ka. Gha.
Where did he dwell?—
There is no [place], there is no [place]— gha.
The mind is located there; this is the peak of the mountain of form. ka. gha. etad rūpaparṣata-ka. gha. cittaṃ gatatrasthakūṭā-ga.
Thus it is indicated—
namely, (Snelagrovamahodaya)—
see Hevajratantra 1.8.50.
The form of Vajradhara is not conventional—ka. gha. *ga* is not present—ga.
*sāṃvṛtaṃ*—ka. gha.
*Hevajratantra* 2.4.30 [First]:
*Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*. Therein the Blessed One said: "The heart of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, the Lord, the most secret of secrets.

[Vajragarbha replied: "Aho! Vajragarbha, well said, well said! O Great Compassionate One, O Great Bodhisattva! Alternatively, this is the meaning: the letter *E* should be known as the earth, and Locanā is the *karmamudrā*.
She resides in the navel, within the sixty-four-petaled wheel of emanation.
The syllable *vaṃ* should be known as water; Māmakī, the Dharma-mudrā, is established in the heart within the eight-petaled lotus of the Dharma-wheel.

The syllable *ma* is declared to be fire, and the Mahāmudrā Pāṇḍarā resides in the enjoyment wheel (*saṃbhogacakra*) at the throat, within the eight-petaled lotus. The syllable *yā* is said to be wind, and the mudrā Samayatārī resides in the great bliss wheel (*mahāsukhacakra*) within the thirty-two-petaled lotus.
That which is called the "innate" (sahaja) is said to be divided into two types:
the conventional form of the deity from the perspective of the generation stage (utpattikrama).
Commentary: However, from the perspective of the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*), the teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon the two truths, which are of the nature of bliss.
And likewise elsewhere: "The teaching of the Vajra-holders is based upon these two stages: the stage of generation and the stage of completion."
"In this very way, thus was it heard by me at one time," and so forth, according to the previously mentioned explanation. || 1 ||

Remaining there in the midst of the assembly, the Blessed One said: "O Vajradhara, what is that distinguished essence of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas? It is the Lord Vajradhara, the supreme deity; for this very reason, he is the secret of all Tathāgatas. [The Lord Vajradhara]—is he the Lord of *ka-kha* mudrās? Is he the Lord of the heart (*hṛdayabhaṭṭāraka*)? Is he the Lord of the form of the *bha* mudrā? He is the most secret, the maker of secrets."
‘kha’—this reading does not appear in the various manuscripts; it is a correct usage occurring only once:
*ka kṛpā* (ka, kha); *bodhisattva* (ka); *mahābodhisattvasya* (gha); *sattvāḥ* (cha).
But it is established as *ka*, *ga*, *va*,
*aṣṭa*, *gha*, *tu*, and *ga*.
The yoga of the sixty-second Taraṇī-ga.
vivṛtisukha—ka, kha, gha; bhāvanā—ga; deśanā—gha; vyākhyā—ka, gha.

O Vajradhara, Bhaṭṭāraka, according to the doctrine of the deities, listen to the heart-essence of Vajrasattva, the Great Being, the Samayasattva, and the Jñānasattva, known as Hevajra, in the Vajra Tantra. 2.
Vajragarbha said: Why is one Vajrasattva? By what does one become Mahāsattva and Samayasattva? O Blessed One, please tell me how this comes to be.
The Blessed One said: "Indestructible" is called *vajra*; the being (*sattva*) who is the oneness of the three worlds through this wisdom (*prajñā*) and reasoning is known as Vajrasattva. ||4||

Vajradhara is [called] Hevajra because it is more secret than that [vajra], as it is not to be revealed to the śrāvakas and others; considering that those who have faith in it are even rarer to find, the Blessed One, in order to encourage the eager members of his assembly, said:
"O Vajragarbha," and so forth, and enjoins them to listen by saying, "Listen. (2)
Vajragarbha said: "What did he say?
He spoke regarding the meaning of the three questions. (3)
The Blessed One said: "Indestructible," and so forth.
It is called "indestructible" because it cannot be broken;
it is that which cannot be uttered by proponents of one's own or opposing schools.
What is that?
It is the emptiness of all phenomena.
And so the venerable Ācārya Devapāda said: "If someone should offer a rebuttal when the analysis has been performed by means of emptiness..."
Everything avoided by her becomes equal to what is to be accomplished.
First: One who is filled with the essence of great primordial wisdom is called a Mahāsattva; because he is constantly engaged in the commitments (*samaya*), he is designated as a Samayasattva. (5)
One who summarizes the conduct of awakening is called a bodhisattva; through the union of wisdom and primordial gnosis, one is a jñānasattva, a Tathāgata.
Vajragarbha said: "By what means does Hevajra come to have such a compendium of names?
What is signified by the syllable *he*, and what is expressed by *vajra*? (6)

And so it was said by the Blessed One in the *Vajraśekhara*: "Firm, essential, without decay, characterized by being uncuttable and indivisible, neither burnable nor destructible—emptiness is called the vajra."

"Sattva is the unity of the three realms of existence" (*sattvaṃ tribhavasyaikatā*). "Sattva" is the state of being (*sato bhāvaḥ*), which is the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) characterized by dependent origination (*idampratyayatā*); it consists of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Thus it was said by the Blessed One: "O Brahmin, 'being, being' refers to the five aggregates; these are the three realms of existence, and they are body, speech, and mind. Their unity is their non-duality, resulting from the attainment of the culmination of luminosity.
This is through this wisdom and reasoning.
By means of this investigation into the Middle Way of the Perfection of Wisdom, he is thus described as Vajrasattva, the Dharmakāya. || 4 ||
"By the essences of great gnosis," and so forth: "great gnoses" refers to the teachings (dharmas) set forth in the Mahāyāna; their "essence" is their savor.
He is "filled" by them.
This is what is meant.

Within the interior of a peaked pavilion constructed of supremely radiant and variegated jewels, his body adorned with the perfectly pure primary marks and secondary signs, he was satiated by the flavors of the enjoyment of great bliss through the forms of the withdrawal and radiation of infinite hosts of yoginīs. Thus wandering until the end of cyclic existence, he remained tireless.
In the *Vajra-tantra*, the Blessed One said: "O, 'He' refers to great compassion, and 'Vajra' is said to be wisdom.
The Tantra consists of the nature of wisdom and means; listen as I proclaim it to you. (7)
The wise know that the great *mudrā* for attracting through vision possesses manifold powers,
such as paralyzing, expelling, immobilizing armies, and performing malevolent rites (*abhicāruka*).
The cause of the birth and maintenance of the Yoginīs according to the rule, their power, their knowledge and realization, and the manner in which the deities arise. ||9||
The meaning is that he is eternal by virtue of his permanence.
He alone is the Great Being (*mahāsattva*), the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) of the Buddhas.
"Eternally," and so forth.

"Samaya" (the commitment) is the going everywhere through the yoga of vibration. It is the going throughout the three realms by means of various forms according to the specific methods for those to be trained; because it proceeds constantly therein, it is the "Samayasattva. The infinite variety of the Buddhas' emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) is designated by the term "Samayasattva. (5–6)
Vajragarbha spoke thus.
What did he say?
He spoke for the sake of that meaning which was indicated by name as the cause of Hevajra’s being the Holder of the Vajra (Vajradhara).
Regarding "Hevajra":
by reason of such a name as "Hevajra," it is subsumed as being of the nature of wisdom and means, and so forth.
"Tantra" means a continuous sequence.
And that [tantra] is threefold: the *hetutantra* (cause-tantra), the *phalatantra* (result-tantra), and the *upāyatantra* (means-tantra).
Herein, the cause is sentient beings belonging to the Vajra family; the result is the fully perfected form of Hevajra.

The means is the path with its associated equipment to be described hereafter. That has been spoken by me, the Vajradhara, beginning with the words "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) and so forth. Now, through the introductory formula (*nidānavākya*), he causes [the audience] to listen to what is being pointed out and applies them to what has been heard. (7)
To explain what was merely indicated, he says:

"by the drawing-in through vision," and so forth. "According to rule" means by the sequence of weak, medium, and intense as stated in the *Devatāpaṭala*. "Arising" refers to color, configuration, and so on. "Abiding" refers to the support.

ka. gha | That which does not exist—kha | consisting of wisdom and means—khaga | threefold—kha; the tantra is threefold—ga | having the characteristics to be described—kha. ga | by means of sentences—kha; by sentences—ga | therein—ga | "No," he says—kha; "and mantra," etc.—ga | seen—ga | the visarga is not present—kha | there is no visarga—kha | the support—kha; there is no visarga—ga | First: *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*. First of all, there should be one [tantra] which is the cause for the arising of Heruka.
O Vajragarbha of great compassion, they are liberated by the very nature of existence itself.
Beings are bound by attachment to existence and are liberated through the thorough knowledge of it.
A wise person should contemplate existence through its cultivation and non-existence through its thorough knowledge;
likewise, one should contemplate Śrī Heruka through his cultivation and non-existence through its thorough knowledge.

The cause consists of the seeds and symbols of the moon and sun; capacity is the power born from the excellence of recitation and meditative cultivation; knowledge refers to astrology and the like; and higher cognition (*vijñāna*) refers to the training of the master in the deities such as Hevajra and others, their arising according to their manifestation and according to what is appropriate.
"First," and so forth.
Why "first"?

For here, in the Mantra Mahāyāna, it is taught that for the sake of the initial entry of beginner practitioners (*ādikarmika*), it is by means of the very form of the deity (*devatāmūrti*) that [the path] is described. As it is said: "For beginner practitioners, there is the meditation on the form of the deity."
It was taught first in the Tantra for the sake of accomplishing all activities.
With reference to the indication of the second stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*) which will be explained later, "the great means" is one cause.
Regarding the phrase "by existence alone," etc.: "existence" (*bhāva*) means that which comes into being or arises; it refers to the transition from one state of existence to another.
By that very thing—the body characterized by the five aggregates—they are liberated. He addresses [the disciple] as "O Vajragarbha, O Great Compassionate One."

Some describe liberation as characterized by the non-existence of the aggregates within the realm of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Anticipating this view, he says: "If liberation were indeed through an existent entity (*bhāva*), then by what would there be bondage? He then explains: "They are bound by the bond of existence. In that context, "bondage" refers to grasping—that is, attachment to things and the conceit of their reality; the meaning is "by that. How, then, are they liberated?

"By the thorough knowledge of that" means the thorough knowledge of it; this is wisdom (*prajñā*), which consists of the investigation described in the *Tattvapaṭala* with the characteristics to be explained, such as "form does not exist by way of its own nature, nor is it seen," and so forth. By means of the thorough knowledge of the five aggregates as being characterized by non-arising, they are liberated.

"One should meditate on the one entity"—*ga*, *ja*, *bho0*. "In compassion"—*ka*, *kṛpaṃ*—*kha*, *kṛpaḥ*—*cha*. "Having fully understood"—*ka*. "Wisdom"—*ka*, *prajño*—*cha*, *ja*, *prajñaṃ*—*jha*. "Those to be fully known"—*ka*. "In the same way, Heruka"—*ka*. "And the entity"—*ka*, "of non-existence"—*ja*. "Light and so forth"—*kha*. "In this Secret Mantra Mahāyāna"—*bho0*, "here in the Secret Mantra Mahāyāna"—*gha*. "Entity and so forth"—*ga*. "Arises from existence"—*ga*. The word "thus" (*iti*) is absent—*ga*. "Is liberated"—*ga*. "They describe"—*gha*. "Anticipating that [objection], he says"—*ga*, "anticipating that, he says"—*gha*. "By the bondage of entities"—*ga*. "Full knowledge"—*ga*. "The investigation is finished"—*ga*. "Beginning with 'tyādi'"—*ga*; "the extraction should be seen"—*he0 ta0*: "In the *Vajratantre*: 'And the great gnosis residing in the body is free from all conceptual constructions.'"
Pervading all things, though residing in the body, it is not born of the body. — [From the *Hevajrakulapaṭala*] What are the channels (*nāḍī*)?
Vajragarbha said: "O Blessed One!"
"Regarding the Vajra Body, O Blessed One, what is it? He replied: "There are thirty-two channels;
these thirty-two carriers of bodhicitta flow into the place of great bliss."
Among them, three channels are principal: lalanā, rasanā, and avadhūtī.
For this reason, the state of being (bhāva) should be that which is to be meditated upon (bhāvya).
"O Wise One" is the address.
The form of the deity, born from the transformation of the seed-syllables and symbols of the moon and sun, is generally what should be meditated upon; the meaning is that this is logical.
And "non-existence" (abhāva): non-existence must necessarily be fully understood. It is called non-existence because it does not come into being; it is non-arising (anutpāda).

And thus it was said by the Blessed One in the *Laṅkāvatāra*: "He who understands things as both existent and non-existent never becomes attached to any phenomena; he who is never attached to any phenomena touches the signless samādhi."
In the same way, Hevajra should be meditated upon with the characteristics as previously described;
furthermore, non-existence must be thoroughly understood.
To indicate that even that [knowledge] is non-existent, he speaks of the second stage, beginning with the words "situated in the body" (*dehastham*) and so forth.
It is situated in the body, thus it is "situated in the body" (*dehastham*).
It is both great and knowledge, thus it is "great knowledge" (*mahājñānam*).
If it resides in the body, how can it be that great gnosis?

He says: Because all phenomena are manifested through the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), which is characterized by being co-emergent with uncontaminated great bliss (*anāsrava-mahāsukha*) and is pervasive throughout all things;
therefore, although it resides in the body, it is not born of the body.
The body is not its cause, because the body possesses the nature of being deceptive and illusory.
And so he will say: therefore—there is not—cha.
ja | [it is] bound by the vajra—ga |
Pervasive—ka;
residing in the body—kha; born of the body—ka.
Which ones? Ka, Kha, Ga, Gha. Which [are they]? Ṭa, Nā, Ā, Gha. Of the channels (nāḍī): Gha.
Carrying the bodhicitta—Ka; carrying the bodhicitta upward—Kha; the carriers—Ga.
sravantyaḥ—ka, kha, ga, gha;
madhya—ka, kha, gha, ṅa;
triṇi—ka, kha; trīṇi—ga, gha, cha, ja.
The Blessed One said: "Lalanā" is *ga*; "avadhūtī" is *ka*, and "dhūtī" is *kha*; "prajñā" is *ka* (and *gha*).
-sañjate - ga. gha;
spṛśate - gha;
abhāvañjeti - ka. gha.
Indicating this, he says: "g" | — "Abiding in the body, innate knowledge, and great knowledge" — "ga" | "Pervasive" — "ga" |

[The first: In the *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*, it is said: "Lalanā, by her nature as wisdom (*prajñā*), and Avadhūtī, situated in the middle region by way of means (*upāya*). [Variants: *anāvasravamahā0* — ka, gha; *dharmatāyāḥ* — ga; *anabhinirvṛtteḥ* — ga; *dharmikatvāt* — ka, gha. *Lalanā*, by her nature as wisdom (*prajñā*), and *Avadhūtī*, situated in the middle region by way of means (*upāya*).
Free from the grasped and the grasper.
Lalanā brings Akṣobhya; Rasanā is known as the bearer of Prajñā and the Moon; and Avadhūtī is the bearer of blood.

There is no smell, no form, no sound, nor even taste; there is no purity of mind. There is no touch, no mental object (*dharma*); through the purity of all things, he proclaimed the nature of the Pure Realm—so I believe.

Thus, having indicated in this opening statement the two sequences—of arising and of the arisen—as suggested by the words heard, [the author] asks regarding Hevajra, who is known as the "perfected sequence": "The body itself is the support-mandala (ādhāramaṇḍala), while the channels (nāḍīs) are the supported (ādheya), being the nature of the fifteen yoginīs. However, it is not known how many these are, how they are arranged, and what kind of realization (abhisamaya) they constitute.
Thus he asks, beginning with "O Bhagavān," etc.; "carriers of the bodhicitta" means those that flow with the innate (sahaja).
"Three channels are primary.

This is the intended meaning: the mere thorough knowledge of the union of these three channels is sufficient, because therein the innate characteristic (*sahajalakṣaṇa*) of the *vajra* is preeminently perceived.
He states the nature of those three [channels] beginning with "Lalanā," etc., which is easy to understand.
In the Vajra Tantra, the chapter on the family of Hevajra states: Viyogā, Premaṇī, Siddhā, Pāvakī, and likewise Sumanā;
Vṛttā, Kāminī, Gehā, Caṇḍikā, and Māradārikā.
Vajragarbha said: "Bhagavān, you have mentioned these thirty-two channels; Bhagavān, what are they like?"

All [phenomena] are transformations of the three realms of existence, devoid of the grasped and the grasper; or else, by every means, they are conceptualized as the characteristics of existence. Now, the divisions of the vows (*saṃvara*) are explained: *Āli* (vowels), *Kāli* (consonants), Moon, Sun, Wisdom (*prajñā*), Means (*upāya*), Dharma-body, Enjoyment-body, Emanation-body, Great Bliss-body, Speech, and Mind.
Thus have I [heard].
“O Blessed One,” and so forth, he asks.
The underlying intention is this: do these [channels], when cultivated solely in the form of channels, bring about the state of the glorious Vajradhara, or rather otherwise?
To that, he says: “They are the transformation of the three realms of existence.”
The three realms of existence are all phenomena, because they are comprised within body, speech, and mind. They are transformations thereof and possess that same nature;
for this very reason, they are devoid of subject and object.
The word "or" (*athavā*) indicates an alternative position.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the serpent-method" (*sarpopāyena*): for the reason that all these [channels] are methods for attaining the state of Vajradhara, they exist within this wheel as the very nature of the channels (*nāḍī*). Thus, Lalanā is of such a form, Rasanā is of such a form, and Avadhūtī is of such a form; they are conceptualized through their characteristic states for the sake of favoring disciples.

Regarding the phrase "the breach of the vow" (*saṃvarabheda*) and so forth: if a yogin should ascertain that which belongs to the internal state of those external, coarse [elements], that constitutes their vow (*saṃvara*), because it is restrained (*saṃvṛta*) and because it is the excellence of contraction (*saṃkṣepavara*). Its breach consists of many [factors]. [First: *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*: By the letter *e* is the goddess Locanā; by the letter *vaṃ*, Māmakī is remembered. By the letter *ma* is Pāṇḍarā; and by the letter *kā*, Tāraṇī is remembered.
In the nirmāṇacakra there is a lotus with sixty-four petals;
in the dharmacakra, eight petals;
and in the saṃbhogacakra, sixteen petals.
In the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), there are thirty-two petals;
this is the arrangement according to the sequence of the number of wheels.
The method: "Āli and Kāli," and so forth; the sixteen vowels beginning with the letter *a* are *āli*;
the thirty-four consonants beginning with the letter *ka* are *kāli*.
These very *lalanā* and *rasanā* are the moon and sun, wisdom and means.
"Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa" refers to the Dharma-chakra, the Sambhoga-chakra, and the Nirmāṇa-chakra.
In the heart, throat, and generative organ respectively,
these are the three wheels known as body, speech, and mind:
the body wheel is in the generative organ, the speech wheel is in the throat, and the mind wheel is in the heart.
The Mahāsukha-cakra at the crown of the head should be understood as having the nature of the thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*) of the three.
Within these very four wheels, the four mudrās, which have the nature of the elements earth, water, fire, and air, are thus designated by me.
Now follows the statement regarding the number of petals on the lotuses in the *nirmāṇa* and other wheels.
Regarding the phrase "in the *nirmāṇa*-wheel" and so forth:
there is a sixty-four-petaled lotus; in the eight central petals, [the syllables] *a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa* are arranged in counter-clockwise order (*vāmāvarta*).
The syllable *aṃ* on the pericarp;
the syllable *aṃ*.
In the heart is an eight-petaled lotus facing downward, with *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* on its four corner petals.
In the directions and intermediate points are the four [vowels] ā, ī, ū, and ai;
at the pericarp is the syllable *hūṃ* facing downward;
and at the throat is a sixteen-petaled lotus.

To be bathed (*snāpye*)—*ka*; *snāpe*—*ga*. Of the maiden (*kumāryyā*)—*kha*, *cha*, *ja*; *kramāya*—*ga*; *kumāryyān*—*jha*. *Prahṛta*—*ga*. Absent—*ka*, *ga*, *gha*. Absent—*ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*. *Veḍuā*—*ka*, *kha*; *veduyā*—*ga*; *veduā* (once)—*gha*. When this is said (*ityakte*)—*gha*. *Hastika*—*ka*, *ga*, *gha*. Absent—*ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*. *Vyāghra*—*ka*, *kha*, *gha*; *vyāghra*—*ga*. Absent—*ka*. When this is said (*ityuktai*)—*ga*. *Gaṇḍa*—*gha*. (*Note: These two asterisks are absent in the reading of 'ka'.*) When this is said (*ityakte*)—*kha*. *Sarpa*—*kha*. (*Note: These two asterisks are absent in 'ka'.*) *Oṃ Dhanapāla*—*kha*; *Dhanapāle*—*gha*. *Asvā*—*ka*; *Śvāna*—*kha*, *ga*, *gha*. Following this, the additional reading "this is the mantra of the heart of the animal" (*iti paśuhṛdayo mantraḥ*) appears in *ka*; the additional reading "the mantra of the animal-heart" (*paśuhṛdayāmantraḥ*) appears in *kha*; the additional reading "the animal-heart mantra" (*paśuhṛdayo mantra*) appears in *ga*. *Saptamyāṃ*—*ga*; *trayodaśyāṃ*—*kha*. In the *Vajratantre*, the Chapter on Mantras: Vajrā, Gaurī, Vārī, Vajraḍākī, and Nairātmikā; through the yoga with Bhūcarī and Khecarī, the practitioner shall perform immobilization and other rites. (34)
The second chapter on mantras:

This is the mantra-yoga beginning with "Vajrā Gaurī" and so forth. Having visualized Vajrā as white, arisen from the syllable *Āṃ*, mounted upon a corpse, and holding a curved knife (*kartī*), a skull-cup (*kapāla*), and a khaṭvāṅga staff—one should recite *Oṃ hūṃ svāhā* one hundred thousand times for the purpose of preliminary service (*pūrva-sevā*).

Afterwards, having written the syllable *maṃ* with chalk inside an unbaked clay bowl, and having written within it "Oṃ hūṃ Devadatta, paralyze! Hūṃ svāhā," fill it with cremation-ground ashes. Enclose it with another unbaked clay bowl, and upon that, draw a pair of Māhendra-maṇḍalas adorned with the directional vajras. Having placed this on the ground and stepped upon it with one's foot, remaining in meditative absorption as before, one should recite the mantra: "Oṃ hūṃ vajre Devadatta, paralyze! Hūṃ svāhā. One should recite it one hundred and eight times or one thousand times.
He becomes paralyzed.

Having thus visualized Gaurī, who is produced from the syllable *iṃ* and is red as saffron, holding a noose and a goad; and having meditated upon the syllable *aṃ*, red as a bandhūka flower, in one's own heart, one should recite *oṃ aṃ svāhā* one hundred thousand times for the purpose of preliminary service (*pūrvassevā*). Then, visualizing the person to be subdued (*sādhya*) in front of oneself, naked, red in color, and with disheveled hair; and having visualized the syllable *aṃ* in the color of fire within her vulva—or else within the heart of the male [target], visualizing him agitated and being scorched by the fire of the syllable *aṃ*—one should perform the recitation while thinking: *oṃ aṃ gaurī amukīṃ me vaśamānaya aṃ svāhā*. Having bound her by the throat with the noose and pierced her heart with the goad, one should visualize her dragged forth and fallen at one's feet; she will certainly become submissive.

In the same way, having meditated upon Vāriyoginī, who is produced from the syllable *Iṃ*, blue in color, and holding a mallet and a threatening gesture (tarjanī) in her hands, and having seen the blue syllable *Khaṃ* on the sun at one's heart, one should recite *oṃ khaṃ svāhā* one hundred thousand times for the sake of prior service (*pūrvasevā*). [Secondly: Having meditated upon the object of practice (*sādhya*) as naked, with disheveled hair, blue in color, and mounted upon fangs, and having meditated upon him fleeing while being struck by cruel ones with clubs in their hands facing south, one should rotate the mantra: *oṃ khaṃ vāriyogini, [name], uccāṭaya khaṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. Within seven nights, he will certainly be expelled.

In the same way, having meditated on the yoga of Vajraḍākinī by means of the syllable *u*, and having meditated on a blue-colored syllable *jrīṃ* upon the sun at the heart, one should recite *oṃ jrīṃ svāhā* one hundred thousand times.

For the sake of preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), having meditated on the two targets mounted on a horse and a buffalo and fighting with one another, one should perform the recitation in that same manner: *oṃ jrīṃ vajraḍākinī devadatta-yajñadattayor vidveṣaṃ kuru jrīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. This will certainly cause them to hate each other.

In the same way, having visualized Nairātmyā, who is produced from the syllable *Aṃ*, with a distorted form and holding a skull-cup, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a flaying knife, and having seen a blue-colored syllable *Buṃ* upon the sun at her heart, one should perform the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*). Then, having drawn a six-spoked wheel in a Brahma-skull using poison, vermilion, and blood, and having written the syllable *Hūṃ* in the corners, one should write in the center: *Oṃ Buṃ [Name] jvaraya Hūṃ*. For various calamities, one should interpose the name and heat those two in a fire of chaff.
One should perform everything for the cruel rite; in all cases, at the end of the mantra, one should append *Hūṃ Hūṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ*.

In the same way, having visualized Khecarī, fully perfected from her own seed-syllable and mounted upon a corpse, and having performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), one should meditate on the victim as distressed atop a circle of wind and fire. Then, emitting rays of red-colored flames from the seed-syllable in the heart, one causes them to enter through the right nostril of the victim, pierce the heart, and exit through the left nostril; drawing them back into the heart-seed syllable while inhaling with the breath, one should recite the mantra. Thus, one certainly effects the summoning.

In the same way, having meditated on the yoga of Bhūcarī as emerging from her own seed-syllable, appearing like the color blue, and having performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), one should meditate on a blazing vajra produced from the syllable *Ghuḥ*, being driven into the waist-region of the victim with its point facing downward, and then recite the mantra:

*Oṃ ghuḥ bhūcarī [name] māraya ghuḥ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. It certainly kills. Thus ends the second chapter, the Mantra Chapter, in the *Hevajrapañjikā* composed by the venerable Kṛṣṇācārya, within the *Yogaratnamālā*.

The third chapter: The Chapter on the Deities. We shall now explain the Chapter on the Deities: One should first cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*), then compassion (*karuṇā*) in the second; one should cultivate sympathetic joy (*moda*) in the third, and equanimity (*upekṣā*) last of all. (1)

Therefore, once again: first is the realization of emptiness, second is the gathering of the seed-syllable, third is the accomplishment of the image, and fourth is the placement of the immutable syllable. ||2||

Regarding the "Chapter on the Deities": the chapter on the deities—namely the Hevajras and Vajrayoginīs—concerning the generation yogas (*utpattiyoga*) of Hevajra and the others as described in the *Vima-laprabhā*, we shall explain here specifically.
"First," and so forth:
it is called "first" with respect to [the sequence beginning with] compassion.

First of all, having stayed in a delightful place and sat upon a comfortable seat, one should recite three times, "Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," for the sake of protecting the site and oneself through yoga. Then, having worshipped the Blessed One in the form [depicted] on a cloth or other support, and having consecrated the water-offering (argha) with his own mantra, one should perform the confession of sins, the rejoicing in merit, and the going for refuge to the Three Jewels. Having established the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), one should first, in the first moment, cultivate loving-kindness (maitrī) toward all sentient beings in the form of bringing them unsurpassed happiness; in the second moment, toward those same beings, cultivate compassion (karuṇā) in the form of removing all suffering; in the third moment, toward those same beings, cultivate sympathetic joy (muditā) in the form of ensuring that divine happiness never ceases; and finally, one should cultivate equanimity (upekṣā) toward them all in the form of applying the path that serves as the antidote to all primary and secondary afflictions (kleśa-upakleśa). Thus it continues. || 1 ||
This describes the preliminary equipment (*parikara*) for the first yoga, which constitutes the body of all yogas that are like an illusion (*māyopama*).
Therefore, [the text says] "again" (*punarapi*); following that, it continues with the instruction "one should meditate" (*bhāvayet*).

What is that awakening to emptiness? He says: having mentally apprehended all phenomena, [one realizes] "this is mind-only" when external objects do not exist. In the *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*: Having visualized the sun in front by means of the syllable *ra*, one should visualize a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) arising from *hūṃ* within that light. With that very vajra, one should visualize a rampart and a lattice-binding. (3)
First, the wise one should meditate on the corpse as being of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*; the yogi, standing upon it, should visualize himself as Heruka. (4)
It appears through delusion, just as in a dream.
One should perceive that very mind, which is the nature of appearance, as being devoid of a singular or manifold self-nature, free from appearances, and consisting of luminosity.
This is the second [stage], the "collection of seeds."

Within that very luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), having visualized the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the deity surrounded by a garland of rays upon the solar and other mandalas as appropriate, and having accomplished the welfare of the world through the infinite emanations of the *yoginī*-families from that seed-syllable, one should meditate on their reabsorption back into that same seed-syllable; this is the "collection of seeds" (*bījasaṃgraha*).
This is the third [stage], the "accomplishment of the image" (*bimbaniṣpatti*).

By means of that seed-syllable, there is the accomplishment of the body of the deity—seated upon a corpse atop the solar and other mandalas located in the pericarp of a lotus with a thousand petals, performing the *tāṇḍava* dance in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*). This is the accomplishment of the image.
One should meditate upon that.
Regarding the fourth placement as the syllable:
then, one should visualize the seed-syllable situated within the solar and other mandalas in one's own heart.
Thus ends the meditative concentration of gentle yoga. || 2 ||
Now, with reference to the second yoga-samādhi, he says:
"By means of the letter *ra*, etc.
Here too, the preliminary preparation (*parikara*) up to the realization of emptiness and awakening should be understood as being the same as before.

With the two verses beginning with "tadadhikaṃ repheṇa" (more than that, by means of the letter *ra*), he explains the protection. Having visualized a solar disc by means of the letter *ra* which has the color of fire, one should meditate upon a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) arising from a blue *hūṃ* above it; from those two, a horizontal vajra-fence, a vajra-canopy above, a ground consisting of vajras below, and outside, vajra-flames of fire. This is the meaning of the verse.
Then, one should consecrate that with the mantra.
Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. || 3 ||
"First" means first from the body of the yoga.
One should visualize a corpse upon a mandala consisting of a sun disk and so forth, atop a thousand-petaled lotus in the midst of a vajra-fence.
Why? Because this is the seat of the deities.

In the Vajra Tantra, [the chapter on the deity]: Then, one should meditate upon the syllable *repha* within one’s own heart; right there, one should visualize the syllable *hūṃ*, black in color and most terrible, situated in the center of the vajra-navel, and further, possessing the nature of wisdom and means. ||5||
One should visualize the syllable HŪṂ arising from that as a solar mandala, born of the vajra—the reality of HŪṂ. (6)

Having seen [the seed-syllable] transformed from the syllable *hūṃ*, one should visualize it as having the nature of hatred. One should indeed meditate upon the Great Black Vajra-born, resembling a blue lotus, or rather, with a dark-blue and reddish luster, according to one's desire.
Having beheld the Lord, the Great Compassionate One born from the Vajra, in the sky, one should worship him with the eight goddesses who wear all ornaments. (8)
He said: "They know [the deceased] as being of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
For the dead person is indeed selfless (*nirātman*), and selflessness is the *dharmadhātu*.
And the *ḍākas* and *ḍākinīs* have the *dharmadhātu* as their ultimate goal."
The practitioner is the meditator (*bhāvaka*).
Having resolved that he himself is situated above that [lotus], he should establish his own state as Heruka.
This is the equipment for the middle yoga, beginning with "in one's own heart," and so forth. (4–5)
"One should contemplate one's own nature as hatred" means that one should visualize oneself in the form of Heruka.
In this tantra, the yoga of all the deities is introduced with reference to the leader, Hevajra.

For the others, it should be understood according to the circumstances through the transformation of their own respective seed-syllables and marks. Regarding "the blue lotus," it means resembling a blue water-lily; one should meditate on it with faith in whatever way one’s own mental appearance finds pleasing. || 7 ||
Concerning the third yoga, he says: "In the sky," and so forth.
Just as there was an elaboration (*parikara*) in the second [yoga], so too in the third;
however, there is an addition at the beginning.

He said to him: "Having seen the Blessed One drawn into the sky by rays from the seed-syllable in the heart, and having worshipped him mentally with various offerings, one should worship him with the eight deities, Gaurī and the others. (8)

[Third: *Vajrapañjikā* and *Yogaratnamālā*: Caurī holds the moon; Gaurī, the vessel of the sun; Vetālī has water in her hand; Bhaiṣajyā is a consumer of food; Pukkasī holds a vajra; and Śavarī likewise holds mercury. Caṇḍālī plays the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*). By these [goddesses], the Lord is worshipped. His neck is embraced by Ḍombī; he is impassioned with great passion (*mahārāga*). The seed-syllables of Candra, Āli, Kāli, and Mārtaṇḍa should be situated in the center. They say that this very one is the *Sattva*, whose nature is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). 9 || 10 || 11 ||
"Mṛgalāñchana" is camphor; "mārtaṇḍa" is *sihnaka*.

The term "container" (*bhājana*) is to be connected with each [item]. "Water" (*vāri*) is Akṣobhya; "medicine" (*bhaiṣajya*) is the fourfold equal mixture (*catuḥsama*); "vajra" is that produced from *śāli* rice. || 9 ||
"Rasa" is honey, and "ḍamaruka" is a skull-bowl.
"By the Ḍombī" means he worships while embracing her by the neck; he worships in such a manner.
Having thus performed the worship of the Blessed One, one should perform everything up to the visualization of the corpse-seat, as in the case of the second retinue.
This is the preparatory section for the third yoga. || 10 ||
Furthermore, the body of yoga here is the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*).
He explains it with the words "the lunar line" (*candrālī*) and so forth: the fifteen vowels beginning with *a* are the *āli*;
the thirty-four consonants beginning with *ka* are the *kāli*.
And that [seed-syllable] is the moon transformed from the letter *ā* in the heart;

the "moon-line" (*candrāli*) is the sun transformed from the letter *kā*, which is the *mārtaṇḍa*. The seed-syllable should be situated in the middle; thus, the seed-syllable is above the moon and the sun, and the emblem produced from its transformation follows.
That medicine consists of *dhatrī*—*gha*—and *dhātrī*—*ṭa*.
Ghasmarī: gha; Pukkaśī: ka, kha, ṭa; Pukkasi:
ga, cha, jha; Savarī: ka; Ḍamarukaṃ: ka, kha, ga, gha, cha, ṭa; vādayet: ga, gha, cha.
pūjyete – kha, ga, gha; kandharam – ka, kha, ga, gha; rāgānurāgataḥ – ka, kha, ga, gha; caṇḍālikālimantrabījam – ka; caṇḍālikālimārtaṇḍam – kha, ga, gha;
madhyagate – jha.
*sattvam*—ka, kha, ga, gha, cha, ja, jha;
*paramānandasvabhāvakam*—ka, cha, jha, ṭa; *paramānande svabhāvitam*—gha; *svabhāvaka*—ja;
*akṣobhyām*—kha.
Madhu: Kha | Vatkāmanādhi-kha, vatmṛtakā-ga | Śarīraḥ-khaga |
Awakening through the five aspects and so forth—kha, ga;
the transformed sun—kha, ga; Kāli-Mārtaṇḍa—kha, ga.
Above the moon and sun—[variant: *kha* and *ga*];
the phrase "born from the transformation of that" is absent in *gha*.

In the *Hevajra Tantra*, [the chapter on the deities]: "The radiance of one's own body flashes forth, covering the entire expanse of space; by means of the process of withdrawal, the yogi should dissolve it into the heart and become the very essence of Hatred."
He has a complexion of blue and reddish luster, with tawny hair and topknot standing erect, and eyes like the red bandhūka flower; he is adorned with the five mudrās.
The wheel, the earring, the necklace, the bracelet on the hand, and the girdle—these are proclaimed as the mudrās through the purification of the five Buddhas.
The seed-syllable should be in the *varaṭaka* (the central part of the lotus); this means one should meditate upon it.
That very thing they call "sattva," and that itself is the seed. He speaks of the Causal Vajradhara—what is its specific characteristic?
It has the nature of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).
"Visphurantī" means they flash forth, pervading the entire universe. These are the radiances resembling the body of Hevajra.
From that very seed-syllable, one should withdraw them back into the heart.
Having withdrawn those very [elements], he should cause them to enter into that very seed-syllable.

Thereupon, that yogin becomes of the nature of hatred; through the transformation of the moon, sun, seed-syllable, and emblem, he takes the form of Heruka. By this much, there is the awakening in five aspects (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*).

And so it will be stated in the eighth chapter: "The moon is the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*); the seventy-seventh is equanimity (*samatā*). The seed-syllables and the emblem of one's own deity are called the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇa*)."
The single performance by all is the manifestation of the image, which is the perfectly pure dharmatā.
"Neither blue nor reddish-brown in appearance," and so forth.
These three are yogas of the solitary hero (*ekavīrayoga*), common to all deities.
In the system [of the *Guhyasamāja*], there is no "self" (*sva*); the heart is in the *ga* [family]; the yogin is in the *ga* [family].
Red-colored with eyes like the *bandhūka* flower;
having reddish-brown hair standing upright and tawny eyebrows;
adorned with the five mudrās.
The reading "nāstyayaṃ pāṭhaḥ" is not found in manuscript Ga.
"Kaṇṭhe" is found in manuscript Ka; "kaṇṭhi" is found in manuscripts Kha and Gha. "Mekhalam" is found in manuscripts Ka and Gha.
The five mudrās—ka. There is no *visarga*—ka, kha, gha.
This portion does not exist in the manuscript ‘ga’.
The word "hetu" (cause) does not exist—O! Vajradhara alone said: "O!"—those very [words]—kha. ga; [the syllables] "candrasūryacihnabījapari"—kha.
It would be—kha. ga; "adarśa" (not seen)—gha;
possessing equanimity—kha.
The reading in the root-text (mūla) is "saptāśvikaḥ. The word "bimba" is absent; there is only "niṣpattiḥ"—in manuscripts kha and ga.
Regarding "śuddhidharmatā," the reading in the root-text is "śuddhadharmatā"—in manuscripts kha and ga.
"Blue and reddish-brown in color," and so forth—*ka*; "color," and so forth—*ga*. "Filled"—*gha*. [Third: With a wrathful gaze, wearing a tiger skin, [the *Vajrapañjikā*, the *Yogaratnamālā-sara*].
Having the appearance of one sixteen years of age,
he holds a vajra and a skull-cup in his left hands, and a khaṭvāṅga staff also in the left; in the right hands, he holds a black vajra, consisting of the utterance of the syllable HŪṂ.
The Lord sports in the cremation ground, surrounded by the eight Yoginīs; by this reasoning, it is designated as "the cremation ground" (śmaśāna).
Having four arms due to the purity of having conquered the four Māras, and possessing the color and form previously described, he arises from the syllable *HŪṂ*. Now,
the indication of the four Hevajras and of Nairātmyā— the fourth yoga consisting of the maṇḍala circle— is made in the passage beginning with "in the cremation grounds," and so forth.
Just as there is the equipment for yoga in the third [chapter],
so too in the fourth:
within the vajra-rampart are the eight terrible cremation grounds, and in the interior of the peaked palace situated in their midst dwells the Lord Hevajra.
Surrounded by the eight yoginīs beginning with Gaurī, he dwells [there];
the etymological derivation of the word *śmaśāna* as "the dwelling place of corpses" (*śavānāṃ vasatiḥ*) involves the elision of syllables.
The meaning is "the abode of corpses.
Furthermore, this term *śmaśāna* (cremation ground) serves as an indication of what will be explained in the eighth chapter regarding the *utpannakrama* (arisen stage):
"In the cremation ground, in the bodiless body, is the Lord (*nātha*)."
How can the body, which dwells in supreme bliss, be a cremation ground?
By the reasoning that it "breathes" (śvasati), it is designated as a cremation ground (śmaśāna).
Now, in order to state the specific characteristics of the four-armed Hevajra, he says: "The four-armed one, who has conquered the four Māras," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "having the form of the Blessed One": she should be visualized as having two arms, with the color and physical form [of the deity], holding a flaying knife and a skull-cup;
there is no tiger skin—[this is the reading in manuscripts] a, ka, ga, gha, ja; whereas in cha and jha, it reads "not wearing a tiger skin."
This reading follows manuscript 'ṅa'; that which is enclosed within brackets in manuscript 'gha' is not at all necessary; 'sa' is absent in manuscripts ka, kha, ga, gha, cha, ja, jha;
the form of an eight-year-old—ka, kha;
the vajra-kapāla—kha.
There is none—gha; situated on the skull-topped staff—kha; the right—ga.
The face—kha; the blue vajra—ga;
*huṃ*—ka; *ga*—kha; consisting of the self (*ātmakam*)—kha, gha;
does not exist—ka; while playing—kha; they play—ga.
nātha—ka. gha;
pariṇataḥ—kha;
sva—ka. gha
yuktā (yukta- in gha); caturbhuja-caturmāranirjitasya (caturbhujaṃ caturmāranirjitaṃ in ga);
pūrvoktarūpavarṇa (in ka, kha, ga, gha).
The state of *hu~* is compassionate in nature—*ka*; the state of *hu~*—*kha*;
the preparatory effort (*parikara*) in yoga should also be observed—*khaga*.
ga: within the interior of the eastern [enclosure]; gha: within the interior of the enclosure wall;
kha: he dwells in a pavilion in the midst of that.
This reading follows the manuscripts *ka*, *kha*, and *ga*; in manuscript *gha*, the word *parivṛttaḥ* is enclosed within brackets. That which has been praised is not at all necessary;
[this is] the arisen four-armed Hevajra—*kha*, *ga*.
He states the mouth: "kha. ga niri" and so forth—gha kartṛ—ka. gha.

In the *Vajratantro* [Deity Chapter]: In the first left arm is a human skull-cup filled with the blood of gods and asuras; in the first right arm is a vajra; embraced by wisdom with the remaining two arms, the consort Vajravārāhī has the form of the Blessed One.

He has six arms and three faces; the left is red and the right has the luster of the moon and dawn. The first [face] is blue. He is naked, possessing the colors and form previously described. The six arms represent the purity of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). In the first left arm is a trident, in the first right arm a vajra, in the second left arm a bell, and in the second right arm a curved knife (*kartī*).
With his remaining two arms, he is embraced by Vajraśṛṅkhalā;
just as the Bhagavān is, so too is Prajñā, holding a curved knife and a skull-cup in her right and left hands respectively.
Trampled by the corpse whose nature is the three realms.
The third chapter: the deities of the Hevajra of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas.
In the same way, Vajraśṛṅkhalā is the consort of the six-armed [Hevajra].

However, in this tantra, for the two-armed Hevajra, Nairātmyā alone is the consort (*prajñā*), because that is established as the general rule. For all [the deities], the offering goddesses are indeed Ḍombīs; it is the tradition that they are not [ordinary] *mudrās*.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Chapter on Deities, in the *Hevajra-pañjikā* composed by the venerable Kṛṣṇācārya, within the *Yogaratnamālā*.
First, the left [hand].
And the skull-bowl (kapālaka) is completely filled;
first, [the syllables] ka, kha, ga, gha in the right [hand].

In the Vajra-tantra, the knower of yoga, who is devoted to reality, should always worship the mother, the sister, the washerwoman, the goldsmith, the outcaste woman, and likewise the Brahmin woman, according to the ritual of wisdom and means. || 2 ||

They perceive all phenomena as non-existent in their own nature, appearing before them like the hairs perceived by one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*), but the Noble Ones (*ārya*), whose eyes of wisdom are free from the stain of ignorance, do not see them so.

Thus, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin praised the Blessed One: "O Protector, at the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, you have revealed that all phenomena are primordially peaceful, unarisen, and by their very nature in a state of *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, it is established that form and the other aggregates do not exist in their own nature."
"Not a seer," and so forth: for that phenomenon which is the seer of form, such as visual consciousness and the rest, does not exist either, because all phenomena are unarisen.
The same should be said for sound and the other objects.
"Not mind," and so forth: "mind" refers to perfected consciousness (*pariniṣpanna-vijñāna*); "mental factors" (*caittika*) refer to the dependent (*paratantra*) and the imagined (*kalpita*).

These three do not exist at all from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). How so? For it was said by the Blessed One: "O Sons of the Conqueror, the triple world is mind-only (*cittamātra*). If that is so, how is this [to be understood]?
It was truly said for the sake of causing those to be trained (*vineya*) to abandon their attachment to form and the other [sensory objects].
Regarding this point, the venerable Nāgārjuna said: "The teaching of the Sage that 'all this is mind-only' was for the sake of removing the fear of the ignorant; it is not [the truth] in reality."
Therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality, this mind does not exist.
By this much, the reality of all phenomena has been explained. ||1||
Now he describes the internal yoga, beginning with the words "jananī" and so forth:

the mother is she who desires one's welfare; the sister is affectionate; the actress is one whose movements are skillful; the washerwoman is devoted to pure deeds; the Vajrī is fond of meditation; the Caṇḍālī, because her pride has been destroyed, is of a patient disposition; and the Brāhmaṇī is devoted to faultless actions. Regarding "prajñā" and so forth: Nairātmyā is wisdom (*prajñā*), and Hevajra is the means (*upāya*).
One who is fond of reality and dear to reality should worship these two in a single form according to the method to be described. || 2 ||

Suffering is endured when unprotected by wild beasts, thieves, fire, and those who roam the earth. || 3 ||
The *mudrā* is said to be the five families for the sake of liberation;
it is called *mudrā* because one is sealed (*mudryate*) by means of this *vajra*. ||4||
O Great Compassionate One, they say that the families are fivefold and supreme: Vajra, Padma, Karma, Tathāgata, and Ratna.

"With effort" (*prayatnena*) means effort (*yatna*) for concealment (*gupti*). [This is done] so that no distinction (*bheda*) arises. Regarding the faults—both seen and unseen—that arise from such a distinction, he says: "Suffering is produced," and so forth.
Explanation of the literal meaning:

"The mother," and so forth. The mother is *avadhūtī*; the sister is *lalanā*, and by the word "and" (*ca*), *rasanā* is included; one should worship these. "Yoga" means union; from the union of those three channels, which are by nature the non-duality of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), great bliss (*mahāsukha*) arises. Therefore, the knower of their yoga—the yogi—should perform the worship consisting of great bliss "always," that is, at all times.

"Naṭī" and so forth: taste and the consciousness thereof are Naṭī; touch and the tactile faculty, along with the consciousness thereof, are Rajakī; the auditory faculty, sound, and the consciousness thereof are Vajrī; the olfactory faculty, odor, and the consciousness thereof are Caṇḍālī;
the visual faculty, form, and the consciousness thereof are Brāhmaṇī.
"Wisdom," and so forth:

wisdom is the emptiness of all phenomena; skillful means is great compassion; the application of these two is the meditative absorption (samādhi) consisting of great bliss. That, moreover, is to be understood from the instruction of the Guru.
"By that" is the meaning.
Should these— sound, form, taste, and so forth— be avoided by the yogin or not? They should be cultivated with effort, that is, with great intensity,
so that there may be no perception of the triad within sound and the other objects, just as there is none in the case of "difference" (bheda).
If such perception were to occur, what fault would there be?
He says: "Unprotected," and so forth; [the practitioner] is overwhelmed by worldly sufferings such as those from *vyāḍas* and the like.
*Vyāḍas* refers to snakes, tigers, and so forth.
The earth-dwellers are the Piśācas and so forth. || 3 ||
How is it that these [senses], such as the eye and so forth, are designated by the word "mudrā"?
It is because these very [objects], such as form and so forth, constitute the five families (*pañcakula*).
Nevertheless, they are not understood; for that purpose, he says: "By the vajra," and so on.
Vajra is indivisible gnosis; by means of this, one is sealed (mudryate). Joy (muda), meaning delight or great bliss (mahāsukha), is produced; for that reason, it is called a mudrā. || 4 ||
"Vajrapadma," and so forth;

subsequently, they become threefold through the division of body, speech, and mind. Families consist of the five elements and have the nature of the five aggregates (*skandha*).

"And this family" refers to the Vajra, Lotus, and so forth. "Gone into suchness" means having entered into the clear light (*prabhāsvara*).
"Glorious" means being fully endowed with the accumulations of merit and wisdom.
"He has arrived" means he has emerged from the clear light in order to act for the benefit of the world.
Regarding the passage beginning with "the families" (*kulāni*) and so forth:
the six families consist of Śāśvata, Ratneśa, Vāgīśa, Amogha, and the two Sāttvikas; these are the five Tathāgatas in their condensed forms as Vajrasattva.
Their condensations, in turn, are Śāśvata, Akṣobhya, and Vāgīśa.
This is what is meant: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are the six families.
In brief, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the five Tathāgatas.
Body, speech, and mind are the three families of the yogin. (9)

Because all phenomena have *tathatā* (suchness) as their intrinsic nature, the triad of the object to be cultivated, the cultivator, and the act of cultivation is not perceived from the perspective of ultimate truth.
To the question, "How then is it seen in the world? he says:
"By virtue of having a nature free from conceptual proliferation (*niḥprapañcasvabhāvata*).

Conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is characterized by manifoldness; and since that [manifoldness] is devoid of a nature that is either one or many, that suchness (*tathatā*) which is their characteristic of non-arising exists precisely in that form—this is the meaning. (11)
"Vairocana," and so forth:
he himself is Vairocana because he consists of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*);
he himself is Akṣobhya because he is not agitated by the afflictions (*kleśa*).
He alone is Amoghasiddhi, because he accomplishes the welfare of the world in all its aspects;
he alone is Ratneśa, because he is the support for all the jewels of the Buddhas; he alone is Vairocana, because he discerns those very [Buddhas] in all their forms.
That very [self] is of the nature of sattva, because it consists of the fivefold knowledge. || 12 ||
"Brahmā," and so forth.

He alone is called Brahmā and the others; how so? It is said: "by way of cessation" (*nirvṛtitaḥ*), because he is of the nature of that which is the cessation of all afflictions (*kleśa*)—namely, the knowledge of liberation (*mokṣajñāna*).
He is the Buddha because he is the reality (*tattva*) of the Buddha; therefore, he alone is the Buddha.
"Because of entering" means because of entering into that very [reality] through identity (*tādātmya*).

The *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*, Chapter Five: And because reality is awakened to as the state of supreme bliss through the awakening of passion, and because it arises within the body, it is therefore called "deity" (*devatā*). (14)
Because he possesses fortune (*bhaga*), the Buddha is called "Bhagavān.

They say that there are six kinds of fortunes, consisting of all qualities such as sovereignty and so forth; or else, he is called Bhagavān because he shatters the Māras, beginning with the afflictions (*kleśa*). (15)

[The Chapter on Reality: He alone is Śiva.
Regarding the passage beginning with "all," etc.:
how is it that he alone is all?]
Because he exists pervading all that is moving and unmoving, therefore he is "all" (sarva). || 13 ||
"By means of true bliss" (satsukhena) means because it has the nature of untainted bliss (*anāsrava-sukha*).

"He alone is the awakened reality" (*tattva-vibuddha*) means that because he experiences that very unsurpassed joy and bliss, what was previously described as Brahma and so forth is here designated [as such].

If this [reality] is all-pervasive by its very nature, then by what means is it to be practiced, or where is it to be practiced? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It arises in the body," and so forth. It arises precisely in the body; therefore, its practice must be performed within the body.
For this reason, it is called a "deity" (*devatā*); Hevajra and the Vajrayoginīs are the deities.
For this very reason, non-dual gnosis consists of great bliss, and that resides in the body itself. || 14 ||
In the ultimate sense, he alone is the Buddha, the Blessed One.
"The Blessed One," and so forth. || 15 ||
