Because it is beyond the range of the sense faculties (*indriya*), it is designated by the term *ḍombī*.

If everything is included within the meditative absorption of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama-samādhi*), then what of that which has been taught regarding recitation, meditation, mudrās, maṇḍalas, and so forth—is that non-existent altogether, or does it indeed exist?
It exists for those disciples who are beginners, because they are favored by the instruction on reality (*tattva*).
And so it has been said: "In these three, both the mantra and the deity are of a non-conceptual (niḥprapañca) nature. (18)
If this is so, how are recitation, meditation, and so forth to be performed according to the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*)?
To that he says: "Speech," and so on.
Speech, attainment, and retention.
Regarding the body (*kāya*):

the examination of the coming and going of the winds within the channels of the left and right petals of *āli* and *kāli*, and the retention of those very [winds] according to the teacher’s instruction, is *jāpa*; that alone is expressed by the term "vajra-recitation" (*vajrajāpa*).
As for the phrase "the mandala," and so forth:
The "essence" (maṇḍa) is said to be the core; it is great bliss and gnosis. In the Vajra Tantra, the snapping of the hands is the mudrā, as is the clenching of the fingers.
[This is from the Chapter on Reality: That which is to be meditated upon and that which has been contemplated is meditation (dhyāna), because it is the act of deep reflection. || 20 ||
That happiness which was attained by one's father is experienced by oneself;
that happiness by which death is met is called meditative absorption (dhyāna). || 21 ||
The Fifth Chapter: On Reality.
It is called a *maṇḍala* because it takes (*lāti*) or grasps (*gṛhṇāti*).

What is that? It is the footprint of the feet. The firm contraction of the two big toes—because of this pressing (*malanāt*), it is called a *maṇḍala*; the verbal root *mala* means "to hold" (*dhāraṇe*). Because it holds great bliss (*mahāsukha*), it is called a *maṇḍala*, and this instruction is the means for maintaining great bliss. || 19 ||

Regarding "cracking the hands" (*karasphoṭa*): the pressing of the thumb against the ring finger is *karasphoṭa*; that itself constitutes the mudrā. Likewise, the snapping of the fingers is so called.
"Regarding 'the fingers,' 'the tongue,' and 'the linga': their crushing and upward joining—this is what should be meditated upon," and so forth.

"That" refers to that which was contemplated by the entire section on reality (*tattvapaṭala*) as having the characteristic of non-arising; that is what should be meditated upon, because that contemplation is the most supreme essence.
Therefore, one should meditate upon that very [nature] which has luminosity as its characteristic by means of reflecting upon it. || 20 ||
The father is Vajradhara;
the locative case is used in the sense of the instrumental: one enjoys that bliss which was attained by Vajradhara.
"By oneself" means together with an external mudrā;
it is enjoyed for that long. "By oneself" [in the second sense] means it is enjoyed entirely independently of an external mudrā, through the majesty of yoga.
That which is to be meditated upon is explained as the meditation on luminosity by the passage beginning with "that which is contemplated."
In that state, because of the absence of the triad consisting of the meditator, the meditation, and the object of meditation, how is it to be meditated upon? [The answer is: "Death," and so forth.

Death is liberation; for it is precisely therein that the mind, mental factors, and those characterized by ignorance set. That very [state] is death, by means of which bliss—that is, by means of great bliss (mahāsukha) characterized by the exhaustion of all primary and secondary afflictions. || 21 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter, on Reality, in the *Hevajra-pañjikā* composed by the venerable Kṛṣṇācārya, within the *Yogaratnamālā*.

The sixth chapter on Conduct. Hereafter I shall explain the supreme conduct that has reached the further shore, by which one proceeds to the *siddhānta* through the cause of accomplishment in the Hevajra [tantra]. (1)
The practitioner should wear divine earrings on his ears, a circlet upon his head, and two bracelets on his wrists. (2)
On her waist she wears a girdle, and likewise anklets on her feet;
on the base of her arms she wears armlets, and a garland of bones around her neck.
Wearing a tiger skin as a garment, consuming the nectar of the five [senses], the dwelling place of the person in the yoga of Heruka is among the five colors. ||4||
Now, since there is no swifter awakening for a yogin who is devoted to constant cultivation than through the practice (*caryā*), he speaks of it, beginning with "Beyond this" and so forth:
the practice is the performance of difficult vows by the command of the Gurus and Buddhas; that I shall proclaim.
"Reached the further shore" means transcending the world.
"Varām" means the most excellent; "gamyate" means it is understood or realized. By what? By me. What is it that is realized?
It is the "siddhānta," meaning the definitive conclusion.
"Siddhihetunā" means for the sake of accomplishment.
Whether or not there will be accomplishment in this very life can be determined by obtaining the [auspicious] signs. || 1 ||
"By the practitioner" means by the yogin of conduct; it is "divine" because it consists of being without clothing. || 2 ||
"Half of ten amṛtas" refers to the five amṛtas.
"Of the Heruka-yoga," and so forth; "wandering" means roaming for alms and the like.
"The five colors" refers to those of lower status. || 4 ||
In the Vajra Tantra, however, the chapter on conduct states:
"That which is endowed with five colors is a single color; for no distinction is perceived between the manifold and the single color. (5)
The auspicious meditation is said to be practiced under a solitary tree or in a cremation ground,
as well as in a delightful mother’s house or in a lonely wilderness.

But when some degree of warmth has been attained, if one desires to engage in the conduct, and if there is a wish to attain accomplishment through this conduct, one should practice by means of this very conduct.

The notion that there are five colors is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpita*). Because of the adherence to this as being real, it is considered to be associated with defects such as [the distinction of] caste and so forth; however, in its essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), there is only one color.
Why is this? He says: because no difference is perceived between the many and the single color.
Living beings of different species possess different forms, such as elephants, horses, and birds.

Those of the same species, however, have identical forms; for example, cows among cows, and elephants among elephants. They are not distinct from one another in color, because their shapes are the same.

Thus, even according to worldly convention, the uniformity of the castes (*varṇa*) is established; how much more so by the conventional perspective of the yogis, since in beginningless saṃsāra, everyone possesses the nature of all castes. (5)
He describes the place appropriate for the practice, beginning with "under a single tree" and so forth.
A "single tree" is one whose shade is not encroached upon by another tree, and which does not encroach upon the shade of another.
The meaning is that this practice, which prioritizes uninterrupted yoga, is to be applied in solitude precisely in such places as under a single tree. (6)
And he teaches that this should not be done impulsively out of restlessness, saying "something" and so forth.
[From the *Vajrapañjikā*, the *Yogaratnamālā*: Chapter Six] [One should take] a beautiful-faced woman with large eyes, adorned with beauty and youth, and endowed with compassion.
He awakens. || 8 ||

Having taken this Vajra-maiden, whose body is dark like a blue lotus and who has been consecrated by oneself, one performs the practice; since she does not belong to the Vajra family, she is taken from the family of one's own chosen deity, or else one may take her from another family. || 9 ||
If this song, consecrated by the planting of the seed of enlightenment, is sung with joy, then it is supreme and endowed with the vajra.
If one dances when bliss has arisen for the sake of liberation, then the concentrated yogi should perform the dance with vajra steps. (10)
The power born from the mantra of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is such that, once it has been attained, [the following] must be performed; this is the intended meaning.
Snakes, wild beasts, humans, non-humans, and so forth have no power over him, and they protect him; he does not fear them either, nor is he afflicted by hunger, thirst, and the like.

If there is a desire to attain the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā-siddhi*) in this very life, then one should practice according to this conduct (*caryā*); this is the intended meaning. || 7 ||
"Vajrakanyām," and so forth.

[It means] a maiden of the Vajra family; she is "awakened" (budhyate) or "joined" (yujyate) because of the excellence of her lineage and because she cannot be approached by others. She is "refined" (*saṃskṛtā*) by the "implanting of the seed of awakening" (*bodhibījanikṣepa*), such as the consecrations (*abhiṣeka*). "Endowed with the vajra" (*vajrānvitam*) refers to the vajra, which is the gnosis (*jñāna*) of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). (8–9)
That which expresses this is "by means of vajra-steps" (*vajrapadaiḥ*).
*Vajra* refers to Hevajra.
His "steps" consist of the *ālīḍha*, *pratyālīḍha*, the maṇḍala stance, the even-footed stance, the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*), and so forth. || 10 ||

In the Vajra Tantra, Akṣobhya is in the form of the wheel; Amitābha is the Lord of Jewels; Amoghasiddhi resides in the necklace on the neck and in the girdle on the hand; and Prajñā is in the form of the hand-drum (ḍamaru). The Yogin is the nature of the earrings; Vairocana is thus remembered. (11) [Caryāpaṭala]
She has the form of a khaṭvāṅga [staff], due to the purification of hatred. || 12 ||
Established through the purity of mantra, song is known as chanting and dance as meditative cultivation; therefore, the yogi should always, at all times, perform both song and dance. 13.

One should always consume the medicine and drink the water; thus, old age and death shall not afflict one, and one will be constantly protected by the *bhūtas*. There, one should apply the crown made of hair from a thief, with the syllable *HŪṂ* arising therein. One should wear the five skulls of the Buddhas; this is the purification of hatred, which is the purification of the Vajra. || 12 || || 14 ||
By means of the practice of yoga. || 15 ||
"Always, always" means eternally, eternally.
The medicine is the fourfold equality.
Water is Akṣobhya.
"Permanence" means eternally.
"Becoming a protector" means being invincible to piśācas and other such beings.
With hair like a thief's,
with hair tied up,
born from the syllable HŪṂ, he is the form of Hevajra.
The five skull-cups are the fivefold yoga, having as their intrinsic nature the five Buddhas beginning with Akṣobhya.
The union of wisdom and means is the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*); for that purpose, there is play, which consists of external and internal worship.
*amṛtābha*—ka; *rūpeṇā*—kha, ga; *rūpeṇāmitābha*—gha; *cakri*—ṭa; *cakrarūpeṇa*—he, paṃ, mu, va;
*ratneśa*—ka, kha, gha;
*mālāyāḥ*—kha.
*vairocanosmṛtāḥ*—ka; *vairocano mataḥ*—kha; *rucaka vairocanaṃ*—gha; *mataḥ*—jha. *mekhalāyo*—gha. *sthitā*—gha.
rūpiṇi - ka, rūpīṇi - kha, rūpiṇī - gha;
ḍamarukopāye - ka, ḍamarukopāyena - kha, ḍamarukopāyarūpeṇa - ga, gha, ḍamarukopāya - cha.
The Yoginī is Kha and the Yogi is Gha;
through the purification of Kha and the purification of Ga.
Gītā: "ga kṛtā" means "ka he paṃ mu va"; "kṛtāḥ" means "ga. gha."
And it is sung: "Who performs [this]?"—*ka*; *ga*, *gha*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha* always—*ga*; "always abiding"—*gha*.
ca - ka:
proficiency; ṅa: permanence; ga: [the letter] ga.
Death does not oppress—*na* (not) *bādhyate* (is oppressed)—*ka*, *bādhyante* (are oppressed)—*ga*, *bādhyete* (are oppressed)—*gha*, *bādhet* (would oppress)—*cha*.
*ja* [variant]: *bhūtā* (beings)—*ka*, *gha*; *bhūta* (being)—*ga*.
kṛtā—ka, kha, ga; made by Cauryakeśa—gha; cauryakeśā—ṭa; makuṭī—ka, gha;
that—ka.
huṃ bhava (ka. kha. gha; bhāva cha.
ja. jha); yojyate (ka. ga; yojayata kha; yojyete gha);
kapālāni (ka; kapālaṃ ga).
It should be maintained—*ka*, *ga*; it should be maintained—*kha*;
the yoga of the moon—*ga*; of yoga and conduct—*gha*.
Immediately after "constantly," there is an additional reading in *bho*: "The liver, the white hair, and so forth will arise. (*Rgas Pa Ni głer Ma Dan sKra dKar hByuñ Baho*)
Yoga—O Sixth! [From the *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*]: Having fashioned a fragment of a five-fingered skull, it is always worn upon the crown;
likewise, the yogin bears two girdles, ashes, hair, and the sacred thread (*pavitra*), by virtue of their being the nature of wisdom and means.
By means of conduct.
Meditative Cultivation (Bhāvanā)

The sound of the hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*) is the recitation (*jāpa*); the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) is wisdom (*prajñā*). This should be the object of meditation and the practice to be cultivated through the conduct of the vajra-skull. One should avoid greed, delusion, fear, anger, and shameful actions. Abandoning sleep and the self, one should perform the conduct; of this there is no doubt.
Having given the gift of the body, one should thereafter undertake the spiritual practice; therefore, no gift is given with a calculation of what is one's own share and what is not.
The sense is that he carries a skull-fragment with five protruding fingers;
*kacaḍorī* means a hair-rope; *bhasma* refers to the smearing of ashes;
and *keśapavitra* refers to a sacred thread made of hair.
Shame and modesty, sleep—a great obstacle to yoga—and likewise even concern for the body and life must be abandoned; "without doubt" means having become free from uncertainty.
"Body," and so forth:

from the very beginning, having given his body to all Buddhas and all sentient beings according to their inclinations, he has bestowed it by giving without expectation, having abandoned the discrimination between the worthy and unworthy or the fortunate and unfortunate.
There is no *ṭa* or *kacaṃ*—*kha*, *yogi*—*kha*.
*gha*: "kapālaṃ ca khaṇḍaṃ"—*ka*; "pañcāṅgulya"—*kha*; "kapālaṃ khaṇḍaṃ ga"; "pañcāṅgule"—*gha*.

This reading follows the recensions of Ka, Kha, Ga, and Gha; that which is enclosed within brackets in manuscript Ca is not strictly necessary. "Mukuṭyā ka" and "mukuṭā ga" mean "it is worn on the head"—Ka, Ga, Gha.
"Nāstika," "sadāḥ"—Ga.
Kaccatorigha dvivegha;
having entered Bhasmakeśa, ga; the purifier of Bhasmakeśa, gha.
vibhṛti – ka; vibhartti – kha; vidharti – gha; caryyayā – ka; caryayāḥ – gha;
jāpaṃ – ka.ga; jāpa – gha; japo – ṭa.
The sound of the *ḍamaruka*—ka, jha; *ḍamaruka-śabda*—ga, cha, ja;
the *khaṭvāṅga*—ka, ga, gha, cha, ja, jha;
meditations (*bhāvanāḥ*)—ga, gha.
jāpaṃ—ka. gha; jāpā—ga;
bhāvaṃ—ga gha;
bhavedetaḥ—ga.
By means of conduct— ka, kapāla-ga.gha * —
this verse does not exist— kha—
greed and delusion— ka, kha, ga, gha.
— *bhayakrodha* — ka. gha; *bhayakrodham* — ga.
*kāyañ ca* — ka. ga. gha.
*vajrayet* — ka; *varjayat* — ga; *vajrīyet* — gha.
Who would abandon me from sleep? Sleep might abandon me.
[The word] *caryā* is found in manuscripts *gha*, *cha*, and *ja*.
[The word] *kriyate* is found in manuscript *ka*; *kriyan* in *kha*; and *kriyate* in *ga*, *gha*, *cha*, and *ja*; *kriyen* in *jha*.
Because of doubt;
[the variants] *nāstika*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*;
*pañcācaryā*—*kha*, *pañcācarya*—*ga*, *caryā*—*gha*.
One should practice with discernment—kha, ga; enjoyments—gha; fortune and misfortune—he, paṃ, mu, va;
he, paṃ, yo, ra, mā are given—gha.
There is no *pavitra*—this reading follows manuscript *kha*; according to manuscript *gha*, it is "paritaḥ"; this reading follows manuscript *ka*, and *kha* considers it doubtful.
There is no such thing as "space" or "portion of space.

Regarding the chapter on conduct (*caryāpaṭala*): one should consume whatever is obtained—whether it be solid food, soft food, or drink—without making any selection here based on the conceptual distinction between what is desirable and what is undesirable.
The mantra-practitioner should not entertain any conceptual doubt regarding what is fit or unfit to be eaten, likewise what is fit or unfit to be drunk, or what is fit or unfit to be approached.
Even a disciple who has attained accomplishment and illuminates perfect knowledge, if he pays homage to the guru out of pride, he must be abandoned for that reason.
Freed from both training and initiation, as well as from the duty of shame, the yogi of great compassion should wander according to the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Transcending fire-offerings, sacrifices, and ascetic penances, devoid of mantras and meditations,
and liberated from the vows and commitments of the *samaya*, the one possessed of excellent yoga performs the conduct.

"He pays homage" means he should salute; [this is stated] for the purpose of avoiding the consequence that one who does not pay homage would be cooked in the Avīci hell on account of being a person to be shunned.
The training in eating at the proper time and so forth,
and the initiation into the vows such as shaving the head and so forth, are performed with the nature of all phenomena— that is, in all circumstances, with the vajra-ego-sense.
"Oṃ hoḥ," and so forth:
this very resolve regarding Hevajra is his excellent yoga;
therein he makes it firm.
External fire offerings and the like must be avoided in every respect;
why?
Because for this one whose self is Hevajra, whatever eating there is constitutes the fire offering (*homa*), and the service of wisdom (*prajñā*) constitutes the yoga.
Every action of the body is austerity—
even the sounding of the hand-drum and the carrying of the khaṭvāṅga staff are mantra and meditation;
even the vajra-dance and song are mantra and meditation.
Likewise, whatever he does is his very commitment (*samaya*);
[regarding] eating—ka, ga, gha; [regarding] eating—kha; drinking—gha.
*kha*: "prātuṃ tu bhakṣayat"; *ga*: "prāsu tu"; *gha*: "prāptavantu"; *ka*: "graha mantra na"; *kha.ga.gha*: "graha mantre na"; *cha.ja*: "grahamatra"; *jha*: "grahanamaṃtra";
*ka*: "prakalpitaḥ".
*bhakṣābhakṣa*—ka, ga, gha; *bhakṣābhakṣavicāre*—kha, ca;
*vikalpam eva*—kha; *vikalpanaiva*—gha.
Even though he has attained accomplishment, he does not speak of it— ga; he is perfectly accomplished— gha— ga, gha.
*avīcātyāja* — ka; *avicyām* — kha; *avicyā hetunām* — ga; *svavicyātyāje* — gha;
*sikṣā* — ka; *vinirmuktā* — kha; *sikṣādikṣāvinirmuktaḥ* — ga; *dikṣā* — ca; *rajā* — ka; *lajjā* — ga, gha, ṭa.
caḥ—gha;
vicaraṃ—ka; cared—ca;
yogi—ga.
Jāga—ka, kha; yāga—ga, he; paṃmuva—ṅa; jāgatapotīto—gha; tyāga—ca, ṭa;
vinirmukto carya—ka; vinirmuktaḥ caryyā—ga; vinirmuktasvayaṃ—gha; suyogavini—ga.
In the Avīci [hell]—
one would fall into the void—
O Initiation! "Vow" is not present.
The liberation of Hevajra and others,
as well as the sound of the hand-drum (ḍamaruka), the vajra-song, and the vajra-dance— kha.
Sixth: Even if a demon equal to Śakra should certainly appear before one, one should not feel fear; one should roam about in the form of a lion. (25)
The yogi, ever devoted to the drink of yoga for the sake of all sentient beings, constantly drinks compassion; he does not indulge in immersion in any other drink. 26.
The sixth chapter: On Conduct.
That which one does not perform is itself one's restraint (*saṃvara*) in this tantra.
Here, four mudrās have been previously indicated according to the distinction between beings who are weak, middling, superior, and most superior.

Among these, for a certain most superior being, the realization of Mahāmudrā occurs at the very moment of receiving the fourth empowerment; therefore, no separate conduct has been taught for such a person.

Therefore, for disciples of weak, middling, and superior faculties, there is no more rapid awakening without conduct (*caryā*). Thus, conduct is also said to be threefold: elaboration (*prapañcatā*), non-elaboration (*niṣprapañcatā*), and absolute non-elaboration (*atyantaniṣprapañcatā*). This conduct of non-elaboration is taught for those of middling faculties.

Furthermore, he will speak of those with superior faculties in the fourteenth chapter, beginning with "O, O Yoginīs," and so forth, regarding the practice of absolute non-elaboration (*atyantaniṣprapañcacaryā*).

He will provide a mere indication of the practice of elaboration (*prapañcatācaryā*) for those of dull faculties in the seventh chapter of the second *kalpa*. Regarding the passage beginning with "compassion" (*karuṇā*):

compassion is cultivation with an object; by means of that, the tasting of the flavor of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is the "drinking. That very [bliss] is drunk constantly, day and night, for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of the world.
He says this very thing: "Yoga" is samādhi; that itself is the "drink," and therein alone is "delight" (prīti).

Therefore, a practitioner of the conduct (caryā-yogin) must not indulge in immersion through the drinking of other intoxicants such as liquor, for due to the predominance of delusion (moha), it would constitute a great obstacle to yoga; thus he instructs. || 26 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter, on Conduct, in the *Hevajra-pañjikā* composed by the venerable Kṛṣṇācārya, within the *Yogaratnamālā*.
There is no "kaṃ" existence—cha; one should avoid [it]—jha; by means of the cause—ga; the sixth chapter on conduct—gha.
kha: yogapānata;
ga: yogi;
gha: majjanaḥ.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Chapter on Conduct, in the glorious Hevajra Tantra.
And [the one] of superior intellect— by means of the form of non-existence— ka.
paryyat ka, paryyataḥ - kha, paryyatataḥ - ga, lepayat- gha;
piyete - ka, piyate - kha, ga, piṣate - gha;
nānyeṣāṃ - ga, nānyapāne - gha.

Sixth: [The sixth chapter on conduct (caryāpaṭala) is designated as "ka" in manuscript A; as "kha" in manuscript B; in manuscript C it is noted that it was previously indicated; in manuscript D it is noted that it occurs at the same time; in manuscript E it is noted that there is a separate conduct for each of them; in manuscript F the word "taṃ" does not exist.]
Without practice—kha;
threefold—kha, gha; state of conceptual proliferation—ka, gha.
Furthermore, those with extremely unobstructed faculties are of weak or middling capacity.
In the fourteenth [chapter]: "kha dra. heta. . dīnā" — kha.
For her,
there is no desire for sexual pleasure.
By means of yoga—due to its predominance—this reading follows the manuscript *kha*; it does not exist in manuscripts *ka* and *gha*. *kha*
The Seventh Chapter on Secret Signs (Chomāpaṭala). Now we shall explain the chapter on secret signs, by which one’s brother and sister are recognized without a doubt.
If one shows a single finger, it means "you have arrived";
with two fingers, it means "a very warm welcome.

One should recognize the Kṣemamudrā by pressing the left thumb; to him who offers the ring finger, one should offer the little finger; to him who shows the middle finger, one should offer the index finger. (3)

The *chomā* (signs) are for the *mlecchas*; the communication regarding the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) by means of the secret code (*saṃketa*) of the *yoginīs* should also be understood as a supreme method.
Therefore, it is said: "Now, the *chomā*," and so forth. This is the chapter revealing the *chomās*, as has been stated; "brother" refers to the *yogī*, and "sister" refers to the *yoginī*. || 1 ||
The index finger (*tarjanī*) represents "one" (*ekāṅgulī*). Regarding the phrase "he who," it should also be understood as "by whom.

As for "with two," one should display the gesture of a turban (*paṭṭi*) with the index and middle fingers; with those very same two fingers, one should display the hand gesture (*hasta*) of binding a turban upon the forehead. || 2-3 ||
The chapter on the *choma*—ka, gha;
by the brother—gha, ca;
sister—ga, gha.
And also—ka, ga, gha;
"one finger"—ka, ga; "one finger" gha; "he [said] pammuva"—this portion does not exist in ka, ga, gha, ja;
*—* this verse does not exist in kha.
A warm welcome—ga gha.
The *mudrā*—ka. One should recognize it—ga; one should understand it and press it—ka gha.
There is no little finger—ka, gha; likewise the little finger—ga; the little finger—gha, the middle finger—ka, gha.
darśayadyātu - kha; darśayedyātu - jha;
dadyāttasyā - jha;
pradasikāṃ - kha; pradeśīkāṃ - ga; predaśikaṃ - gha.
"— *Chommā* means *icchā* (will).
*Kha-chommā*, etc.— *kha* is the light (*jyotaka*), *gha*..."
Sister—
[gesture with] one finger, the index finger— outside, twice. Master.

Regarding "ye" (*yetyapi*)—this reading follows manuscript *ka*; "ye (ne)" is according to manuscript *kha*, while in the *Snelgrove* edition it is *gha*. "Ya" (*ya iti*) should be understood as "yena" (*yena draṣṭavyam*).
"With the index and middle fingers"—this is *ka*; "with the index and ring fingers" is *kha*; "with the index and middle [fingers]" is *gha*.
"One should display the *paṭṭisa*" is *ka*; "one should display" is *kha*.
[Hevajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā, Chapter 7: To one who shows the gesture of binding a turban, one should show the neck;
to one who shows a cloth, one should show a trident. ||4||
He who shows his breast, one should show him the boundary;
he who shows the earth, one should show him the discus. || 5 ||
The *triśūla* (trident) [mudrā] is formed by pressing the little finger with the thumb and making the gesture of a trident with the remaining fingers. || 4 ||
"Sīmāntam" means the hairline; "cakram" refers to the gesture of the wheel (*cakrābhinaya*);
"bhṛkuṭīm" is the knitting of the eyebrows; "śikhāmokṣa" and so forth.
The explanation of the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) is as follows: "One should show a single finger," and so forth.

If one should show or point toward the lotus of wisdom (*prajñāravinda*) with a single finger—the index finger—or with two fingers—the middle and index fingers—then from that [act], one would become a "Welcome" (*svāgata*).
‘Śu’ means semen (*śukra*); the meaning is that it becomes drawn forth by the application of the fingers.
Regarding “the seal of security” (*kṣemamudrā*) and so forth: it is the seal of security, the culmination of well-being, the realization of the *dharmadhātu*; one should understand that.
He explains how this is so: "By pressing with the left thumb.
Here, *vāmā* refers to wisdom (*prajñā*); the thumb within her lotus is the *vajra*.
By pressing with it once the state of emission has been attained, [the flow is restrained].

"Anāmikā," and so forth: "anāmikā" refers to the consecration of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*). "To whom" means to that person for whom one should give it according to this sequence; "to him" [one gives] the "kaniṣṭhikā"—that is to say, the fourth, the proximate consecration. How should one give it? He says: "The middle one"—the Guru who shows the *avadhūtī* to the disciple, meaning the Guru who demonstrates the *avadhūtī*, which is called the fourth instruction, along with its location, should give the *anāmikā* [finger] to the *lalanā* and *rasanā*. As for the one who would show the neck by prostrating at the feet and so forth—that is, the disciple who correctly [serves] the Guru—to that disciple he should explain it; such is the intended meaning.
Regarding "the *paṭṭīśa*," and so forth:
with two fingers, one performs the gesture of binding a turban; this is the *paṭṭīśa*, which indicates wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*).
One shows that very [gesture] right here, and thus asks; one should show the trident (*triśūla*) to him.

The trident symbolizes the non-duality of wisdom and means; [the teacher] should show it to him by dividing [it into its parts], such as the *lalanā*, *rasanā*, and *avadhūtī*. As for the disciple who shows or describes the breast—which symbolizes the experience of those two [wisdom and means]—in the *Vajra-tantra* it is prescribed that one should display a frown (*bhṛkuṭī*) and the loosening of the topknot (*śikhā-mokṣa*).
He who shows his forehead should show him his back.
He who shows the sole of his foot, playing out of curiosity, they say that he breaks the seal by means of a counter-seal through the pledge (samaya). ||7||
There, the Yoginīs say, "O son, O you of great compassion!
If they show the hand holding a garland, they are signaling that one must assemble there. || 8 ||
One should show the *sīmānta*, the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*); thereafter, one should show the earth, the wheel of emanation (*nirmāṇacakra*), to him.
One should show him the wheel, the Wheel of Dharma. || 5 ||
"One who shows the brow, which is the *saṃbhogacakra*, to him"—thus it is further stated that "the loosening of the topknot (*śikhā*) is prescribed";

for the sake of liberation, it is stated that "the vital beings of the topknot are to be slain by you," and so forth; and "one should show the forehead" means one should perform this again for the purpose of salutation.
"One should show the back with the hand"—this is the intended meaning:
one should not merely touch with the hand, but should show the sole of the foot toward the circle of the earth;
joined by this yoga, one should say, "Dwell upon the earth as you please."
But he who, having been thus granted permission by the Guru, dwells and sports—this is the yogi Nanduka, the Blessed Buddha;
together with him, he is gradually adorned with such a multitude of qualities. This is the explanation according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). || 6 ||
"By means of the counter-seal," that is,
by showing two fingers and so forth, one opens the hair-treasures.

"Drawing the garland" means holding the garland in one's hand; its dispatching toward [the practitioner] is both [actions] performed directly. Having dispatched the garland according to the *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*, saying "Abide in the pledge (*samaya*), O you of good vows!
Enjoy!"—there, in that assembly (*melā*), one relies upon the divine sphere.
For whatever the Yoginīs say, all of that indeed must be done. || 9 ||
Vajragarbha said: "O Blessed One! What are those places of assembly?

The Blessed One replied: "They are the *pīṭha* and the *upapīṭha*, the *kṣetra* and the *upakṣetra*, the *chandoha* and the *upachandoha*, the *melāpaka* and the *upamelāpaka*, as well as the *pīlava* and the *upapīlava*, and the *śmaśāna* and the *upaśmaśāna*. (10)
These are the twelve stages;
the Lord, the master of the ten stages, is not described by these nor by others. || 11 ||
This should be understood through gesture, and all of this should be shown with the left hand. || 8 ||
By means of the garlands, he states the intended meaning: "O Samaya," and so forth;
"stay" means perform the service; "divine yoginīs, worship" means perform the service. || 9 ||
"O Blessed One," and so forth; these twelve, beginning with the *pīṭhas*, are called "grounds" (*bhūmis*) because they serve as the basis for [the realization] of these [states].
In the Vajra Tantra, Vajragarbha said: "O Blessed One! What are those sacred seats (pīṭhas) and so forth?
The Blessed One replied: "The sacred seat known as Jālandhara, and likewise Oḍḍiyāna; the sacred seat Pūrṇagiri, and likewise Kāmarūpa. (12)
Upapīṭha is declared to be Mālava, as well as Sindhunagara; the field (kṣetra) is renowned as Munmuni, and the field Kāruṇyapāṭaka; likewise Devikoṭa is a field, and Karmārapāṭaka is a field. ||13||
Kulatā is declared to be an upakṣetra, as is Arbuda; likewise, Godāvarī and Himādri should be briefly summarized as upakṣetras.

[The Chapter on the Grounds]: In sequence, they are Muditā (Joy), Vimalā (Stainless), Arciṣmatī (Radiant), Prabhākarī (Luminous), Sudurjayā (Very Difficult to Conquer), Abhimukhī (Facing Toward), Dūraṅgamā (Far-Reaching), Acalā (Immovable), Sādhumatī (Excellent Intelligence), Dharmameghā (Cloud of Dharma), Samantabhadrā (Universally Auspicious), Nirupamā (Incomparable), and Jñānavatī (Possessing Wisdom). The thirteenth ground, that of Vajradhara, consists of the realm of non-abiding nirvāṇa; therefore, it is not mentioned here.
The connection is that the Bodhisattva, the Lord, who is the master of the ten grounds, is called a Buddha.
"By which stages?
means "by these [seats] and so forth," such as the *pīṭha* and others. || 10–11 ||
"O Blessed One," and so forth;
[he went to] Pullagiri, [also known as] Pullīramalaya. || 12 ||
The city of Pāṭaliputra. || 13 ||
The *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*, Chapter Seven: Chandoha and Harikela, born from the midst of the salt ocean;
likewise Lampāka, Kāñcika, and Saurāṣṭra. (15)
Kaliṅga is the upachandoha, and the island of Kokaṇa, endowed with gold, is the upachandoha; this is stated in brief. || 16 ||
O Vajragarbha of great compassion, [he taught] Pīlava situated at the edge of the village, Pīlava of the city, Caritra, Kośala, Vindhyā, Kaumārapaurikā, and Upapīlava as its settlement.
A cemetery is a gathering of the departed; the shore of the ocean is also a cemetery; and a garden or the bank of a pond is declared to be a secondary cemetery (upaśmaśāna). || 18 ||
And I shall now describe the excellent assembly of yoginīs during the day, according to the *Hevajra* Yoginī-tantra, for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings. (19)
"In the midst of the salt ocean" is an epithet of Harikela; "endowed with gold" refers to Suvarṇadvīpa, which is situated there. (15–17)
"Reservoirs, oblong ponds, and likewise the day," and so forth. (18–19)
In the *Vajra-tantra*, in the chapter on secret signs (*chomā*), Vajragarbha said: "O Blessed One, what are those days?
The Blessed One replied: "On the fourteenth day of the fortnight of the hungry ghosts (*pretapakṣa*), and likewise on the eighth. (20)
One should eat a banner, that which has been struck by a weapon, and the seven-fold turn; having diligently generated compassion, they know that the act of killing is performed. ||21||
The fortnight of the departed spirits (pretapakṣa) is the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa);
by this much, the external [classification] has been explained. || 20 ||
Now, in order to subdue the wicked, he speaks with a single voice to explain the yoga of the disciples regarding both the external and the internal: "The banner" refers to its destruction;
one who has been slain by weapons or struck down in battles and the like is "seven-fold," meaning one who has undergone seven births.
"Compassion" (kṛpā) means having reflected upon the worldly suffering of that very [being];
"by the wise" (viduṣā) means by one who knows—this is one explanation;
the "banner" (dhvaja) is the mind with its objective support (sālambana).

Having cut down that which is struck by weapons with the weapon of wisdom— that is, rendering it devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvīkaraṇa) through the investigation of whether it possesses a single or multiple nature— the phrase "by the weapon" indicates that even the investigating mind itself is rendered devoid of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, the expression "sevenfold" shows that it is repeatedly turned over seven times and then consumed, thereby being made devoid of intrinsic nature.
To this extent, in such a place, the supreme protection of both oneself and others would have been accomplished;
even snakes and other creatures will not approach, and the samādhi of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) becomes manifest— thus [it is said] "compassion" and so forth.

"Compassion" (*kṛpā*) is an elliptical expression; it implies that one must first diligently cultivate the four divine abodes (*caturbrahmavihāra*). Regarding the statement "the wise ones know," if the slaying of the world is the realization of its non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha*), [one might ask]: why must the cultivation of the four divine abodes be performed at the outset? To this he says, "compassion," and so forth:
if the cultivation of the four divine abodes were not always present at the beginning, there would be no accomplishment in the form of a perfectly enlightened Buddha (*samyaksambuddha*).
Through the cultivation of emptiness alone, there might at some point be liberation by means of the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas and others. || 21 ||

In the subduing of the wicked, everything is accomplished through the primary ritual procedure. || 22 ||
In this regard, it should be understood as follows: "The Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, is day, and wisdom is said to be night. (23)

There is nothing that should not be done, nothing that is always unfit to be eaten, nothing that is inconceivable, and indeed nothing here that is unspeakable, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious. ||24||
Just as with oneself, so toward other beings; having reflected that "I am the self and others are the same," one whose nature is yoga should undertake eating, drinking, and other activities. || 25 ||

He concludes with the words "therefore, from that" (atastasmāt) and so forth. [The term] "corrupt" (duṣṭāḥ) refers to those who hate the teaching of the Sugata, such as the Kaulas and others; it was said for the purpose of enjoining them to the Mantra Vehicle.
"By way of affirmation," and so forth;
"In this case, it is established precisely by way of affirmation. (24–25) // 22 //
Wherever words such as "killing" and so forth are seen to be employed, there one should understand it to be as follows:
"The Blessed One, the Vajrī, is Time," and so on. || 23 ||
"Always" means at all times; therefore, furthermore, banners and so forth must be avoided in front of worldly people,
whereas in the *gaṇacakra* and other such occasions, they may be enjoyed in a secluded place—
thus, it is not inconceivable, and so on.
Thinking otherwise is "inconceivable" (acintya). || 24 ||
Just as the identification with Hevajra (*hevajrāhaṅkāra*) is to be performed in relation to oneself, so too should it be performed in relation to sentient beings.
By the conjunction "likewise in oneself," [it means]: "I am this Hevajra; I am supreme. Thus, one should regard both oneself and the other [as Hevajra]. || 25 ||
It is conceived—ka, gha; it is prescribed—ga;
that which is to be brought about—ka; that which is to be consumed—ga; always—gha.
There is nothing that is inconceivable;
there is nothing that is inexpressible.
*sattva*—ka, kha; *sattvo*—gha (in the reading of Snelagrove); *yathā sattve tathā*—ga;
he concludes with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*) etc.—ka; he concludes with "therefore"—khaga.
The wicked one says: "There is no [fault]," [according to] Kha and Ga;
by that [method], Kha.
The meaning of *niyoganārtha*— [the reading] *gha* is "from the primary," while *kha* shows [the reading] *cakrī* and so forth— *ga*.
The self is refuted— [as stated in] Kha and Ga. (Kha and Ga)
Māraṇa-dāya: - Ga, in a secluded place; - Kha, it should be eaten;
- Ga, within the essence.

In the Vajra Tantra, [the Chapter on Secret Signs]: "Indeed, as many as there are movements of the limbs and expansions of speech, so many are the mantras and mudrās for one established in the state of Śrī Heruka. (26)

The syllable *Śrī* is non-dual (10), which is gnosis (10); the syllable *He* (11) is the emptiness of causes and so forth (12); the syllable *Ru* is free from conceptual elaboration (*prapañca*) (13); the syllable *Ka* (14) is not established anywhere (15). For whichever beings (16)—whichever creatures (16)—their flesh is eaten by the wise (18), those very beings (19) come under control through the yoga of the Vajra-Kapāla (20). This is the seventh chapter on Mudrās (21). Regarding "established in the state" and "non-dual": it is the emptiness of all phenomena (22). That itself is *Śrī*, because its nature is luminosity (*prabhāsvara*); thus, it is the cause, the reason (23).

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is included; emptiness (śūnyatā) is the state of being devoid [of self-nature]. "Reasoning" (ūha) refers to discursive thought (vitarka); by that, it is "gone away from" or abandoned. "Ka" refers to that which is extinguished through non-abiding nirvāṇa (apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa). By this much, the meaning of emptiness, signlessness (animitta), wishlessness (apraṇihita), and lack of volitional construction (anabhisaṃskāra) is stated as the meaning of the term Śrīheruka. || 26-27 ||
"Beings" (jantavaḥ) are those born within the six realms of existence;

"flesh" (piśita) is their intrinsic nature (svabhāva). It is "eaten" (aśnīyate), meaning it is rendered free from appearances (nirābhāsīkriyate), by the wise—namely, by those engaged in the yoga of Hevajra.

"Those various sentient beings" refers to those various entities that come under one's control; that is, they attain mastery in each respective case through emanations of diverse forms and so forth, because of the disciplining of the entire world.
*Vajra* is Hevajra;

she who protects (*pālayati*) *kaṃ*, which is bliss (*sukha*), is Nairātmyā. The union (*yoga*) of both emptiness and compassion is *samādhi*; from that [arises the result]. (28) Thus ends the seventh chapter, the Determination of the Secret Signs and the Seats (*chomā-pīṭha-nirṇaya-paṭala*), in the *Yogaratnamālā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Hevajra* composed by the venerable Kṛṣṇācārya.

The equality of phenomena—
there is no [self]—

There is no [meaning of] signlessness, lack of volitional formation, and wishlessness— ga; [rather,] the meaning of the term *heruka* is the object of signs, volitional formations, and [wishful] activity— gha.
