The Chapter on the Chomāpīṭha — Gha:

The Eighth Chapter, titled "The Circle of Yoginīs," concerning the Assembly of Great Yoginīs. Now we shall explain the Circle of Yoginīs (Yoginīcakra). Having meditated upon the bhaga within the element of space (khadhātu), one should perform the visualization in its center:
first the circle according to the rule, and then the deities according to their arising. (1)
First, the wheel [is the earth], then water, then fire according to the rule; the great wind is the generator of the deities, arising according to its proper sequence. ||2||

"Now," and so forth: "cakra" means the mandala, the primordial abode of the Supreme; it has the same meaning as the "city of great liberation. Therein, the two-fold mandala—both the support (*ādhāra*) and the supported (*ādheya*)—must be explained here. This consists of the yoga of the *ādiyoga-maṇḍalarājāgrī* and the *karmarājāgrī-samādhi*. Since the yogas of the solitary hero (*ekavīra*) have been introduced in the Deity Chapter, [the subject here is] the Yoginī Nairātmyā; her "cakra" is the Yoginī-cakra.
"In the space-element," and so forth:
within the space-element inside the vajra-fence and canopy, one should visualize the *bhaga*, white as the autumnal moon, triangular, known as the *dharmodayā*;
one should perform the meditation upon it in the center.
In the midst of that, one should perform the meditation on the four elements which serve as the cause for the generation of the *ādhāra-cakra*.
To explain how this is done, he says: "First the wheel," and so forth; this is the brief statement (*uddeśa*). || 1 ||
The exposition beginning with "the wheel, the earth," and so forth, is as follows:
"earth" refers to the terrestrial sphere (*pṛthivī-maṇḍala*).

Prior to this is water, the watery sphere (*vāruṇa-maṇḍala*); prior to this, according to the proper order, is fire, the fiery sphere (*hutāśana-maṇḍala*); and prior to that, for the practitioner, is the sphere of the deities, namely the airy sphere (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), which exists in its very form as it arises. Thus, here first, in the center of the *dharmodaya*, is the airy sphere, transformed from the syllable *yaṃ*, resembling a bow, blue in color, and marked at its two tips by fluttering banners.
Above that, from the syllable *raṃ*, arises a triangle marked with the letter *ra* at its corners;
in the *Vajratantre*, it is taught that the wheel arising from the *dharmodayā* is indeed free from affliction and has two enclosures:
one by means of the filaments and the other by the triangle. || 3 ||
In the center of that, one should contemplate the corpse consisting of fifteen seats; above that shall be the moon, and above the moon, the seed-syllable.

[The Melāpakapaṭala: One should visualize the fire-maṇḍala; above that, the water-maṇḍala arising from *vaṃ*, which is white, circular, and marked with a jar; and above that, the earth-maṇḍala arising from *laṃ*, which is yellow, square, and marked with vajras at its corners. || 2 ||

"Dharma" and so forth refers to the *dharmodaya*; that itself is the triangular mudrā. "Arising therein" means arising within that [triangle] through the transformation of the four mandalas beginning with wind.
As it has been said: "The wheel is the foundational mandala, endowed with qualities such as being square and so forth;
and thus he will say: 'This wheel described by you is adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, four-cornered, with four gates, and embellished with vajra-lines.'"
"Two-fold" means two layers:
one by means of the pericarp—that is, the central eight-petaled lotus—and the other by means of the triangle, which encompasses the *dharmodayā* and is square. || 3 ||

Within that, in the middle of the two-chambered gabled palace (*kūṭāgāra*), are the seats of the fifteen Yoginīs; one should contemplate a corpse-seat (*śavāsana*) at each of their respective locations.
Within the heart of that central corpse-seat is the moon, which is the transformation of the letter *ā* (the first vowel), and upon that is the seed-syllable, namely the first vowel [A]. || 4 ||

In the Vajra Tantra, the wise one should meditate on the fivefold forms as they have been described: the union of *āli* and *kāli*, and for the mass of Vajrasattva arising from the syllables, the two syllables *HŪṂ* and *PHAṬ*. [This is the section on the assembly, the seat. If these two are not desired, one should visualize the Lord of the Maṇḍala arisen from the image of the sentient being. || 8–9 ||
As before, [he is characterized] by the face, symbols, and so forth, with the luster of a moonstone gem. ||9||
Thus, all are perfected by way of the nature of wisdom and skillful means. || 10 ||
The wise and learned one [should visualize] the five forms, beginning with the mirror;
the union of *āli* and *kāli* is the pair of lunar and solar mandalas.
"Viṣṭara" means a seat;
"vajra" is the emblem; "sattva" is the seed-syllable.
The meaning is that it is the seat of that Vajrasattva. || 8 ||

Regarding the phrase "born from the syllable" (*akṣarodbhava*) and so forth: "syllable" (*akṣara*) refers to the primordial syllable; "born from that" refers to the *piṇḍa* (the condensed form) of the Lord of the Maṇḍala. Regarding "HŪṂ" and so forth: this refers to the syllables HŪṂ and PHAṬ. From the word "and" (*ca*), [one understands] the syllable ĀḤ, the melting of the body of Prajñā and Upāya as the *praṇava*, and so on, for the purpose of generating the Lord in the Nairātmyā-maṇḍala. If there is no generation due to the occurrence of melting, from what then does it arise? To this he says: "the image of the sentient being" (*sattvabimba*) and so forth.
"Sattva" is the seed-syllable, "viśva" is the symbol;
from these two arises the Lord of the Mandala, meaning Nairātmyā, who is the leader of the mandala. || 9 ||
"As before" means as Vajraśṛṅkhalā was described in the Devatāpaṭala: "in the right and left hands, a knife and a skull-cup," and so forth,
by way of faces, symbols, and the rest.
The face is the mouth;
the marks are the curved knife, skull-cup, and khaṭvāṅga staff.
[Eighth: According to the *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*, because of the piercing of the moon and sun, they are the means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
And from this arise Gaurī and the others, distinguished by their various colors. ||11||
First, the knower of yoga should always meditate upon the five yoginīs residing within the inner enclosure as being the very nature of the five aggregates.
Indrāṇī is in the east, Gaurī in the south, Vāriyoginī in the west, Vajraḍākinī in the north, and Nairātmyayoginī in the center. || 13 ||
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), garments and ornaments are included.
"Possessing the luster of a moonstone" (*candrakāntimaṇiprabham*) means that its radiance is like that of a moonstone;
the meaning is [the presence of] moon-thrones and moonlight-halos.
"In this manner" means like the leader of the mandala;
"everything" refers to Vajragaurī and the others.
How are they perfected?
By way of the nature of wisdom and skillful means. (10)

"Gaurī and the others" means that Gaurī and the rest become the deities of the mandala through the transformation of the moon, sun, symbols, and seed-syllables [originating] from the seed-syllable situated upon the symbol on the moon at the heart of the Lord of the Mandala.
What is the seed-syllable? Is it the same as theirs? No; he says "color," and so forth—"color" refers to the seed-syllable, and its "differentiation" (bheda) [is what follows].
The meaning is that each seed-syllable is distinct;
as he will state in the *Sarvatantramudraṇapiṇḍārthapaṭala*: "The first [syllable] of Āli is Nairātmyā, the second of Vajrāli, and so forth. || 11 ||
Now he describes the location of the Yoginīs, beginning with "adhyātma" and so forth:
"adhyātma" means within the inner circle;
one should meditate [there] through the purification of the five aggregates (*skandhas*). || 12 ||
Indra is in the eastern direction. || 13 ||

The Chapter on the Assembly: Furthermore, in the outer enclosure are Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, Ghasmarī, Pukkasī, Śavarī, Caṇḍālī, and the eighth is considered to be Ḍombinī. They are known as Adhovatī, Ūrdhvavatī, Khecarī, and Bhūcarī. By their very nature of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, all these goddesses are black in color and extremely fierce.
In the case of these two [mantras], both deities are present. ||15||
Adorned with the five mudrās, they have one face and red eyes, holding a flaying knife and a skull-cup in their hands. || 16 ||
The wheel, the earring, the necklace, the bracelet, and the girdle—these five are the pure mudrās through the purity of the five Buddhas. || 17 ||
In the outer enclosure, Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, and Ghasmarī are located at the gates in the east and other directions,
and in the corners starting from the northeast.
Pukkasī, Śavarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī. || 14 ||

Because she protects—that is, guards—the lower part, she is the "lower-protecting" (adhovatī) Bhūcarī; likewise, she becomes the "upper-protecting" (ūrdhvavatī) Khecarī, and so forth, through the purification of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. || 15 ||
"By means of the purity of the five Buddhas" means by way of the essential nature of the five Buddhas; "seals" (mudrā) refers to those who are sealers (mudrakāḥ). || 17 ||

[The Eighth: The *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā* states that all [the goddesses] are described as being like Nairātmyayoginī: they hold a single skull-cup in their hands, and in their right hands, they carry flaying knives. || 18 ||

Holding a khaṭvāṅga staff in her left hand, with her waist covered by a tiger skin, mounted upon a corpse, blazing with light, possessing two arms, and having tawny hair—[these are the goddesses]. (19)
Likewise, the small knife stands ready to cut the six defects such as pride, while the lotus vessel holds the head of the conceptualization of existence and non-existence. (20)
And the blood of the four Māras is drunk for the sake of accomplishment; it is conceived through the means of a corpse by way of the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) and emptiness. || 21 ||
By means of this, one should meditate upon the wheel and swiftly attain accomplishment; first, one should meditate on the black [form], and secondly, indeed the red.
"Of such a kind" means "in that manner.
"Blazing and radiant" means blazing with their bodies and radiant in their minds. (18–19)
Likewise, by the words "pride and so forth," he describes the essential nature of the agent and the other factors. || 20 ||
"By this" means one should meditate in this manner;
"light" means quickly. || 22 ||

There is no [attainment] for Māras by means of a khaṭvāṅga or a sword; rather, one should meditate on the wheel through every possible means. First, one should visualize it as black; second, one should visualize it as red, blazing and radiant with the light of pride, and so forth. This reading, contained within the floral ornament, is not found in the Cambridge manuscript. In the *Vajra-tantra*, third, one should visualize it as yellow; fourth, likewise as green; fifth, as blue-colored; and sixth, as having a white body. (23)
The yogi should meditate on the six-limbed yoga, ending with the stage of cessation; likewise, he should practice both the sequential generation stage and the completion stage. (24)
Relying upon the two stages, the Vajra-holder has taught the Dharma; the section on generation has been explained, and now I shall speak of the perfected stage. (25)
"In the element of space" refers to the lotuses; "wisdom" is known as the *bhaga*; "meditation" is the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), and its bliss is called the "wheel. || 26 ||

[The Melāpaka Chapter: Now, for the sake of empowering the mind, he teaches the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga): "By the six colors" is for the purpose of indicating the equality with the six universal monarchs; and again, "afterwards" means that which ends with the cessation (viramānta), namely, mere innate bliss (sahajānanda). || 24 ||

Having now explained the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), he speaks in order to introduce the second, the stage of completion (*utpannakrama*), beginning with the words "the sequence" (*krama*) and so forth. What is the sequence? It is a method (*prakāra*). What is its sequence?

"Arising" (*utpatti*) is the accomplishment of the form of the deity through the transformation of the signs of the moon, seed-syllables (*bīja*), and so forth within meditative absorption (*samādhi*). The "arising stage" (*utpattikrama*) is that meditative absorption in which this [arising] exists. "The arisen" (*utpanna*) refers to the very nature of reality; that yoga in which this very [nature] is resolved upon as the form of ultimate reality and is cultivated is the "arisen stage" (*utpannakrama*). Relying upon these two stages, the teaching of the Dharma by the Vajra-holders—the Buddhas—is the teaching of meditative absorption. By means of this verse beginning with "In the element of space" (*khadhātāv*), the portion concerning arising—that is, the side of the arising stage (*utpattikramapakṣa*)—is explained. By implication, it is stated that the "arisen stage" (*utpannakrama*) is being discussed. || 25 ||

He says of that [practice] with the words beginning "in the space-element" (*khadhātu*) and so forth: "In the lotuses" means in the lotus of wisdom (*prajñā*); "having meditated on the knowledge-vajra" means having caused [it] to enter. One should perform the meditation upon these three—the first being the two innate [joys]—in the middle of these two. The third [lotus] is yellow, the fourth green, the fifth blue-colored, and the sixth is the bodily [lotus]. Meditating on the six limbs, the yogi likewise [meditates] up to the Hero (*vīra*). Thus is the sequence of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*). Relying upon these two stages, the teaching of the Vajra-holders has been declared; from this point onward, there is no further remaining portion of the knowledge regarding the generation part.

Even in the meditation on "bhaga," for the sake of performing the function [of union], this reading follows the manuscript *kha*; he says "to introduce": this reading follows the manuscript *gha*, which has arisen as "utpanna"; one is resolved upon it as the nature of reality—this reading within the flower-marked brackets is not found in the Cambridge manuscript; [End of] the Eighth [Chapter]. *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*: Bodhicitta is to be personally realized according to the rule; the deity arises as semen according to its emergence; therefore, the innate (*sahaja*) is of two kinds. || 27 ||

Wisdom (prajñā) is indeed the woman, while skillful means (upāya) is traditionally held to be the man; subsequently, these two are each twofold, distinguished by their nature as the manifest (vivṛti) and the concealed (saṃvṛti). || 28 ||
For in the male there is indeed a twofold nature: semen and his pleasure; and just as it is with the male, so it is with wisdom—semen and its pleasure. ||29||

Samāpatti is the practice of meditative concentration (*samāhita-pratipatti*), which is "setting in motion. The bliss produced by that cultivation is called the "wheel" (*cakra*); it is designated by the word *cakra* for the yoginīs because they are gathered together through that very great bliss (*mahāsukha*). || 26 ||

He explains what that bliss is like: "according to its own nature" (*yathānyāyam*) means it is self-cognized (*svasaṃvedyam*), not dependent on another, and to be realized within oneself; this is the meaning of "intrinsic nature. That very self-cognized state is *bodhi* (awakening); the mind whose intrinsic nature is awakening is *bodhicitta*. The word "but" (*tu*) is used for conjunction. Because she herself dwells as the deity within the body, [it is said] "according to its arising" (*yathodayam*), meaning according to the actual way it arises. It is independent of subject and object, white like the moon, and liquid in form. Since it is thus, the innate (*sahaja*) is twofold: innate bliss is of two kinds. (27)

If this [bliss] is innate (*sahaja*), then what will become of woman and man? To this he says: "Woman," and so forth. The word "of these two" (*anayoḥ*) is in the locative case. How is there a twofold nature of bliss? He says: "Manifestation" (*vivṛti*), and so forth. Manifestation is the form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*); concealment (*saṃvṛti*) is according to its arising, because it is concealed by even a slight trace of form. For this very reason—because of that twofold nature of those two—there is a division of the four; that is, a division of the four together with their general classification. [Objection: But surely the four joys (*ānanda*) are recited in one way, whereas here they are otherwise; how is there no contradiction? [Response: He says: "Innate," and so forth. The four, beginning with joy (*ānanda*) and supreme joy (*paramānanda*), arise in sequence; this is the position of the "arising stage" (*utpannakrama*). That very twofold nature of the innate is to be known by oneself according to its own arrangement, self-cognized (*svasaṃvedya*). The deities are the semen (*śukra*); the twofold nature is remembered as the innate woman and the means-man (*upāya-puruṣa*). As for manifestation, that twofold nature does not exist even in the white [semen] within the Wisdom Consort (*prajñā*); the yoginī’s semen is like a jasmine flower (*kundasaṃkāśa*). Thus he says "woman. This reading, which is within the "flower-sign" (*puṣpacihna*), is not found in the Cambridge manuscript. In this very *Hevajratantra*, there is indeed a division of the four joys; since the innate is fourfold from the perspective of the arising stage: *sahajaṃ caturvidhaṃ yasmād utpannakramapakṣataḥ* || 30 || (30) Because the innate is fourfold from the perspective of the arising stage.

[The Melāpakapaṭala: "It is said to be fourfold"—this is one explanation. Regarding the phrase "in the space-element" (*khadhātāv*) and so forth: within the lotuses, there is the gnosis (*jñāna*) of the four [consorts] beginning with Locanā; it is called "the vulva" (*bhaga*) because it shatters the Māras such as the afflictions (*kleśa*). "Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) refers to the simultaneous descent through the union of the lotus and the vajra with an external consort (*mudrā*); that bliss is "bliss of attainment" (*samāpattisukha*), and it is called a "wheel" (*cakra*). Thus, the meaning is that the fourth is spoken of among the wheels. "According to the rule" (*yathānyāyam*) means it is spoken of in sequence. "To be personally experienced" (*svasaṃvedyam*) means the bliss found in the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), characterized by the master-initiation (*ācāryābhiṣeka*), which is to be personally experienced in the first wheel according to the guru’s instruction; this is designated as "to be personally experienced. That which arises in the dharma-seal (*dharmamudrā*) is the "awakening-mind" (*bodhicitta*); the meaning is that its bliss is the awakening-mind. That which is perceived in the commitment-seal (*samayamudrā*) is the bliss of the deity. In the great seal (*mahāmudrā*), the untainted bliss (*anāsravasukha*) arises; that wheel, characterized by arising in due order, is the "semen" (*śukra*). As for the syllable *śu*: it shatters (*krakacavat*) the worldly suffering of grief (*śoka*) like a saw, hence it is "semen. Regarding the "twofold nature": therein, due to the experience of the four seals, there is a twofold bliss. One is the innate (*sahaja*) having the form of great bliss, and the second is the form of semen. Thus, the twofold nature of the innate is stated through the division of the seals, such as the action-seal and the dharma-seal. Is this produced only in a single person, or in both woman and man?
To that end, he says: "A woman," and so forth.
"Precisely for this reason" means that it is the differentiation of the four joys (*ānanda*) and the four seals (*mudrā*).
In this *Yoginītantra*, just as with women, so too men are to be favored through initiation (*seka*) and other means, according to the distinctions of weak, middling, and intense [capacities].

Let there be, indeed, a distinction among the four mudrās; however, he asks: "From what [source] is the distinction among the four joys? He replies with the words beginning "sahaja" (the innate), meaning that it is by way of the characteristic of the arising of bliss in the *utpannakrama* (the stage of completion).
This is the second explanation.
All of this is to be understood through the instruction of the Guru.
Therefore—ka. kha. ga. gha. mu.va.; hyānanda—ka;
catṛṇām—ka, catasṛṇām—ga.
When there is no outflow—emptiness; when there is nothing—emptiness; bliss—emptiness.
Kha reads *ṣāṭayāti*, which has been noted here; however,
since this portion is found in the manuscript obtained from Kāṭhmāṇḍu, we have presented the Sanskrit reading here according to that source— Editor.
It begins again, in two ways:

*mahāsukhākāram ekaḥ* (one [form] having the aspect of great bliss) — Ga; *mahāsukhākārātmakam* (consisting of the aspect of great bliss) — Ka, Gha, Bho; *karmamudrādibhedena* (by means of the divisions beginning with the action-seal) — Gha.
The innate is said to be twofold—either "ka.
gha" or "āhośvit-ka. gha," or else "ata-kha."

The meaning is that the classification of the mudrās has been made—[the reading] "classification" (prabhedanam) is found in manuscripts kha and gha; [the reading] "of men" (puruṣaḥ) is in kha, while "even of men" (puruṣāṇām api) is in ka and gha.
Thus: kha, ata-kha. Puruṣo 'pi—kha; puruṣāṇām api—ka, gha.
Regarding the term "of the characteristic" (lakṣaṇasya)—[variant readings: ka.
gha]—in the *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*, chapter eight:
"The Hero is the first bliss; the Yoginī is supreme bliss."
He is the omniscient one, the means for attaining all that bliss which consists of the joy of union.
Through *ānanda* there is some pleasure; *paramānanda* is greater than that.
Through *virama*, detachment (*virāga*) occurs; and from what remains, *sahajānanda* arises.
The first is practiced out of a desire for touch; the second, out of a longing for pleasure;
the third, because of the destruction of passion; by that, the fourth is cultivated.
Now he states the threefold nature in its entirety, beginning with "Bliss" (*ānanda*) and so forth.
"Hero" (*vīra*) refers to the practitioner (*sādhaka*), because of his having initiated heroic effort (*vīrya*).
"Yoginī," however, refers to supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), because without her there is no arising of bliss.
The bliss of union (*suratānanda*) is the characteristic of the co-emergent (*sahaja*); the meaning is that all three are indeed one and the same.
He explains this very point: the means is the instruction on the *mudrās*, and the bliss produced by the cultivation of that is "that bliss," which is the Omniscient Vajradhara.
In the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), four joys (*ānandas*) are observed for the purpose of indicating the co-emergent.
In the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*), however, only the innate (*sahaja*) [nature] is to be cultivated.
Regarding this point, he states three arguments in three verses beginning with "By bliss" (*ānandena*).

As for the phrase "but innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) from the remainder," it follows by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*): since these three [other types of bliss] have the nature of cyclic existence (*bhava*) and nirvāṇa and are delusive, they lead to *saṃsāra*.
For that reason, the innate bliss is that which brings about the goal to be accomplished—the Great Bliss characterized as the *dharmakāya*.
And he alone is to be meditated upon.
Why, then, do these three not bring about liberation? He says: "The first," and so forth.
"Sparśa" refers to the lotus and the vajra; the second is due to the desire for greater pleasure than that;
and the third is the *viramānanda* (bliss of cessation), because it is the destruction of passion (*rāga*), that is, because it is of the nature of detachment (*vairāgya*).
The fourth is called the innate (sahaja); it is "cultivated" (bhāvyate) by means of that, hence it is called "cultivation" (bhāva).
Ānanda—ga. gha;
Paramānanda—ka. mu. va;
Suratananda—ka. ga; Sahajānanda—gha.
"Samastam vai" — [found in] Ka, Ga, Gha, Mu, Va; "cetad" — Cha; "cestat" — Ja; "ca tat" — Jha.
"Tatsukhopāya" — Ka, Ga, Gha, Cha, Ja, Jha.
"Sarvataḥ" — Ka; "sarvavidit" — Gha; "sarvavitā" — Cha.
This verse does not exist in manuscript kha;
"Ānanda" in manuscript ga; "paramānandaṃ tu cādhikam" in manuscripts ka and gha; "paramānandādhikaṃ" in manuscript gha.

*Viramānanda*: ka. kha. cha. ja. jha; *viramānande*: ga. gha. mu. va; *virāmena*: ṭa. *Sahajānandaṃ tu*: ka. kha. ga. gha; *sahajānandastu*: mu. va. *Kāṅkṣa*: ka; *kāṅkṣī ca*: kha; *kāṅkṣi*: ga. ja; *sparśanākāṅkṣa*: gha; *sparśakarānta*: jha.
The second is—Gha;
by one's own desire—Gha;
the third is—Gha.
The state of destroying passion—ka;
because of having initiated vigor—kha;
the Yoginī—kha.
nāsti—ka. gha; paramārthe—bho;
śeṣa—ka. gha.
By elimination—gha;
indeed only one—kha;
by the desire for more than that—ka, gha.
"Because of the destruction of passion, that [is so]"—ka. gha;
"the fourth"—kha; "to be cultivated"—ka. gha.
In the Vajra-tantra, existence is said to be supreme bliss, and nirvana is from the absence of passion;
but the innate is free from these, being merely the intermediate bliss.
There is neither passion nor dispassion, and no middle state is perceived; herein there is neither wisdom nor means, due to the realization of perfect reality.
The innate (*sahaja*) is not described by another, nor is it found in anything else; it is known by oneself through merit and by serving the lineage of gurus.

"Supreme bliss" (*paramānanda*) and so forth refers to *bhava*, characterized by cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); "from detachment" (*virāgataḥ*) refers to *viramānanda*, which is said to be *nirvāṇa*, because of the longing for the innate (*sahaja*).

"Madhyama" refers to that which is devoid of these aforementioned [states]: namely, mere initial bliss (*prathamānanda*) and mere common pleasure (*sukhasādhāraṇa*). It is the *sahaja* (innate), whose nature is unstained by the defilement of faults regarding both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; therefore, one should meditate upon that alone and nothing else—this is the meaning.

If innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) is the means for attaining the state of the Great Vajradhara who is to be realized, then since it is experienced within the lotus of wisdom (*prajñāravinda*) itself, one would have already accomplished what was to be done; for what purpose, then, should it be cultivated? To this he says, "Not by another," and so forth.

The meaning is that it cannot be attained through anyone else—such as a Guru or a Vajradhara—because even when there is contact with the lotus of wisdom within any of the four wheels (*cakras*), that which is to be personally realized (*pratyātmavedya*) transcends the domain of verbal conceptualization.
If that is so, how then can there be its teaching or its hearing?

This is by way of conventional designation (*udbhāvanā-saṃvṛti*), but not in its own intrinsic nature (*svena rūpeṇa*). Just as one hears of the experiences of pleasure and pain of gods and hell-beings, how then is that [the self] known? To this he says: "By oneself," and so forth.

It is perceived by the self alone through a specific cultivation (*bhāvanā-viśeṣa*); thus, cultivation is not in vain. Therefore, because it is impossible to realize it directly without the perfection of cultivation.
O Supreme Bliss!
What is saṃsāra?
What is nirvāṇa? Kha.
There is no [such thing as] "non-existence"—kha;
"delighting in the innate" (sahajābhirviva)—kha; "the innate is devoid of friends"—gha;
"there is no dispassion, nor is the middle state of dispassion perceived"—kha, cha, jha; this portion of the verse does not exist—ja.
Due to the realization of the perfection of skillful means (upāya-kha-sampannatva-bodhataḥ), [and] due to the realization of the perfection [of wisdom] (sampannatvāvabodhataḥ).
I believe this verse does not exist in the *Ka*, *Ga*, or *Gha* manuscripts, nor is it found in the *Muktāvalī* or the *Yogaratnamālā*, as there is no commentary on it.

[Chapter] Eight: *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*. Whether they be inferior, middling, or superior, whatever other [teachings] there may be, all these should be regarded as equal by those who cultivate reality (*tattva*). (37)
The inferior is the subtle object, while the superior is said to be the state of being; the middle is devoid of both, and "others" refers to the six sense organs. (38)
"The path which I have taught for the extraction of the thorn of craving—such is the duty; the Tathāgatas are the proclaimers thereof.
Thus, indeed, this is the method regarding the initial cultivation of the maṇḍala-cakra and so forth;
however, innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) is perceived as a direct experience.
For instruction from another is not appropriate regarding an object that is directly perceived;

therefore he says, "from merit," thinking as follows: it is not merely the worldly innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) that is to be accomplished, because it is already established, and because it is defiled by outflows (*sāsrava*) for those in cyclic existence. Rather, it is the innate *dharmakāya*, which is to be personally realized (*pratyātmavedya*) only by the Tathāgatas, that is to be accomplished here.

Since there is no other alternative state, he gains conviction in this very worldly innate bliss (*laukika-sahajānanda*) according to the instruction; through the maturation of cultivation, it is known by oneself and not previously [so known].
Therefore, hearing, reflection, and cultivation are not in vain here—this is the means, the path. Its "service" is correct cultivation; its "many stages" means many varieties.
A *parvan* obtained from a guru is a "guru-parvan," which is that which is bestowed by the guru according to the prescribed rule upon a worthy disciple; the meaning is "instruction. || 36 ||
How is innate cultivation (*sahajabhāvanā*) to be performed? Is it to be done in only one part, or rather pervading the entire universe? To this he says: "The inferior," and so forth.
This is the brief statement (*uddeśa*); its explanation (*vyākhyāna*) follows: the subtle entities are the self's mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*), and the state of the self is the body.
"By two" refers to the limbs of one's own body and the six sense organs, such as the eyes and so forth, which reside within the body. (37–38)

In the Vajra Tantra, [the Melāpaka Chapter]: "Whatever things there are, whether stable or moving—all these are indeed myself; they possess equal activity through meditations on reality that are of a single flavor. (39)
"Equal" (sama) is said to mean "even" or "identical"; its wheel is known as "flavor" (rasa).
Thus, by this meaning, it is called "of equal flavor" (samarasa), which signifies a state of oneness. || 40 ||
For this entire world originates from me; all this originates from me and is pervaded by me. This threefold world is seen as nothing other than myself. ||41||
Thinking thus, the yogi who is well-composed in practice attains perfection; of this there is no doubt, even if he is a man of little merit. || 42 ||
"Stable and moving" refers to external things, both sentient and insentient.

"Not indeed 'I'" means that it is not only I who am of the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), the Vajradhara; rather, all these [things] share the same activity and are of an undifferentiated nature.
To the question "How so?", he says: "By the cultivation of reality" (*tattvabhāvanaiḥ*); the explanation of this is "by those of equal flavor" (*samarasaiḥ*). (39)
The explanation of this [verse] begins with "equal" (*sama*) and so forth; the meaning is "similar. Regarding the word "of that" (*tasya*), it refers to the inferior, middling, and so on.
"Taste" (*rasa*), "essence" (*sāra*), and "state" (*bhāva*) are synonyms.
What is this taste?

The *cakra* (wheel) has the characteristic of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), meaning it is the innate (*sahaja*). He states the collective meaning [of the term]: "the state of being of one nature in equal flavor" (*samarasa*) and so forth. || 40 ||
Furthermore, how should one cultivate that state of equal flavor?
"Mad" and so forth;
having thought thus, meaning having determined it to be so.
"Thoroughly concentrated" means in all states. || 41-42 ||
[Chapter] Eight: *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*. Whether eating, drinking, bathing, awake, or even asleep, one should contemplate [this] constantly; then the seeker of Mahāmudrā attains it. (43)

For the entire world is meditated upon by the mind; that which is not meditated upon is the thorough knowledge of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-parijñāna*), which is indeed no meditation at all. Whether things stable or moving—be they supreme entities or mere grass, shrubs, and creepers—they are meditated upon as the reality (*tattva*) which is the very nature of the self (*ātman*). (45)
For them, there is no other supreme [state] than that great bliss which is self-cognized;
for accomplishment is self-cognized, and indeed, meditative cultivation is self-cognized.
To clarify that very point, he says "eating, drinking," and so forth;

"continuously" means flowing spontaneously; "the Great Seal," and so forth, refers to the meaning of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). By this, the yoga of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-yoga*) is stated. || 43 ||
Now, regarding this point, he speaks of the stabilization of the mind, beginning with "For they are meditated upon," and so forth.

"The entire world" refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) and the world of the environment (*bhājanaloka*). Why are all of them meditated upon? He says: "By the mind," that is, by conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*).

If they are not conceptualized, then they are not cultivated; thus he says: "The thorough knowledge of all phenomena" means that there is no cultivation at all, because of their innate nature. || 44 ||
Regarding the verse beginning with "sthiracala" and so forth:
all things are indeed the supreme reality (parama-tattva) and are to be meditated upon as having that nature of reality; what, then, is that supreme reality?
"Self," and so forth, refers to the essential nature of the self, which is one's own mind characterized by the coemergent (*sahaja*). || 45 ||
Of these, "one" refers to the reality characterized as the innate (*sahaja*);
what, then, is that one? It is to be personally realized (*svasaṃvedya*).

Now, one might object: "Is not the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) the true nature of all phenomena? There is no reality beyond this. To this he says: [It is] self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*). [The variants read: *svayaṃ vedyaṃ* (ga), *vedya* (cha), *vedye* (ja). 16–16. Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*) (ga). 17. From that which is self-cognizable (*svayaṃ vedyāt*) (ga, gha); from that which is self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedyād*) (ṭa, Pañjikā-yogaratnamālā). 18. Existence (*bhavaṃ*) (ka); existence (*bhava*) (ga); becoming (*bhavo*) (gha). 19. Accomplishment (*siddhi*) (ka, ga). 20. Self-cognizable (*saṃvedya*) (ka, gha); self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedyaṃ*) (kha, Pañjikā-yogaratnamālā); self-cognizable (*svayaṃ vedya*) (ga). 21. Meditations (*bhāvanāḥ*) (gha). 22. Supreme indeed (*parameva*) (ka). 23. The nature of the self (*ātmabhāva*). 24. Carried by the essence of flavor (*surasavāhitaṃ*) (gha); "by itself" means it exists by its own innate nature (*nijasvabhāvena*) (Bhoṭa). 25. Thus it is said, etc. (Bhoṭa). 25. Having form (*sarūpaṃ*) (ka). In the *Vajra-tantra*: "The action consisting of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedyamayaṃ karma*) arises from the subduing [of obstacles]. Itself the destroyer, itself the doer, itself the king, itself the lord. —[Melāpakapaṭala]—
Passion, hatred, envy, delusion, and likewise pride— all these are not worth even a sixteenth part of that beautiful state.
The wisdom arising from the source of phenomena (dharmodaya) is equal to space and endowed with its means;
for within it, the three worlds are born by virtue of the nature of wisdom and means. 49.

Regarding the phrase "from that which is to be experienced": the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā arises from the very mind consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Regarding the phrase "to be self-experienced": the mind characterized by great bliss is itself the meditation in the context of the *utpannakrama* (completion stage). || 46 ||

Regarding the phrase "consisting of self-awareness" (*svasaṃvedyamaya*): whatever is perceived—the manifold diversity of sentient beings, such as the stationary and the moving, which is produced by the ripening of their karma—that itself is karma.
If karma arises here from self-awareness, how then is the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā attained?
To address this, he says: "because of awakening" (*bodhanāt*).

Awakening (*bodha*) is the act of perceiving in the form of subject and object; from that, action (*karman*) arises, and not because the universe possesses a single innate flavor (*sahajaikarasabhāva*).

For this very reason, since action consists of the innate, one is oneself the destroyer and oneself the agent. Because there is no other agent distinct from that [awakening], one is oneself the agent of well-done and ill-done deeds.
One is a king (*rāja*) because one shines by oneself.
He is the Lord (prabhu) because he himself has the power to bring about the destruction of all afflictions. || 47 ||
"Passion," and so forth.

Passion and the like do not equal, nor do they attain, even a sixteenth part of that state—the state of self-awareness—within the practice of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), for the purpose of bringing about illumination. 48.
Now he describes the nature of that which is self-cognized, beginning with "arising from the source of phenomena" (*dharmodayodbhava*) and so forth.
"Phenomena" (*dharma*) refers to the noble qualities (*āryadharma*); that in which their arising occurs is the "source of phenomena" (*dharmodaya*), which is the *dharmadhātu*.
Here, it is the lotus of the consort who is its seal (*mudrā*).
Consisting of that which is self-known;

[Eighth: In the *Hevajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*, it is said: "The Blessed One is of the nature of semen (*śukra*); that bliss is known as the *kāminī*."
This is the separation from the one and the many; it is the supreme bliss arising from the moment. ||50||
This knowledge is to be personally realized and its sphere transcends the path of speech;
for this is the sequence of empowerment, consisting of the very essence of the knowledge of the Omniscient One. 51.
Dharmodaya.
Thus, because its arising occurs therein through the power of resolute conviction (adhimokṣa), it is the "knowledge arisen from the source of phenomena" (dharmodayodbhava).
Of what kind is it?
"Equal to space" means having the nature of the sky; "means" refers to the path.

That [path] is of many kinds, as has been stated and will be stated [further]. Even by means of many methods, in the context of the *niṣpannakrama* (completion stage), only the innate (*sahaja*) alone is to be cultivated. To the question, "How is the state of the Great Vajradhara attained through that? he says: "In the three worlds," and so forth.

The secrets of body, speech, and mind of the Buddhas residing in the ten directions and the three times are each infinite; these three worlds constitute their aggregate, which is Trailokyamahāvajradhara. He is born therein. One should meditate on the gnosis born from that.
In what form?
In the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). Wisdom is sublime knowledge, which is the *dharmakāya*.

The means for accomplishing the welfare of the world consists of the two bodies—the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*)—which are its natural outflow (*niṣyanda*). This means that their very nature has arisen from that [ultimate reality]. || 49 ||
He explains how they are born by their own nature with the words beginning "śukra" (semen) and so forth.
"The Blessed One" refers to the means (*upāya*), which is said to encompass the two bodies.
"That bliss" refers to that bliss which is described as knowledge equal to space; the meaning is that this is the consort (*prajñā*) who possesses desire.
"Single or multiple," and so forth.

"This" refers to the aspect of the means (*upāyabhāga*), which has the form of semen (*śukra*); because it is devoid of a nature that is either single or multiple, it is "without intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*), meaning it is empty of analytical investigation.
For this reason, it is not to be cultivated, because it is impossible to attain awakening swiftly through such falsity.
Regarding the term "moment" (*kṣaṇa*):

the single *rati* (delight) is the innate knowledge of great bliss (*sahaja-mahāsukha-jñāna*), which is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*). The meaning is that this alone is the supreme (*parā*) and most excellent (*śreṣṭhā*) state to be cultivated. The underlying intention is that, therein, the conceptualization of unity or multiplicity does not exist.
If there is no room for investigation in that case. (50)
How is that known? He says: "It is self-cognizable," and so forth.
It is not described by another; it is to be realized within oneself (*pratyātmavedya*).

Regarding the term "the path of speech" (*vākpatha*): the path (*panthā*) of speech (*vācaḥ*), that is, its means of comprehension, is the "path of speech"; its range is transcended (*atītagocara*). [Variant reading: *tatkāmīni* (kha, ga)].
2. *ekānekāviyogā* — ka; *viyogau* — ga. 3. *vaidyam idaṃ* — ka, kha, gha; *svayaṃ vedyam idaṃ*. 4. *vākpathātīta* — kha, ga.

The sphere of activity—[kha]—in the *Vajra Tantra*, the chapter on the assembly (*melāpakapaṭala*): "Earth, water, wind, fire, and space itself—for an instant, none of these can obstruct the awareness that perceives both self and other. (52)
In an instant, one becomes a single embodiment of the heavens, the mortal world, and the nether regions;
by means of the conceptualization of self and other parts, one can never be obstructed. (53)

Through all the established doctrines of the Vedas, such as the performance of ritual actions and so forth, there shall be no perfection; rather, through purification alone, one may attain [liberation] in another birth.
The meaning is that it transcends all objects.
Regarding the phrase "the sequence of the substratum" and so forth:
because it subsumes the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, it is identical with them. (51)
With these two verses beginning with "The earth," he describes the fruit of the meditation on the Innate (*sahaja*). How is it that one is not obstructed by the earth and other elements?

When the practitioner, desiring this, emerges from and sinks into the earth; passes through walls and mountains without obstruction, coming and going; and is not afflicted by poisons, weapons, and the like; sleeps above and below water; sits, stands, or walks about; and is not afflicted by wind, rain, and so forth. This should be applied similarly to other cases as well.
"Perceiving the cognition of one's own and others' awareness" means that one knows the minds of oneself and others—past, future, and present. || 52 ||
"Of heaven and mortals," and so forth.
"Single form" means having a single nature. "One's own and others'" has already been explained. || 53 ||
In order to demonstrate the superiority of the *Hevajra Tantra* over other scriptures (*āgama*), it says "all" and so forth.
The Vedas—characterized as the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, *Sāma*, and *Atharva*; the *siddhāntas* composed by non-Buddhist outsiders; the *purāṇas* and so on;

and the *sūtrāntas* of the *Śrāvaka-piṭaka*—constitute "attainment" (*siddhi*) because they bring about the end of rebirth. Based on these, there are the "expansions of activity," such as the *Kriyā-tantras* and others; however, through these, the attainment characterized as described above would not occur.
What occurs in the Pāramitā-naya?

He says: it does not occur—earth and water (pṛthivī āpa), earth and water (pṛthivi āpa), earth and water (pṛthivī āpaśca), and wind (vāyu). (kha, gha, ka). Earth and water (pṛthivī āpa) [in manuscript kha], earth and water (pṛthivī āpa) [in manuscript ga], and wind (vāyu) [in manuscript kha].

[Chapter] Eight:
The Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā. Without that, there is no accomplishment in this world or the next.
For one who has not known Hevajra, all effort is in vain. (55)
Like the flow of a river's current or the continuity of a lamp's flame, one should remain constantly engaged in the yoga of reality day and night. ||56||
The eighth chapter, titled "The Assembly of the Yoginīcakra," concerning the great yoginīs.
Regarding the passage beginning with *bhavet*:

"Purification" (*śuddhi*) is so called because by means of it one's self is purified through the washing away of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstructions to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); it is the path characterized by the six perfections (*pāramitā*). Through that purification, awakening (*bodhi*) certainly occurs.
However, as for "rebirth," the meaning is: by way of a succession of births throughout three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhya-kalpa*). || 54 ||

In that regard, even in the *Yogatantre*, enlightenment is said to be attained in this very life; [the author] asks, "What is its superiority over those [other systems]? and says: "And not without that," and so forth.
Without that innate (*sahaja*) state characterized by self-awareness, there is no accomplishment either in this life or in another life.
[The author] then asks, "What, then, is its distinction from those [others]? and says: "*Hevajra*," and so forth.

Because the *sahaja* (innate) indicated in other tantras is explained in its fully manifest form only in the *Hevajra*, for this reason it is shown that for one who does not know it, even the exertion of hearing, reflection, and meditation upon the *vajra* is entirely in vain. || 55 ||
[Objection: "Is it not true that enlightenment (bodhi) is difficult to attain? How, then, can it be obtained in this very life? To this, he says: "Like a river," and so forth.
"River-stream" means the flow of a river; [it is] by way of being uninterrupted like that. "Lamp-light" means the flame of a lamp; its "continuity" (prabandha) is [the subject].

*nadī śroto* — *ka*, *gha*;

*dīpaśekhā* — *gha*.
This reading follows the Ka.Kha' manuscript; the Pravāha reads "Gha.

In the *Vajra-tantra*, [the Melāpaka Chapter]: "In that same way, one should remain day and night in the constant and uninterrupted yoga of reality (*tattva-yoga*), which is the yoga of innate bliss (*sahajānanda-yoga*).
This being so, enlightenment (*bodhi*) will certainly be accomplished in this very life—this is the meaning. (56)

The Mahāyoginīs are Nairātmyā and the others; their *melāpaka* is their gathering (*melaka*). This occurs in the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) and in innate bliss (*sahajānanda*); thus is called the chapter that illuminates that.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the Melāpaka-paṭala, in the Hevajra-pañjikā composed by the venerable Kṛṣṇācārya, within the Yogaratnamālā.
Nairātmyā and others—Chapter Nine on Purity. Hereafter, we shall explain the Chapter on Purity: "The purity of all things is indeed known as suchness (*tathatā*);
subsequently, it is described according to the individual distinctions of the deities. (1)
The six sense-faculties, the five aggregates, the six sense-bases, and the five elements—though pure, they are veiled by ignorance and afflictions. (2)
Purity, which by its very nature consists of self-awareness, is not liberated through the removal of impurity;
because its objective state is pure, supreme bliss is self-aware. (3)
Regarding the "Chapter on Purity" (*viśuddhipaṭalam*):
it is called purity (*viśuddhi*) because by means of it things are purified; that by which all phenomena (*sarvabhāva*) become free from defects is purity.
The chapter that elucidates that is the "Chapter on Purity."
The pervasive purity of all phenomena is suchness, the emptiness of all dharmas.
It was explained as "mindfulness" in the eighth chapter; now, it is discussed subsequently. (1)
How is it that the deities, such as Vajragaurī and others, are impure, or how are they purified?
[The answer begins with] "the six sense faculties," and so forth.
"By their own nature" means by the nature of suchness (*tathatā*).
If it is already pure, for what purpose is it purified? [The text says] "by ignorance," and so forth.

Ignorance is the lack of thorough knowledge of the intrinsic nature; it is the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Afflictions are passion and the like; they are the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*). It is "covered" or concealed by these. For this reason, it is purified. (2)
Regarding that purity which consists of suchness (*tathatā*), he asks what its nature is and says "to be personally realized" (*svasaṃvedya*) and so forth.
The meaning is that it is not purified by any other kind of purity, as was explained previously in the eighth chapter. (3)

In the Vajra Tantra, the Chapter on Purification: "By whatever means the world is bound, by those very same means one should release that bondage.
The world is deluded; it does not know reality, and therefore, being devoid of reality, it shall not attain accomplishment. || 19 ||

There is no smell, no sound, no form, nor even taste, nor the purity of mind; there is no touch, no mental object (*dharma*), for through the purity of all things, the world is of a pure nature. Thus I perceive the world. This is the ninth chapter, on Purity.

Thus, having first explained purification according to the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), he again speaks of that very same single-flavored purification according to the stage of completion (*utpannakrama*) with the words beginning "by which," and so forth:
"By whichever forms, such as visible form and the rest, the world is bound, by those very same [forms] I am liberated; not by means of meditating on the forms of deities and so forth."

If the world is liberated by each of those very [means], then how is it bound? To this he says: "The world is deluded therein because of its adherence to the notion that 'this is real'; it does not know reality. Non-arising (*anutpāda*) is reality, yet being devoid of reality, it does not know it. Lacking the cultivation of non-arising, one does not attain accomplishment, which is the state of Vajradhara"—this is the intended meaning. || 19 ||
Since this is so, for that reason the meaning is that the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth do not exist at all from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Nor is the purification of the mind to be considered something separate, because it too is of the nature of non-arising;
thus, "purification of all" means the entire world is pure.
By what [means] was it stated? By the purity of the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatāviśuddhi*).
Therefore, since the world has a pure intrinsic nature (*śuddhasvabhāva*), who indeed knows it thus? He says: "I consider the world"—the meaning is that I know it. (20)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, on Purification, in the *Hevajra-pañjikā* composed by the venerable Kṛṣṇācārya, within the *Yogaratnamālā*.

The Tenth Chapter: On Consecration. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the mandala in its proper sequence, as well as the ritual procedure by which the disciple is consecrated. (1)
The yogi, first identifying himself with the deity, should purify the earth;
having diligently transformed it into a vajra with the syllable *HŪṂ*, he should thereafter draw the maṇḍala. ||2||
One should construct the maṇḍala in a garden, in a secluded place, in the residences of bodhisattvas, or in the center of a maṇḍala hall. || 3 ||
Either with a divine streak of powder, or with a middling one, or with powders made of the five precious gems, or with rice and so forth. ||4||

To that end, he says "atha ata" and so forth; this should be understood as follows: [the author will explain] the sequential and unerring procedure, as well as the procedure by which the disciple is consecrated according to the rite. || 1 ||

having meditated on emptiness by means of the syllable *HŪṂ*—thinking "having made it vajra"—one should visualize a sun-maṇḍala by the syllable *REPHA*, upon which is a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) by the syllable *HŪṂ*. From these two, one should contemplate the ground as consisting of vajras, a vajra-fence and canopy, and outside of that, a garland of vajra-fire. Having empowered it with the mantra "A rakṣa HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ," one should draw the maṇḍala. || 2 ||

It is a blending of wisdom and means, a mixture of passion and the absence of passion. ||9||
He alone is the life-breath of living beings; he alone is the supreme syllable;
he alone is all-pervading; he alone is established within every body. ||10||
He alone is that Great Breath; he alone is that which consists of the universe. Existence and non-existence arise from him, as do all other things whatsoever.
"Equal to space" means it is equal to the sky because it is without appearance;
"dustless" because it is free from afflictions;
and "empty" because it transcends conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Existence is arising; non-existence is destruction. That which has these two as its own nature or essence is thus described.

"Supreme" means the form of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), which is the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of all phenomena. Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the means (*upāya*), which is the experience of the equality of oneself with all sentient beings through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Intermingled with those two, because they manifest as a single form:
passion (*rāga*) is the supreme joy (*paramānanda*), and dispassion (*arāga*) is the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*); it is a form intermingled with those two. || 9 ||
Living beings are *sattvas*; for them, that very [essence] is the *jīva*, because without it there is no life.
It is the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*), without beginning or end, because its nature is the *dharmadhātu*;
it is all-pervasive, because all phenomena (*dharmas*) consist of it.

"He is established in all bodies" because living bodies are presided over by consciousness; for this very reason, the world arises, since it originates from the karma and afflictions (kleśa) whose essence is that [consciousness]. || 10 ||

This is what he says: "Existence" (*bhāva*) is the body; "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth; the other six sense-faculties (*indriya*) and those which are external existents such as the stable and the moving—these too have been conceptualized by the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) as being the self (*ātman*) and so on. Demonstrating this, he says: "And all is of the nature of consciousness," according to the Vedāntins. (Note: Regarding the variant readings, *viraja* appears in manuscripts ka, kha, while *virajaḥ* appears in manuscript gha.)
Śūnya (empty) is *ga*; emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is *gha*.
From existence (*bhāva*) comes *ka*; from existence (*bhāva*) comes *kha*.
*Vyamiśra* is *ka*; *miśra* is *kha*; *mīśrī* is *ga*.
Spread by passion and non-passion—ka; mixed with passion, non-passion, and so forth—kha; unmixed—ga; mixed with passion and non-passion—gha;
of living beings—ka; of a living being—kha; of life-force—ga.
All-pervading—kha ga gha sa; that very one is also kha; she herself is gha; and she is of the nature of Māyā in every body—ka, sarvadehe0—ga. gha. ṭa. he0 paṃ0 mu0 va0.
This line does not exist in manuscripts Ka, Ga, Gha, Cha, and Bho;
[the reading] "bhūto" occurs in Ga and Ca;
[the reading] "caḥ" occurs in Gha.

Here, the reading "kha" begins again; the sense is that non-arising (anutpāda) is the nature (bhāva), and because this [emptiness] has that nature, it is so described— as stated in the Ka, Kha, and Gha recensions.
But as for what is adopted according to the Tibetan [tradition], it is the self-attachment toward sentient beings—
ka, gṛhītastu bhoṭānusārī.
Sattva—kha; the living being—ka, gha;
of living beings possessing bodies—kha.
The body—kha;
the six sense faculties—kha; indeed, the self is emptiness (kha).
Establishing this, he says:
"Indeed, it consists of consciousness"—[as stated] in the *Vajratantra*: "And everything is of the nature of consciousness; the Person (Puruṣa) is the ancient Lord (Īśvara)."
He is the self, the living soul, and the sentient being; he is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, as well as time and the person, existing in the form of an illusion. ||12||

The first is mere bliss (ānandamātra), the second is supreme bliss (paramānanda), the third is known as the bliss of cessation (viramānanda), and the fourth is remembered as the innate (sahaja). ||13||
The Sāṃkhyas [assert] that the person (*puruṣa*) is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*);
the proponents of the person (*pudgalavādinaḥ*) [assert] that it is the person (*pudgala*);
and the proponents of established tenets (*siddhāntavādinaḥ*) [assert] that it is the eternal creator of the world, God (*īśvara*).
The proponents of the self (*ātmavādins*) maintain that it is the self alone that is born, lives, dies, is bound, or is liberated;
the Digambaras call it the *jīva*,
while the proponents of the *sattva* call it the *sattva*.

Regarding those who propound time (*kālavādinaḥ*), it is said: "Time ripens all beings; Time destroys all creatures; Time remains awake while others sleep; for Time is indeed insurmountable. [They hold that] existence is filled by actions and wanes through their exhaustion. Likewise, the proponents of matter (*pudgalavādinaḥ*) maintain that all things—both mundane and supramundane—are of the nature of illusion (*māyārūpī*), like a creator of diverse emanations. || 12 ||
Then, regarding how that state of equal flavor (*samarasa*), which is once again within the range of experience for disciples, should be brought about, he says:
"But the mere first bliss" (*prathamānandamātraṃ tu*); "mere bliss" means common pleasure.

Regarding "the two numbers": the second and the third are to be understood as distinct applications [of the term]. "That which is called cessation" (*virama*) refers to the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*);
"the innate" (*sahaja*) refers to the nature of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). This is one interpretation, beginning with the words "the first," and so forth.
In the first [initiation] and others, such as the initiation of the master (*ācāryābhiṣeka*), mere bliss (*ānandamātra*) arises from the external union of the lotus and the vajra.

Why? Because mere bliss is the common form—[the text notes that] *sarvasattva* (all beings) is the reading in versions ka, ga; *sattva* in kha; and *sattve* in gha; while *na rūpaṃ* (not a form) is the reading in cha.

*ātma*—ka.

That nature is *asau-ga*; that nature is established as *asau-gha*.
There is no *ka*—*ka* is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*)—*ga gha*.
Incalculable—ka, kha, gha;
that which is called Virama—ka, gha; Vīramā—kha; Vīramānanda—ga; Sahaja—kha, ga.

Such is the state of equal flavor—
for the disciple— [this phrase is not present in manuscripts *ka* and *gha*].
Regarding how such a state of equanimity (*samarasa*) should be made accessible to disciples, he says:
"O, first," and so forth.
The meaning is: "kha" refers to mere commonality with bliss (*sukha*). "kha" [end].
The yoga of separation is to be performed according to its own form—
first, and so forth.

[Chapter Ten: The Consecration] *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*: Having heard this, all the wise ones, Vajragarbha and the others, were struck with supreme amazement; they fainted and fell to the ground. (14)

The world is the joy of initial bliss (*prathamānanda*), and likewise the world is the supreme joy (*paramānanda*); the world is indeed the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*), yet the innate joy (*sahajānanda*) does not exist within these three. (15)
Thus,
because others also experience such bliss through the union of the lotus and the vajra, it is described as mere bliss (ānandamātra).

"Supreme bliss," and so forth: "supreme" (*parama*) means most excellent; because it is experienced through the secret jewel (*guhyamaṇi*) by means of the guru’s instruction, it is the second consecration, as indicated by the number "two.

"The third," and so forth: "the distinguished subsequent joy" (*virama*) is characterized by the wisdom consecration (*prajñābhiṣeka*), because great bliss is experienced through the jewel situated within that [wisdom].

"Fourth," and so forth: the fourth is the fourth consecration (*caturthābhiṣeka*), which is the "innate" (*sahaja*), because it is experienced as having the nature of the realm of non-abiding nirvāṇa. || 13 ||

Thus, when sahajānanda alone—which is to be made the object of the disciple—is indicated by various synonymous terms such as *samarasa* (equal flavor) through its different characteristics, the compiler [of the tantra] describes how the Blessed One was surrounded in that assembly: "In this way," and so forth;
"with astonishment" means through the attainment of wonder; "fell upon the earth" means they fell on the ground. || 14 ||

To explain why they have fallen [into these states], he says: "The first bliss is the form of the world," and so forth. Because the world is an object of cognition (*vedya*), its form is the world; because it exists as the nature of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) by virtue of being the path, it is "thus" (*tathā*); the meaning is "exactly so. Furthermore, that which is described as the nature of the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*), consisting of the penetration of the extremely subtle mind—that too is the world, because even the mere mind, whose nature is conventional truth, is included within the category of conventional truth.
The particle *eva* is to be understood as restrictive.

The mundane (*laukika*) is threefold alone; it is called "the world" (*jagat*) because it is known by the world. It does not exist (*vidyate*) as innate (*sahaja*) within these three, nor is there any innate [nature] to be perceived within them, because they are of a different character—this is the meaning.
The word "iti" refers to the compiler of the collection (*saṃgītikāra*).
The phrase "having thus become filled with wonder" serves the purpose of concluding the statement. || 15 ||
There is none—ka; all—gha;
the wise [know] Vajrarāga and the others—ka.
Then all the Tathāgatas, headed by Vajragarbha— having attained wonder (variant readings: *vismayasampannāḥ*, *vismayamāpannāḥ*)—
fainted (*mūrcchitāḥ* or *mūrcchritāḥ*).
Pratibhāvanau—O Khaga!

Paramānanda—Ka. Kha. Ga.

*viramānanda*—ka, kha, gha; *vidyate*—ka, kha, gha.

Hevajra, the single embodiment of all Buddhas, [bestows] divine removal of doubt for the awakening of Vajragarbha. 16.
Neither passion nor dispassion, nor even the middle way, is perceived;
by the very abandonment of these three, it is called innate awakening (sahaja-bodhi). 17.
Alternatively, he is the soul of all, or else he is devoid of all; he is perceived at the beginning of the Cessation (virama), [in the chapter on consecration], as being devoid of the three joys.
The Blessed One said—this being the words of the compiler [of the scripture]: "Together with all Buddhas, he is of non-different body, a single form.
"Doubt is removed" means that by which doubt is removed; [he spoke] for the sake of divine, supreme awakening and practice. (16)
"Not passion," and so forth.
Passion (*rāga*) is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*); dispassion (*virāga*) is the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*); and "the middle" (*madhyamā*) is the initial bliss (*prathamānanda*).
These three are not perceived as having the nature of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
"Of the three" means by the avoidance and separation from these three. "Innate" refers to innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), because it is the cause of perfect enlightenment (*saṃbodhi*).
"Not passion" (*na rāga*) is said because [innate bliss] has passion as its object.
The first consecration is [the first].
Because it has as its object distinguished bliss, detachment (*virāga*) is the third consecration.

Regarding "in the middle": because the second consecration is not perceived between those two as being the immediate cause of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), for this reason it is said, "by the avoidance of the three."
"Sahaja" refers to the sahajābhiṣeka; the meaning is that it is the fourth [initiation].
It is called "awakening" (sambodhi) by way of metaphorical attribution of cause to effect.
Why is it not mentioned in other [contexts] regarding the other initiations?
The meaning is that it is the cause of causes.
For this very reason, it is said to be "devoid of the three [other] joys.
If it did not exist altogether elsewhere, then that innate moment (sahajakṣaṇa) would not possess pervasiveness; therefore, the innate awakening (sahajasambodhi) is called the primary cause. || 17 ||
Now, he says "virama" and so forth, in order to somehow reveal the innate (*sahaja*).
Is this very [state] supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) at the beginning of the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*)?
No, he says.

"Devoid of the three joys"—by implication, this means: "The first [state], devoid of the three supreme joys, appears like a cloud; once established, it becomes like *māyā*; suddenly it appears like a dream, as if there were no distinction between sleeping and waking. (19)
"When the characteristic of non-duality is established, the practitioner of the mudrā-yoga attains perfection";
thus the Teacher spoke, [describing] the mandala as four-cornered and brilliantly radiant. (20)

"Beyond Nanda," as it will be stated in the thirteenth chapter: "I am of the nature of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), [consisting of] the supreme (*parama*) ending with the cessation (*virama*) and so forth" (*Hevajratantra* 2.2.40).
This is one interpretation.
One should understand "at the beginning of *virama*" (*viramādau*) as referring to the third initiation and so on, and should practice according to what is appropriate.

To explain what that [state] is distinguished by, he says: "devoid of the three joys" (ānandatrayavarjita), meaning it is free from the joys of Ānanda, Parama, and Virama; for its essential nature is distinct because its form is different from them. || 18 ||

When the co-emergent (*sahaja*) has been thus correctly discerned, for one who meditates by means of instruction—meditating by means of instruction—the various concentrations (*samādhi*) arise. He describes them as being like a cloud, like an illusion, like a dream, and like a dream-awakening.
Regarding the first: at the time of initial practice, why is it "like a cloud"?
Because, like the full moon obscured by clouds, it is not perfectly clear.
How is it like an illusion?

For one who is immersed in the essence of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), the world appears as if it were an illusion; when this becomes manifest, then there is accomplishment (*siddhi*). "Suddenly" means that after that, it is like a dream.
How is it like a dream?

Because of the non-perception of self and other, it is therefore comparable to dreaming and waking; for there is no distinction between the states of waking and dreaming, as they are equally composed. || 19 ||

Thus, regarding how the yogin achieves accomplishment through the perfection of the four meditative concentrations, he says "non-differentiation," and so forth. Non-differentiation (*abheda*) is the absence of distinction among form and the other [sensory objects].
How is there an absence of distinction?
There is an absence of distinction when their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are established.

"Characterized" (*lakṣaṇa*) means that by which something is characterized; [it refers to] its own-nature (*svabhāva*). In the accomplishment of that, all phenomena are rendered devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) by way of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
"The practitioner of the mudrā" means that the practitioner of the Great Mudrā (*mahāmudrā*) attains accomplishment.
"Thus" (*iti*) means: such is the accomplishment of the Great Mudrā.

In the Vajra Tantra, there is a great palace with four doors, adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, provided with garlands, variegated chowries, and beautified by eight pillars; it is joined with vajra-lines and adorned with incense, lamps, and various flowers. [Chapter on Consecration: 21]
Likewise, it should be provided with perfumes, eight jars, and so forth. || 22 ||
And they should have tips with young shoots, their necks covered with cloth;
one should present the Vijaya [vessel], encircled by the five jewels, in the east.
The wise one should mark out the lines with a beautiful thread, [visualizing] himself in the form of his chosen deity.

One should recite the mantra of the Lord of the Mandala one hundred thousand times and that of the deities of the mandala ten thousand times; with the previously mentioned mantra, the wise one should purify the ground.

Because [the goal] does not arise without empowerments, and for the reason that the empowerments must be bestowed, the Teacher Vajradhara spoke of the mandala for that purpose: "Blazing brightly, adorned with various jewels. (20)
"With variegated chowries" means with chowries of various colors. || 21 ||
"Those whose necks are covered with cloth" means those whose necks are wrapped in new cloth.
"The five jewels" refers to coral, pearl, lapis lazuli (rājāvarta), gold, and silver.
"One should give" means one should place them [there]. || 23 ||
With the words "of the Lord of the Wheel" and so forth, he describes the preliminary service (pūrvasevā). || 25 ||

This is because all entities do not arise from themselves, from another, from both, or from neither.

Emptiness has the characteristic of non-arising, and that itself is supreme wisdom (*prajñā*).
