One should offer flowers and other articles produced from the syllable *hūṃ*;
the water for honor (*argha*) and the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth, should be presented as before, according to the sequence of procedures in the previous tantra.
For pacification (śāntika), the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is circular; for enrichment (pauṣṭika), it is square;
for killing (māraṇa), it is said to be triangular; one should accomplish the remaining rites within these very same shapes.
For the rite of pacification (śāntika), it should be one cubit or half a cubit in height and width;
for the rite of nourishment (pauṣṭika), it is considered to be two cubits by one cubit in height and width.
Twenty-one finger-breadths in length, it is used for killing;
for pacifying, it should be white in color, and likewise yellow for nourishing.
In the rite of killing, [the color] is black; for subjugation, it is proclaimed to be red.
As it is in subjugation, so it is in summoning; as in killing, so it is in causing hatred and the like.
Sesame is for pacification, curd for nourishment, and likewise the thorn (kaṇṭhaka) for killing;
the thorn is prescribed for hatred and the like, while the lotus is for subjugation and attraction.
Oṃ! To Agni, of great splendor, who accomplishes all desires;
you who have acted for the benefit of sentient beings out of compassion, be present here!
"Sesame," and so forth.
There is no part of it.

One should offer the vessel and other items with the syllable *hūṃ*. As before, the previous mantra is used for pacification (*śāntika*) and enrichment (*puṣṭika*); however, there is no mantra for killing (*māraṇa*). [The fire-pit] should be twenty finger-breadths wide, or half that, or higher; killing is not [performed] in white color. Likewise, killing is proclaimed [for specific purposes]. For subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), [use] sesame, *karṇaka*, and thorns; in *karṇaka* and thorns, [there is] great splendor. In the fire, [one performs] the propitiation for the sake of sentient beings. The invocation of the fire is as follows: "O Goddess, you are the witness here; O Hevajra-Krodha, you who are worshipped! Wearing various jewels, I, the holder [of the lineage], named so-and-so, shall draw the mandala."
O Consumer of Oblations, go forth to accomplish both your own purpose and the purpose of others!
You shall return at the proper time; grant me all success! *La la la!* This is the mantra for propitiating Agni.
Oṃ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hāḥ khaṃ raṃ is the mantra for the water of honor (*argha*). Nī rī hūṃ khaḥ is the mantra for the water for the feet (*pādya*).
Dhvaṃ dhvaṃ dhvaṃ is the mantra for the food offering (*naivedya*).
The first chapter: The Determination and Establishment of the Fire Offering (Homa).

The mantra beginning with "tvaṃ devi," etc., is the invocation mantra for the Earth mentioned here by way of introduction; at the end, however, the mantra for the *argha* offering and so forth belongs to Agni alone.

Thus ends the first chapter, on the determination of the fire sacrifice and consecration, in the second kalpa of the *Hevajrapañjikā*, composed by the venerable Kṛṣṇācārya as part of the *Yogaratnamālā*.

"O Goddess, having become a witness, may you who maintain the effort write: 'I am not liberated; once it is accomplished, I shall surely come. *Hoḥ raṃ svāhā dhūṃ dhūṃ dhūṃ*. This is the mantra for the food offering (*naivedya*). Thus ends the first chapter, the Chapter on the Consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), in the *Śrī Hevajra Tantra*. Thus ends the first chapter, the Chapter on the Consecration, in the *Śrī Homa-nirṇaya*. [In the manuscript marked] *kha*: In the second section of the *Hevajra-Ḍākinījāla-saṃvara*, the first chapter is the Chapter on Consecration. Vajragarbha said: "The second chapter, named the Determination of Accomplishment (*siddhi-nirṇaya*): Just as a gourd [floats] upon the ocean, how do sentient beings achieve accomplishment among all phenomena which are like the sky? [They do so] by means of the form of their own chosen deity."

The Blessed One said: "One who desires accomplishment, having disciplined himself in the yoga of selflessness or through the yoga of Heruka, should not remain for even a moment with a mind directed elsewhere."

Vajragarbha asked, saying "Like the sky," and so forth. The unwholesome qualities (*akuśala-dharma*) of sentient beings, accumulated since beginningless time, are like the sky; their antidote (*pratipakṣa*) is the meditation on one's own tutelary deity (*svādhidaivata-bhāvanā*). Consequently, an antidote resembling a small gourd is not capable [of overcoming] a mass of opposing factors (*vipakṣa-rāśi*) that is like the ocean. Therefore, the sense is: "for the sake of crossing over the mass of unwholesomeness. The meaning of the question is: how then do sentient beings achieve accomplishment through that meditation?
Regarding this, the Blessed One said: "Selflessness," and so forth.

*Yoga* is meditative absorption (*samādhi*); one whose self is joined with that is a *yogin*. Alternatively, the glorious *vajrayoga*-joined self is the *yogin* who, having abandoned the entire mass of opposing factors, necessarily attains accomplishment.
Now, one might ask: how can there be a crossing over from a mass of opposing factors (*vipakṣa*) as vast as the ocean merely through the yoga of the deity?

The point is that just as a fire ignited once within a mountain cave destroys a pillar of darkness accumulated over a long time, so too is this specific meditation on Hevajra, who is devoid of self (*nairātmya*).
Nevertheless, if it is asked: "Since the opposing factors are destroyed by the cultivation of the antidote even once, why would there not be accomplishment (*siddhi*)?"
True; for the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā does not arise from the mere destruction of opposing factors alone.
Rather, this belongs only to one who has accumulated the two provisions (*sambhāra*).

To that end, he says: "even for a moment being of another mind. For what is called "non-other-mindedness" is a specific form of cultivation characterized by calm abiding (*śamatha*), and that is to be attained through gradual practice.

Just as the vajra, sky, and ocean are accomplished, so too are they accomplished and fully realized by one joined with the yoga of selflessness (*nairātmya*). The self of the yoga of selflessness, which is the ultimate self of selflessness, belongs to those who desire the glorious Heruka. Since the characteristics of a snake are insentient, how could an adept (*siddhika*) remain [attached] to them? Now, through the mere yoga that is like the ocean, by means of meditation, there is the destruction of the counter-factors; this belongs to one for whom the destruction of the counter-factors has been accumulated. He is indeed accumulated in this state. With a mind focused on nothing else, in the *Vajra-tantra*, a virtuous place is prescribed for the time of the first practice, where situated, the mantra-practitioner, single-minded and composed, attains accomplishment.
In his own home at night, the wise one, with the thought "I am accomplished," should meditate upon the Yoginī or else upon the form of Śrī Heruka.
Washing his feet, eating, sipping water for purification, chewing betel nut, rubbing his hands with sandalwood paste, and covering his loins with a loincloth;
Whether departing, speaking words, walking, standing, being angry, or laughing, the wise practitioner, observing his vow, should serve the Blessed Lady and meditate upon the Yoginī.
Those who are wise and desire accomplishment should strive with effort not to abide with a mind corrupted by ignorance, for the sake of attaining success.

O Vajragarbha, even for a single moment, meditate on that which I have described as being of another form; this meditation destroys all sins. For the sake of accomplishment, you should examine it for even a single fortnight, even out of mere curiosity.
Therefore, he says "first," and so forth.
"At the time of night" means during the night, because at other times there is the possibility of opposing factors arising.
"I am accomplished" is due to a particular form of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
The yoga of meditative concentration at night has been explained.
— || He speaks of uninterrupted yoga at other times [than that]: beginning with "the feet," etc.; "one should serve" means one should propitiate.
Whom should one propitiate?
The Yoginī Nairātmyā.
"Of another form" means having a form that is not distinct from the nature of selflessness (*nairātmya*).
"—Vajragarbha," etc., is the conclusion.
"Sins" refers to faults.
For the purpose of generating firmness, he says: "even out of curiosity."
"Fortnight" (pakṣa) means half a month.

The auspicious [practice] of Mahākāla, situated in the four states, with the mind: expanding the form of Heruka, O Yoginī, there is no rinsing; one should consume the rinsing, the rinsing, the rinsing, and cover oneself with loincloths. Covering himself, the yogi, observing the vow, should examine with the mind: "Be examined," "Examine," "To be examined," "Let it be examined," "Examine! "Examine! "Examine! "Examine! "Examine! "Examine! Having abandoned all thought, with a mind focused on the form of the deity, having meditated continuously for one day, you should examine it again and again. *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā:* Having abandoned all conceptual thought, with a mind fixed on the form of the deity, having meditated without interruption for a single day, you should examine it through repeated meditation.

In this saṃsāra, there is no other means for the accomplishment of one’s own and others’ welfare than this knowledge (vidyā), which, when practiced even once, produces immediate conviction. Furthermore,
the practitioner is never afflicted by fear or madness, nor by sufferings, the afflictions of grief and pain, nor by passion, hatred, and great delusion.
Reflecting thus upon the emergence of the fruits of what is beneficial and what is harmful,
how could those who commit the five immediate transgressions and those who are devoted to the slaughter of living beings remain yogins for even a single moment in Raurava? 12.
Moreover, even those who are low-born, foolish, performers of cruel deeds,
deformed, or have impaired limbs— these too attain success through this meditation.
So too does one who practices the ten virtues, is devoted to the guru, and has conquered the senses.
"Practiced during the twilight" indicates the resulting conviction by means of the words beginning with "fear.
By the words beginning with "thus," [the author explains that] one who is thus patient and of a reflective nature [attains] the arising of what is beneficial and wholesome.
The arising of the unwholesome that is harmful;
"in the worldly conduct of the Raurava hell" refers to worldly conduct which is the cause of hell.
For even those such as the most wicked who behave in this manner, there is the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā.
If it is asked, "What is the opportunity?", he says:
"The five immediate [sins], etc. (verse 13).
Those with deformed limbs or missing organs should reflect by means of the meditation on selflessness (*nairātmya-bhāvanā*).

[The opponent objects: "In that case, those who follow the Dharma would not achieve success. To this he says: "By the ten wholesome [actions]," and so forth. || 14 || [Variants: *parīkṣayā* (ka), *parikṣayaḥ* (kha, ga, gha), *parīkṣatha* (cha, jha), *parīkṣasva* (ja), *pariṣethāḥ* (ṭa); *svaparārthaṃ* (ka); *abhyāsatā* (ka).)]
In the *sādhaka*—*ga*.
In the *vimukha*—*māna* is *ga*.
What was stated in the middle of the *kṣaṇa*—*ka*; [the reading] "in the middle of the *kṣaṇa*" is *gha*.
One who performs the five mantra-less rites—ka;
[the reading] *vadhya*—ka, *prāṇibandhana*—kha, *prāṇivadhe*—gha;
and those of low birth—ka.
It is accomplished—ka; they are contemplated—ka;
practiced—gha.
"One should contemplate"—thus it is said in the *Ka* manuscript.

"By means of the meditation on selflessness"—thus it is said in the *Ka* manuscript. In the *Vajra-tantra*, in the chapter titled "The Determination of Siddhis": "One who is completely freed from pride and anger will certainly attain accomplishment."
Having attained perfection through the yoga of continuous practice, he remains concentrated in meditative absorption.
He should live in seclusion for one month until the mudrā is obtained;
then the practitioner of mantra receives an instruction and is directed by the yoginīs.
"O Vajradhṛk, having taken such-and-such a mudrā, act for the benefit of sentient beings!
Having obtained that large-eyed woman, adorned with beauty and youth,
one should consecrate her— joined with musk and camphor— with the *bodhicitta*."

Beginning with the ten wholesome actions, one should proclaim the Dharma to them. By practicing the visualization of the deity’s form, the samaya, and single-mindedness for one month, she will certainly be attained; there is no doubt in this matter. || 18–19 ||
Since a woman who has obtained a boon is free from all conceptual constructions (*saṃkalpa*),
or else, by means of her own power, she may draw [the deity] forth and fashion the *mudrā*.
Even more so than a *kinnara*.
Having taken up that [practice] from among gods, asuras, humans, and yakṣas, one should carry out the conduct out of confidence in one's own fortitude.
Siddhi is the attainment of samādhi;
for this very reason, one is "composed" (samāhita).
"Month," and so forth.
"Secret" refers to the secret vow; it is enjoined by the yoginīs for the sake of obtaining the mudrās.
"By means of the bodhicitta" refers to the going for refuge and so on. || 15-16 ||
The deity-yoga is the mind in the form of the deity. The pledge consists of that which is to be guarded and so forth. The yoga of the co-emergent is the state of single-mindedness.

"Bhavyā" means one who is capable of attaining accomplishment (*siddhi*). "Having drawn forth" refers to conceptualization (*vikalpa*). "Having drawn her" means having drawn her who has obtained a boon, or who has been attracted; "through the confidence of steadfastness" means having attained steadfastness (*dhairya*).
[Note: *kāmakrodha* is found in manuscripts ka, kha, gha.]
Having attained accomplishment: Kha.
The secret: He0 Paṃ0 Mu0 Va0.
That which is to be taken up: Ka.
0 *mantritam* — gha; 0 *saṃyuktam* — ga gha;
therefore, *ka*.
What is possible? It would not be so here—ga. Better.
Labdha (obtained) is *ka*; *nārī* (woman) is *ca*; that which is devoid of *ka* and *kha* is *gha*.
O Yakṣa, "from what does fortitude arise?

[The answer is: having attained fortitude—(according to the reading *dhairyapratyāditi* in the Snelagrove manuscript); or, according to the second [version], *dhairyapratyayāditi*, meaning for the sake of establishing fortitude.
[From the *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*: "The conduct (*caryā*) is not proclaimed as being for the sake of enjoyment (*bhoga*), that which is known as having a terrifying form."

For the sake of examining one's own mind, [one must determine] whether the mind is stable or moving; therefore, the yogin should constantly abide in the form of the deity. As Vajragarbha said: "Therefore, by the yogin... (22)
For one engaged in the yoga of selflessness, how is the meaning of the *mudrā* distinguished?
How can there be the accomplishment of the *mudrā* through both the [inner] *mudrā* and the [outer] *mudrā*? || 23 ||
The Blessed One said: "Having abandoned the female form, one should assume another form; having removed the breast of the Blessed One, it becomes the *bola* situated within the *kakkola*. (24)
The two banks are the bell, and the filaments are the *bolaka*; the remainder is the form of the Great Being Heruka, the Great Joy. (25)
For a man who practices the yoga of Heruka, the perfection of the mudrā occurs effortlessly through the transcendence of his masculinity, because he is a yogin whose power is manifest. ||26||

He asks "Why? and says "Not the practice," and so forth; that which was previously described in the *Caryāpaṭala* as having a terrifying form because it is exceedingly difficult [to perform]. || 22 ||
He said to Vajragarbha: for what purpose did he say "Nairātma" and so forth?

[The term] "mudrā" refers to the external mudrā; for what purpose is she sought? [The phrase] "by means of a mudrā, with a mudrā" means: how can the accomplishment of the mudrā be achieved through two mudrās? The form of the woman is the form of Nairātma. "Of the Blessed One" refers to Hevajra. "Having taken the breast" means having removed the two breasts, one should make that into a *bola* (phallus); this is the meaning. (23–24)

"By the banks," and so forth: the two sides are the bell (*ghaṇṭā*), which is the testicles; with the filaments, which is the human nose, one should fashion the *bola* (the male organ) of "great passion," that is, of one consisting of great lust. || 25 ||
"Mudrāsiddhi" refers to the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā. Regarding the phrase "by which," it means that through this sequence, the unmanifest [is realized] from the manifest.
[The reading] "cale-gha" does not exist in this text; [it is found only in] Ka, Gha, Cha, Ja, and Ṭa.
Nairātmā— having taken [the letters] ka, kha, ga, gha, ha— [is] situated in the heart; [this is] the Hevajra-pañjikā-yogaratnamālā-saṃsthita (Kha).
By the filament—ṭa; of the Great-Souled One—kha, cha; the Great-Souled Ones—jha;
O Great Lover—ga; O Great Deed—gha.
This much portion does not exist in the "ka" manuscript;
"puruṣatva māyābhya0" in "kha", "puṃstvamāyāti0" in "ga", and "puṃsa māyāti" in "gha";
therefore, [the reading is as in] "ga" and "gha".
For what purpose is it sought? For what purpose does one who seeks it [seek it]?
Having abandoned—[as stated in] the *Vajra-tantra*, in the chapter titled "The Determination of Siddhi"—wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) are not sublated by arising and dissolution.

Therefore, for this [reality], there is no dissolution, nor indeed is there any arising in reality; because there is no dissolution, nothing whatsoever dissolves, and because there is no dissolution, there is no destruction. (28)

Through the yoga of the generation stage, the practitioner of the vow should cultivate the manifold world; having made the manifold world like a dream, he should transcend the manifold by means of the manifold. (29)
For one engaged in the meditation on the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), there is the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā therein, which is the accomplishment of the two bodies of the deity.

Consequently, the body of those such as Brahmā who travel in celestial palaces (*vimāna*) is subject to arising and destruction through the processes of cosmic evolution (*saṃvarta*) and dissolution (*vivarta*). || 26 ||
Therefore, he says—beginning with "utpatti" and so forth—that this is not subject even to the attainment of Mahāmudrā.

Why is it not subject [to change]? He says: "Because of the means (upāya). It is called "sambhava" because it occurs continuously; the meaning is that it is eternal by way of its continuity as long as space exists.

That is the means; that is the fruit upon the completion of cultivation. Therefore, it is *pralaya* (dissolution), for *laya* is the non-perception of all phenomena (*sarvabhāvānām anupalambhaḥ*); that is *prajñā*. Consequently, this [state] brings an end to existence—that is, it brings an end to the clinging to the body. The two bodies, which have become of one flavor with those two, which resemble a dream, a magical illusion, a conjuration, and a mirage, and which extend as far as the limits of space, constitute the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā. || 27 ||
For that very reason, there is neither dissolution nor arising for this;
rather, in reality, nothing whatsoever dissolves.

If it were of the nature of a functional entity (*bhāva*), it would possess both arising and destruction. However, because its nature is non-abiding nirvāṇa, it possesses the characteristics of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Therefore, what is it that dissolves? Since that [entity] does not exist, there is the exhaustion of destruction. Thus, it is established that for one who has attained the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), there is neither arising nor passing away.
And that [attainment] is obtainable only through cultivation. || 28 ||
But what is the nature of this cultivation? To this he says: "Having created," and so forth.
"The manifold" refers to the various kinds characterized by the relationship of support and supported;
"having made it like a dream" means that just as in a dream the mind appears in various forms, so too [has one] made it.
One should make it free from conceptual proliferation by means of "conceptual proliferations," that is, by means of verbal discriminations. || 29 ||

Second: The Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā states: Just as an illusion, just as a dream, and just as the intermediate state (antarābhava) may appear, so too does the mandala shine forth through the yoga of constant practice. (30)
In the empowerments of Mahāmudrā, there is great bliss as it is known;
its power is that very maṇḍala, and not something arising from another. //31//
Bliss is black, bliss is yellow, bliss is red, bliss is white;
bliss is dark-brown, bliss is blue, and bliss is the entire world of the moving and the unmoving. ||32||
Bliss is wisdom, bliss is the means, and likewise bliss is that which arises from *kunduru*;
bliss is existence, bliss is non-existence, and Vajrasattva is remembered as bliss. || 33 ||
He says "yathā" and so forth to explain what occurs for one who practices in this manner step by step: "like a city of Gandharvas" refers to the city of Hariścandra;
the meaning is that it becomes just like that, attaining a state of vivid clarity. || 30 ||

Now, demonstrating that this cultivation of the maṇḍala circle is indeed the very nature of the great bliss (*mahāsukha*) characterized by the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*), he says "Mahāmudrā," and so forth.
"Mahāmudrā-consecration" refers to the wisdom-consort consecration (*prajñābhiṣeka*);
"in those four" means as it has been understood from the guru’s instruction, according to how it is realized.

What is this realization according to the guru’s instruction? It is great bliss, characterized as both the goal and the means; the meaning is that this maṇḍala is its very manifestation (*prabhāva*), and "manifestation" here means being composed of that.

"The mandala is the Hevajra-Nairātmyā mandala; it does not arise from anything else" means that it is not produced from something other [than itself]. Now, one might object: "In the consecrations of wisdom and gnosis (*prajñājñāna-abhiṣeka*), only bliss characterized by the absence of conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) is perceived. How then can it be said that the mandala-circle, endowed with the excellence of all aspects, has arisen from that? It is logical that like should arise only from like."
This is not so;
this is merely worldly convention, namely that "from a similar [cause] arises only a similar [effect].

For just as the proponents of the *ālayavijñāna* describe the *ālayavijñāna* as the substratum for the seeds of the world, so too, in the Mantra Mahāyāna, that very thing—characterized by great bliss (*mahāsukha*) and realized through the consecration of wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*)—is described as the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*) and as the substratum for all the qualities of a Buddha. Demonstrating that very point, he says, beginning with "bliss" (*sukham*), etc.; "passion" (*raja*) refers to the union of wisdom and means. (31–32)
Existence is the nature of the five Buddhas;
non-existence is their very state free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*).
Let there be *bhavatu* (ja), *prajñopāyagha*, *attasambhavaṃcha*, and *astathābhavaṃ jha*.

In the *Vajra-tantra*, the chapter titled "The Determination of Siddhi," Vajragarbha said: "This is the yoga of the stage of completion (*utpannakrama-yoga*); its bliss is considered the Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*).
For one who is devoid of the meditation on the stage of completion, what is the purpose of the generation stage (*utpatti*)? (34)
The Blessed One said: "Aho! ||34||
In the absence of the body, whence can there be happiness? It is impossible to speak of happiness;
for the entire world is pervaded by happiness in the form of the pervaded and the pervader. (35)

By virtue of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the Śrī Hevajra maṇḍala has the form of bliss; however, one might ask how the Nairātmyā maṇḍala can likewise have the form of bliss. To this he says, "Vajrasattva," and so forth: the moon and sun, whose natures are wisdom and method, are joined together; from their union arises a seed-syllable, from which the emblem (*cihna*)—the vajra—is produced. The seed-syllable situated within that [vajra] is the *sattva*. Together with the vajra, the *sattva* is Vajrasattva; he too is bliss.
Thus it is remembered. || 33 ||
Vajragarbha asked: For what purpose did he say this? [The answer is: It is for the purpose of praising the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) itself as being of the nature of bliss (*sukharūpa*).

Regarding the words "the arisen" (*utpanna*) and so forth: "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) refers to the cultivation of the body of a deity; that which is devoid of this is meant. The phrase "what is the purpose of the generation? means that there would be no purpose [for it].

The intention is as follows: [the author] demonstrates his reverence by asking, "What is the purpose of an extensive cultivation of the maṇḍala-circle through the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in great bliss (*mahāsukha*), since the desired goal is accomplished by great bliss alone? (34)
"Destroyed by the force of faith," and so forth.
There is weightiness in the generation stage (*utpattikrama*);
therefore, this [view] is destroyed because it rejects the generation stage.
With the words beginning "deha," he praises that very process of generation (utpattikrama).
As for the question "Whence is bliss?":
the meaning is that bliss cannot be taught anywhere else.

Therefore, it is said that the world is pervaded by bliss; not merely by way of being the pervaded, but also by way of being the pervader, because both possess the nature of the pervaded and the pervader. Just as the body and so forth do not exist without bliss, likewise, bliss does not exist without the body. || 35 ||

Second: *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*: Just as fragrance residing in a flower is not perceived when the flower is absent, so too bliss is not experienced in the absence of form and the other [sensory objects]. (36)
I am existence, yet I am not existence; I am the Buddha because of the awakening to reality.
Those fools who do not know me, and those who are overcome by indolence—[they remain ignorant].
I dwell in Sukhāvatī, within the womb of the true Vajra-consort.
But in the form shaped like the letter E, I have been explained as the Dharma within the jewel-casket of the Buddha. || 38 ||
I am the hearer accompanied by the Suganas;
I am the one to be attained, the teacher of the world, and I am both the world and that which pertains to the world. || 39 ||
"I am," and so forth.

"I am existence" (*bhāva*) by virtue of having the nature of the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, in the form of the *maṇḍala-cakra* and so on; "I am indeed non-existence" (*naiva-bhāva*) by virtue of having the nature of the *dharmakāya*, in the form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
If the nature of existence consists in the form of the *maṇḍala-cakra*, then, because the *maṇḍala-cakra* is devoid of a nature that is either one or many, it is illusory (*bhrāntatva*).
Therefore, the sense is that he is not [merely] "the Buddha.

Hence he says: "I am the Buddha. "Vastūni" refers to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*); their awakening (*bodha*) is the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñāna*). By means of that knowledge, I am the Buddha.
To demonstrate that, for this reason, I am the nature of the two supremely profound bodies, he says: "Me," and so forth.
"Deluded" refers to those who have not heard [the Dharma] and are devoid of attending upon spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra). || 37 ||
In order to manifest that very same profound nature of the two bodies, he says: "I shall dwell," and so forth.
The Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitābha is called Sukhāvatī;
here, however, the "vulvas" (*bhaga*) of Nairātmyā and the others are the "abbreviations of Sukhāvatī" (*sukhāvatī-saṃkṣepāṇi*), because they protect unsurpassed bliss.
Therein I abide; for the purpose of indicating that all phenomena possess the nature of a single great bliss, they take the form of a single *ekāra* syllable.
The Buddhas themselves are the jewels, and [this] is their casket, their place of residence. 38.
Now, in order to illuminate the majesty of such a self, he says "Vyākhyāta" and so forth.
The Dharma, such as Hevajra and others, is that which illuminates this [self]. The "listener" is one endowed with the qualities of a disciple.
"I am the goal to be accomplished. As it is said in the *Vajra-tantra*, in the chapter titled "The Determination of Siddhi":
"I am of the nature of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), the ultimate beyond the limit of cessation (*viramānta*).
O son, proceed in that manner with conviction, like a lamp in the darkness. (40)
The Teacher, endowed with the thirty-two marks and the Lord possessing the eighty minor characteristics, resides in Sukhāvatī within the womb of a woman under the name Śukra. || 41 ||
Without that [the cause], there would be no happiness; and without happiness, that [the effect] could not exist.
Happiness arises from the union with a deity because it is dependent and lacks independent power. (42)
And that which was previously described as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is none other than myself.

I alone am the teacher of the world through the *saṃbhoga* and *nirmāṇa* bodies. Regarding the phrase "the world" and so forth: the world arises from sexual union; the worldly [element] is the fluid of bodhicitta, which serves as its cause. Considering that the world is its purpose (*prayojana*), it has the nature of the *saṃbhogakāya*, and that too is I. (39)
Now, if it is asked: "Since its nature is that of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) by virtue of being primary, what is that? he says: "Innate" (*sahaja*), and so forth.
What is the specific quality of this innate bliss?
He says: "Supreme," and so forth.
That which exists at the end of the supreme [joy] and at the beginning of the cessation [of joy] is the meaning of "I.

Now, one might object: "The goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is that which consists of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), is the essence of all, namely the Blessed One (*bhagavān*); however, the innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) pertaining to cyclic existence mentioned previously is not this goal. Therefore, how can that very thing be the Blessed One?
To this, it says "And thus," and so forth.

The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*); because that very [worldly pleasure] is the means for establishing the cognition of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) through its similarity to the condition of the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*), which is bliss, therefore that alone is primary, while this [present discussion] is merely conventional usage.
He states this very point: "like a lamp in the darkness.

Just as, for instance, for those situated in a place of darkness, a lamp is the means for establishing the cognition of jars, cloths, and so forth, in the same way, worldly innate pleasure itself should be regarded as the means of accomplishment for the goal characterized as Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*), by virtue of serving as an illustrative example. || 40 ||
Clarifying what was previously stated in the passage beginning with "I wander," he says "thirty-two," and so forth: "His body resplendent with the primary marks and secondary signs;
the Lord" means the sustainer of the Buddha-dharmas;
"the woman" is the illustrative example of the Vajra-woman; "in her bhaga I abide by the name of semen. (41)

"Semen" (*śukra*) means pleasure (*sukha*), as well as external semen; without that semen, pleasure is not perceived. This is because, in the absence of semen, other causes lack the capacity to produce such pleasure.
It is said that bliss arises solely from the yoga of the deity; therefore, one who seeks great bliss must certainly cultivate the yoga of the deity. || 42 ||
Second: The Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā states: Therefore, the Buddha would not be an existent entity, nor indeed would he be of the nature of non-existence;
for he possesses the form of arms and faces, yet is formless due to supreme bliss. (43)
Therefore, the world is innate;
its very own nature is nirvāṇa when perceived by a mind in the aspect of purity. (44)
Everything is said to be the innate nature (sahajasvarūpa).
However, the form of the deity-yoga is established as soon as one is born;
yet, due to the positions of the arms, faces, and colors, there is the influence of worldly tendencies (prākṛtavāsanā).
By that very same portion of poison by which all living beings die,
one who knows the true nature of poison may neutralize poison with that very poison.
Since the path is neither existence nor non-existence because its nature is that of seminal bliss (*śukra-sukha*), its fruit—the Buddha—is likewise neither existence nor non-existence.
Why? He says: "With arms and faces," and so forth.
By means of the *saṃbhogakāya*, he possesses form; yet by virtue of supreme bliss, he is not possessed of form.
The *dharmakāya* is not material, and because it is thus of a non-abiding nature, it is established that it is neither existence nor non-existence. || 43 ||

Since it is thus, the world consists of the co-emergent (*sahaja*). What is the meaning of "all sentient beings are co-emergent"? It means that their own nature (*svarūpa*) is being expressed; "the co-emergent" is a synonym for the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of phenomena.
To explain how that itself is *nirvāṇa*, he says "purified," and so forth.
Purity is the attainment of the Dharma, which is the nature of luminosity; therefore, the meaning is that when this purity of the mind occurs, then there is nirvāṇa. || 44 ||

If the world consists of the Buddha because its nature is both existence and non-existence, then why is the meditation on the form of the deity performed? To this he says: "True, it has been said," and so forth. "Deity," etc., means that [the deity is meditated upon] because of the commonality of body, such as having arms and faces, and so on.
Consequently, cultivation would be futile.
However, as for the phrase "but" and so forth, the remainder of the sense is that there is a latent impression (*vāsanā*) of an ordinary body in that [state].

The intention is that, for the sake of abandoning that [ordinary state] and for the nourishment of the latent impressions of the untainted aggregates (*anāsravaskandha*), the cultivation of the deity’s body is performed. || 45 ||
Now, it is difficult to accept that the cultivation of the body is the cause for non-abiding nirvāṇa.
Proving this through many examples, he says "by that very [means]" and so forth.
"One should burst open" means one should strike. || 46 ||

In the Vajra-tantra, the chapter titled "The Determination of Siddhi": Just as one seized by wind is cured by wind, so too is existence—which is pure—cured by existence itself. Black gram (*māṣa*) food is offered because of the application of contrary medicine;
this occurs through conceptualization and its counter-conceptualization. (47)
Just as water that has entered the ear is drawn out by water of a similar form, so too the conceptualization of existence is indeed purified by being drawn out through its own forms. || 48 ||
Just as those burned by fire are steamed [healed], so too those burned by the fire of passion are steamed again by the fire of passion. (49)
For by whatever means beings are bound through their fierce karma, by that very same means they are released from the bondage of existence. 50.
How is it that the downward wind (*apāna*) is the cause of wind? How is it contrary [to the flow]? This is the method of its conceptualization.

"Existence" (*bhava*) is *saṃsāra*; "purity" is completely exhausted. By "by existence itself" is meant that it comes about through the transformation of the marks of the moon and sun; thus, "existence" is the form of the deity. The meaning is that by that very [deity], it becomes exhausted.
Conceptual construction is saṃsāra; the meaning is that it becomes exhausted through conceptualization—that is, through the conceptualization of the form of a deity. || 47 ||
With the words "Water in the ear," etc., he provides an illustration; [he says] "in the same way," etc.
"Bhāva" refers to saṃsāra in the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
"By means of forms" means by means of the forms of the deities; "khalu" (indeed) signifies that there is no doubt. || 48 ||
"Yathā" and so forth:

"Passions" (rāga) are the afflictions (kleśa); these themselves are the fire. By that [fire], they are burnt, scorched, sweated, and ripened by the fire of passion—that is, by the cultivation of great passion (mahārāga), which is characterized by the non-duality of the bodies of wisdom (prajñā) and means (upāya). || 49 ||
"By whatever [means]" and so forth.
"Are bound" means they undergo bondage. "Fierce karma" refers to the harming of living beings and the like.
Skillful means is great compassion. || 50 ||
Second: *Hevajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā* The world is bound by passion; by passion alone it is liberated.
This is indeed a practice of the "perverse" (*viparītabhāvanā*), which has not been understood by the Buddhist outsiders (*buddhatīrthika*). (51)
In the sexual unions (kuṇḍalīs), there are five according to the nature of the five elements;
yet that which is one alone, the Great Bliss, undergoes a state of fivefold division through various distinctions. 52.
Through the union of *bola* and *kakkola*, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of solidity arises from contact;
because that which is solid has the nature of delusion (*moha*), delusion is considered to be Vairocana. (53)

Since the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is fluid, and the fluid element is considered to be the water element, and because water has the nature of Akṣobhya, hatred indeed has Akṣobhya as its leader. ||54||
"By passion" means by worldly passion (*laukikarāga*).

One is liberated by innate passion (*sahajarāga*), for that which is contrary [to it] has the nature of an adversary even to its own side. But in the ultimate sense, it is not merely one type of passion, but rather all worldly phenomena (*laukikadharma*).
"Not known" means that such a cultivation of great bliss has not been known—that is, it has not been realized—by the Buddhist outsiders (buddhatīrthika), such as the Śrāvakas and others.
How are they "Buddhist outsiders"?
Because of their intense aversion toward the Vajrayāna, which is the essence of the Blessed One’s teaching. (51)
By this much, it has been established that the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā arises through the meditation on the maṇḍala-circle.

Now, demonstrating that supreme great bliss itself takes the form of many families (*kula*), he says: "In the *kunduras*," and so forth. *Kunduras* are acts of sexual union (*surata*); "it would be" means they become; "five" refers to the five kinds of enjoyments (*sambhoga*).
"Having the nature of the five elements" means by way of the form of the five great elements, beginning with earth.
What, then, are those? "Only one" refers to the state of being five, that is, the fivefold aspect; "by divisions" means by the divisions of the five great elements. || 52 ||
"Bolakakkoletyādi" [and so forth].

The latent impression of solidity (*kāṭhinyavāsanā*), which is the cognition of solidity, is the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*); that very thing [is so called] because of the firmness of delusion (*moha*). || 53 ||
*Akṣobhya*—ka. kha. gha. ca. ṭa.
This additional reading, "they approach the Buddha as the Teacher," is found in the Tibetan manuscript.
*Kundureṣu*—gha.
The true nature of the elements—earth and so forth.

In the *Vajra-tantra*, in the chapter titled "The Determination of Siddhis": "From the friction and conjunction of the two, fire is always produced. Passion (*rāga*) is Amitavajra; passion arises within fire. (55)
The mind that resides within the *kakkolaka* is of the nature of wind;
for envy is Amoghasiddhi, and Amogha arises from wind. ||56||
Pleasure is passion, and that which is impassioned has the characteristic of space;
space is the Piśuna-vajra, and Piśuna is born from space. ||57||
The one great consciousness alone exists in five forms; from it, thousands upon thousands arise within the five families.
Therefore, this single-natured supreme eternal great bliss undergoes a fivefold state through the differentiation of the five mental states, such as passion and the rest. //59//
"Tejas" (fire) refers to heat; "raktatā" (redness) refers to passion, as fire is characterized by redness.
The form of "samīraṇa" (wind) consists in its possession of motion.
And here, envy [is associated with wind] because of the verbal root reading "īr-gatau" (to go). || 55-56 ||

Bliss (*sukha*) is the joy of sexual union (*suratānanda*); that itself is passion (*rāga*), because its characteristic is attachment; that itself is the "red" (*rakta*) world, because it colors [everything]. Its characteristic is space (*ākāśa*), because it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). Piśunavajra is Ratneśa, for he is "piśuna" (the informer) because he reveals the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). "Great mind" (*mahācitta*) refers to the mind whose form is great bliss; "five" refers to those very [elements] therein. (57–59)

Second: *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*. Equal to the sands of ten Ganges rivers are the assemblies of Tathāgatas within the single families;
indeed, within the assemblies of families there are many families, and within those families there are hundreds of families. (60)
And those hundreds of thousands of families become many great millions of families; within those families are innumerable families born from the family of supreme bliss. || 61 ||
The second chapter, titled "The Determination of Siddhis," from the *Hevajra-Ḍākinījāla-saṃvara*.
"Ten Gaṅgās," and so forth;

"in the single families" means in the families of the Tathāgatas and the families of the Saṃgha—that is, in the families of the Tathāgata-Saṃgha—and within the families of those Tathāgata-Saṃgha families, there are then hundreds of families. || 60 ||
There are hundreds of thousands and tens of millions of families, each distinct; others are beyond counting, yet all of them originate from the family of supreme bliss. || 61 ||

The *kula*s are the *ḍākinīs*, the *vajraḍākinīs*; their *jāla* is the assembly, the maṇḍala-circle. From that comes *saṃvara*, the supreme bliss; from that, the accomplishment (*siddhi*)—this is its definitive determination.
Thus ends the second chapter, the Determination of Accomplishment (*siddhinirṇayapaṭala*), in the *Hevajrapañjikā* composed by the venerable Kṛṣṇācārya, within the *Yogaratnamālā*.
"Equal to grains of sand" (bālukā-tulya), "equal to grains of sand"—Hevajrapañjaramahātantrarāja, Chapter 5, Verse 12;
"in thousands of families" (sahasra-kuleṣu)—K;
"many families" (aneka-kulāni)—Ka, Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Cha, Ja, Jha, Ṭa.

Great—ka. ga;
in the koṭi-families, the number—ka. kha. gha. cha; 0 asaṃkhya0—jha; "'ca" is not present—ka. ga. gha; in the families, the number—cha; 0 in the families, asaṃkhya—ja.
— Thus ends the second chapter, the Determination of Accomplishment (*siddhinirṇaya*), in the *Śrī Hevajra* [Tantra]. (Variants: *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*).
From the families (*kula*) arise further families; their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) become manifold. (Variant: *ka*, *bho*; others: "from the families, then the families arise").
The number of others is... (*ka*).
The Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā: That divine form shaped like the letter *E*, adorned in its center with the syllable *Vaṃ*, is the abode of all blisses and the jewel-casket of the Buddhas. (4)
Blisses arise there, differentiated by the distinctions of moments; from the knowledge of the moment, the knowledge of bliss is established in the syllable EṂ. ||5||
The diverse, the ripening, the crushing, and likewise the distinctive—yogins know these four moments as they truly are. (6)
The "variegated" (vicitra) is known as the manifold [acts] such as embracing and kissing; the "ripening" (vipāka) is the enjoyment of the knowledge of pleasure in the reverse of those [acts]. ||7||
To the question "How is it known that [it] is established?", he says: "It is known from the consecration," and so forth.

It is known through the instruction of the Guru; it is realized. Regarding the term "of the ḍākinīs": the verbal root *ḍai*, meaning "to move through the sky," is employed here; thus, it refers to the accomplishment of moving everywhere in space.

Because it has been explained by the Blessed One that "Ḍākinī" means "by the will of the Ḍākinīs," the Ḍākinīs are the Vajra-Ḍākinī yoginīs; [the work is called] *Saṃvara* because it is their concise compendium. (2–3)
In order to indicate the single form of the body, speech, and mind of all the Tathāgatas, there is the shape of the syllable *e*;

it is "divine" (*divya*) because they sport (*divyanti*) therein. The syllable *vaṃ* is the central hub (*varaṭaka*); that which is adorned and beautified by it is the "abode" (*ālaya*), meaning the support (*ādhāra*).
The "Jewel of the Buddha" refers to the casket of the five Tathāgatas, because it serves as their foundational form. (4)

In that very state, blisses (*ānanda*) arise in a single moment, differentiated by the divisions of *vicitra* and so forth. If it is asked, "If the blisses themselves are what are being differentiated, what is the use of differentiating the moments? he replies with the words beginning with "moment" (*kṣaṇa*).
The sense is that through the thorough knowledge of the essential nature of the moments, there arises the knowledge of the differentiation of the blisses; it is nothing else. || 5 ||
Demonstrating that very distinction of moments, he says "vicitra" and so forth:

"vividha" means various kinds of skill and the preparation of the teacher; "vipāka" and so forth; from that, "viparyāsa" means the opposite; and "of knowledge" refers to the knowledge of great bliss (*mahāsukha*); "bhuñjanam" means experiencing. (6–7)

The verse [is] established in Kha, split [between] Ka and Kha.
In the *Vajra-tantra*, the chapter titled "The Sandhyābhāṣā" states: "Vimarda is said to be the reflection [on the experience], thinking 'I have enjoyed bliss';
Vilakṣaṇa is other than the three, free from both passion and dispassion. (8)

In the *vicitra* [stage] there is the first bliss (*prathamānanda*); in the *vimarda*, the supreme bliss (*paramānanda*); and in the *vipāka*, which is characterized by the absence of marks (*vilakṣaṇa*), there is the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). || 9 ||
The teacher, the secret, the wisdom, and the fourth which is likewise; these joys are to be known respectively by the number of the four sprinklings. (10)
Through the purification by laughter, the Ācārya [is purified] in gazing; likewise, the Guhya in the attainment of hands; and that again, through wisdom, in the practice of the union of couples.

Regarding the passage beginning with "vimarda," *ālocana* is the recollection of what immediately preceded it; alternatively, *ālocana* is the perceptual nature of cognition, such as the ascertainment of a prior experience: "I have experienced pleasure."
"Distinctive" means that it is free from passion and dispassion, and devoid of both cyclic existence and nirvana, as previously stated in contrast to the three [preceding] states. || 8 ||

With the words beginning with "vicitra," he establishes the arrangement of the joys (*ānanda*) within the four empowerments (*seka*); the intention is that each joy also receives its respective name—Master (*ācārya*), Secret (*guhya*), Wisdom (*prajñā*), and Fourth (*caturtha*).

Therefore, he says "the joys and so forth" and so on, [meaning] "in sequence": the joy (*ānanda*) is the Master empowerment; supreme joy (*paramānanda*) is the Secret empowerment; the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*) is the Wisdom empowerment; and co-emergent joy (*sahajānanda*) is the Fourth empowerment.
Thus, in all four empowerments, one should understand that there are four moments and four joys according to the instruction on practice;
in this way, they are to be understood as being numbered as four. (9–10)

With the words beginning with "hasita" (laughter), he explains the purification of the initiations: in some *Kriyātantras*, there is laughter indicating the passion of the deities' wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*); through its purification is the *ācārya* initiation, that is, the master initiation.

In some *Caryātantras*, there is mutual gazing indicating the passion of wisdom and method; through its purification is the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*). In some *Yogatantras*, there is mutual embracing of wisdom and method; its purification is the wisdom initiation (*prajñābhiṣeka*).

The fourfold consecration (*seka*) is proclaimed for the sake of the accomplishment of sentient beings. It is called *seka* because by means of it one is sprinkled (*sicyate*) or bathed (*snāpyate*). [12] —ka| ānandādyāḥ — ka. kha. ga. gha. cha.ja.jha —kha.ga| Third: *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*.
Embracing with both hands a sixteen-year-old Prajñā, the sprinkling by the Ācārya is considered to arise from the union of the bell and the vajra. ||13||
The disciple, who has a beautiful face, large eyes, and is adorned with beauty and youth, should apply [the substance] to the mouth of the disciple with the thumb and the ring finger. 14.
But therein, the teacher should perform that which is of equal flavor within the sphere of the disciple; he should worship Prajñā, and having honored her, he should offer her [to him]. || 15 ||
In some cases, such as the *Anuttara* and other [tantras], there is the union of wisdom and means, which is the coitus (*dvandvasamāpatti*); its purification is the fourth consecration. || 11 ||

For this reason, the fourfold [initiation]—consisting of four types—is proclaimed. How so? Here, in this *Vajra-tantra*, which is authorized because it is the unsurpassed among the *Yoginī*-tantras, there is universal authority. Precisely for that purpose, for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings—that is, for their benefit—he speaks while demonstrating the meaning of the word "abhiṣeka": "That by which one is bathed (*snāpyate*) is an *abhiṣeka*"; it is designated as such in the sense that one is washed and rendered stainless. || 12 ||

With the words beginning "With the two hands," he states the definition of the Master’s Empowerment (*ācāryābhiṣeka*): the union of the bell and vajra in the hands, or of the lotus and thunderbolt, according to the oral instruction, constitutes the Master’s Empowerment. With the words beginning "O fair-faced one," he describes the nature of the Wisdom Consort for the sake of the Secret Empowerment (*guhyābhiṣeka*): with the thumb and ring finger—meaning with the thumb and ring finger of the left hand—one should cause the essence of the meditative union (*samāpatti*) to fall into the mouth of the disciple, preceded by the verses of the Secret Empowerment; this is one interpretation.

Alternatively, the *jyeṣṭhā* is the tongue and the *anāmikā* is the palate; with these two, one should cause the *bodhicitta* of the *prajñā* to descend into the mouth of the disciple’s *vajra*-jewel, and then one should explain that instruction. (13–14)
And therein, "one should act with equal flavor" (*samarasam*), and so forth;
"therein" (*tatra*) means in that very wisdom (*prajñā*), the instruction is stated.

"Equal and equal" (*samasamam*) means one should bring about the union of wisdom and method (*prajñopāya*) as the *bodhicitta* within the sphere of the disciple's experience. [The letters] *ka*, *kha*, and *ga* represent the causal nature (*hetutā*) for the sake of benefit (*hitahetave*). *Ga* refers to the causes.
*snāpyate* (ga), *snāpyete* (gha);
*vidhīyate* (ga);
*samāliṅgaye* (ka, gha), *samāliṅge* (kha).
Furthermore,
she has a beautiful face, a broad forehead, and large eyes.
Adorned with *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, and *tu*.
He causes *ga* to fall, *kha* to fall— thus he causes *ga* to fall.
Ca-ga-ṭa: O Lord, one should treat the disciple as equal to oneself;
[this portion does not exist in the manuscript labeled 'ka'].
He offered [it]—Kha.Ga. In some places, such as the beginning of the Uttara, Ka has "How? (katham); it does not exist in Bho Gaṇṭhāvajra Gha.
Thus it is said: In the *Vajra-tantra*, this is the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Sandhyā-bhāṣā" (Esoteric Language).
The Teacher should say: "O Great Being, take this seal which brings happiness, having recognized the disciple as one who has become great, devoid of movement, and free from anger. (16)
The Teacher commands him: "O Vajra-holder, perform the *kunduru*! I shall now declare the duties of the disciple and the procedure for the consecration. (17)
Having seen the Guru endowed with the mudrā, one should perform praise and worship as follows:
"O Blessed One, solely intent upon the Vajrayoga! (18)
O you who arise from the indivisible vajra-yoga that accomplishes the mudrās, just as you are great-souled beings, O Lord, perform that same act for me as well. (19)
This is the meaning of the secret consecration (*guhyābhiṣeka*).
"The Wisdom [Consort]" (*prajñā*) and so forth refers to one who possesses the characteristics prescribed in the tantras. "One should worship" means first; "the Teacher" (*śāstṛ*) refers to the Guru.
To examine whether or not they are capable of bearing the burden of performing difficult tasks, one should present them with the verse taught in the Tantra and to be mentioned hereafter. || 15 ||
"Take the mudrā"—this refers to the *dharmamudrā*. The *prajñā-abhiṣeka* consists of [the words] "having known," and so forth;
it is that which is great in being, capable of accomplishing the *mahāmudrā*, free from envy and stinginess, devoid of anger, and possessed of great compassion. || 16 ||

"He commands the disciple" means that he delivers an instruction; thus he says, "Perform *kundura*," which means "perform sexual union (*surata*), the attainment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā-samāpatti*);
O Vajradhṛk," meaning O Vajradhara.
Regarding the fourth consecration:
now, for the sake of the consecration, the propitiation of the disciple is described; beginning with "the duty of the disciple," one should offer supplication. (17)
"O Blessed One!"—this is praise of the Guru.
Because he abides in non-dual yoga, he is "greatly peaceful.
The yoga of the vajra, that is, the kuliśa, is a specific meditative attainment (*samāpatti*); he is devoted to that very reality, intent upon it. (18)

"O accomplisher of the mudrās": there are four mudrās; their "accomplisher" is the one who purifies them. Because his intrinsic nature is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), he is the indivisible Vajra Tathāgata. Their "yoga" is meditative absorption (*samādhi*);
"arising therein" means just as you are the cause of the welfare of the world, so too, O All-pervading Lord, O Master. (19)
Having heard the sound "kha" which brings happiness,
[he is] "kha"; having abandoned the great wonder "ṅa," he is "ga."

Kuru, Kundaru, Ka, Gha; and I shall explain Kunduru. Regarding the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one should supplicate as follows: Ka, Ga, Gha; supplicating for the consecration—Kha; one should supplicate: *hepaṃmuva*; *hepaṃ yoraṃā*. Regarding worship (*pūjā*): Ka; auspicious worship—Ga.
One should cause [it] to be made;
the Blessed One,
the Great Teacher.
*tatparaḥ* (kha, gha), *tatparam* (ga);
*samudbhavam* (kha), *bhedasamudbhavaḥ* (ga);
*yūyam* (ka); *mahātmanaḥ* (ṅa, ca), *mahāyānaḥ* (cha).
O you who possess the thunderbolt, you are indeed the earth and the patience [of the earth].
The Tathāgata Gha-vajra said: "Ka.
Gha, it is so; Ka."
[Third: I am submerged in the perilous straits of saṃsāra; O Refugeless One, save me! Delightful food, drink, and edibles, intoxicants, and great strength— ||20||
With incense, food offerings, garlands, bells, banners, and ointments—with these acts of worship and the like—the disciple should worship the Holder of the Vajra. (21)
When supreme bliss, devoid of all diversity, has been attained in that moment, the Teacher should say: "O Great Being, this great happiness is to be maintained. (22)
"O Vajradhṛk, act for the benefit of sentient beings until the limit of enlightenment"—thus does the Vajrin speak to the disciple during the sequence of initiation rites. (23)
"Quagmire" means the quagmire of *saṃsāra*, which is a mass or a collection; "I am submerged therein—save me! implies "save me who am without refuge.
"Sweet" is the general term for food, drink, and edibles that are delicious; "intoxicating" is the specific description of their power as being exceedingly great. || 20 ||
The Guru, the holder of the Vajra, the holder of non-dual gnosis. || 21 ||

Having awakened the disciple by means of the verse beginning with "supreme bliss" (*paramānanda*) and ending with "arisen" (*samutpanna*), which refers to the fourth state called the Innate (*sahaja*) that transcends [the others] and is free from multiplicity, and having addressed him as "Great Being" (*mahāsattva*), he should give the instruction regarding the Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*)— which is to be maintained through the verse to be spoken beginning with "this knowledge is extremely subtle" (*idaṃ jñānaṃ mahāsūkṣmam*)— in accordance with the oral teaching. || 22 ||
By the words "as far as" (*yāvad*) and so forth, he indicates the gnosis whose characteristics are about to be described.
Having consecrated [the disciple] with initiations through the accumulation of all rites—that is, through the collection of rituals—the Vajra-holder, the Guru, should speak thus. (23)
The mire of saṃsāra, the heap, the fear, the refuge, the path, and the destruction of passion— ka, kha, ga, gha.
Mahattara: Gha for incense (kha.ga), Puṣpa for gha, Naivedya for ka.kha.ga.gha.
O bird, one should perform anointment with these [substances]: with these offerings— ka, gha, cha, he, paṃmuva— one worships (pūjataḥ) ga, and for those who worship (pūjānaḥ),
there is supreme bliss (paramānandeṣu) gha.

When it has been attained—ga; when it has been attained—gha; when it has arisen, the great beings (mahāsattva) experience the supreme great bliss (mahāsukha)—hepaṃ yoraṃā ka. gha mahāsukhaṃ—hepaṃ yoraṃā.

Having observed the accumulation of compassion—ṅaca; having initiated those to be initiated with the accumulation of ritual actions—jha, ña; having observed—bho; with the accumulation of all ritual actions—hepaṃ yoraṃā saṃpātaḥ—gha (in the reading of Snellgrove); in the assembly—hetu; and "to be consumed"—this is the designation—gha; "attained"—bho; indeed called "the innate"—ka. This very great gnosis is in the Hevajra Tantra.

[The Chapter on Intentional Language (Sandhyābhāṣā): The Lord, who is established within all bodies, shines as both non-dual and dual in form, consisting of existence and non-existence, and remaining pervading the stable and the moving. Having the nature of *māyā*, he abides pervasively; and through the means of the mandalas, cakras, and so forth, he attains certainty through continuity. ||24–25||

Then, having obtained the forgiveness of all the yoginīs and sisters, Vajragarbha addressed the Blessed One in this way: "What is called the mandala-circle, the city consisting of the essence of all Buddhas?
May the Blessed Ones teach it according to the proper method; an error occurred to me. (26)

The Blessed One said: "The maṇḍala is said to be the essence; it is the great bliss of the bodhicitta. Because it performs that taking up (*ādāna*), it is considered a maṇḍala, which is understood as 'grinding' (*malana*). (27)

To the question "What is that?", he says: "This very [is it]. It is the Great Knowledge (*mahājñāna*) obtained through consecration (*abhiṣeka*), because it is innate (*sahaja*). "In all bodies" means it is established within the body of the four seals (*caturmudrā*).
It is non-dual, devoid of the appearance of the duality of wisdom and means. Its dual form is the nature of those two, consisting of existence and non-existence;
thus, it is the Lord, the nature of supreme joy (*paramānanda*) and the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*), being the primary among the three joys.
The meditation on the *dharmasamayamudrā* is stable, while the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) with the external *mudrā* is mobile;
pervading all of this,
he remains as one who possesses an illusory form (*māyārūpin*), like one produced through various emanations.

If one asks, "By what means, then, does he attain continuity? the author says: "The mandala," and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is an inclusion of the instruction on the two mudrās, the resolve of the solitary hero (ekavīra), and others.
Regarding the word "atha" (then): by the term "maṇḍalacakra," the instruction on Mahāmudrā is meant; "mṛṣitvā" means having asked for forgiveness; "āha" means he questioned.
"Puram" is that which is filled by all the Buddhas;
"kimiti" means "why" or "for what reason."
"Maṇḍala," and so forth. The word *maṇḍala* is a synonym for *sāra* (essence). What is that essence? He says: *bodhicitta*. [Regarding the term *mīlaṃ*: *ka*; *maṇḍalaṃ mīlanaṃ*:

*kha*, *ga*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*, *he0paṃ0 yo0ra0mā0*, *he0paṃ0mu0va0*; *milanaṃ*: *bho0*. Regarding *paramānanda-ananda-viramānanda*: *bho0*. Third: The *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā* states: "The *cakra* is the assembly (*nivaha*) called the *khadhātu* (space-element), which is the purification of the sense objects and so forth."
Through the application of *bola* and *kakkola*, his bliss is realized.

Vajragarbha asked: "By what vow? By what commitment (samaya) should one abide? The Blessed One replied: "You must kill living beings, you must speak false words, you must take what is not given, and you must consort with the wives of others."
Since the single mind is considered the life-force of living beings,
I shall deliver the worlds; that which is called false speech is the semen of women, and what is not given is another's wife— yet one's own consort is beautiful.

"Great Bliss" (*mahāsukha*) is characterized by the joy arising from the destruction of all suffering produced by the primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśa* and *upakleśa*). "Taking up" (*ādāna*) means making it one's own. "That" refers to the gnosis of Great Bliss; "union" (*mīlana*) is the assembly of all Buddhas. Therefore, the meaning is the ultimate mandala.

The "wheel" (cakra) is the characteristic of great bliss; the "multitude" (nivaha) is compassion; the "space-element" (khadhātu) is the emptiness of all phenomena. The purity of the sense objects and so forth is the luminosity (prabhāsvara), which is the single-flavored nature of those two.
The *bola* is the mind-vajra consisting of great compassion;
the *kakkola* is the primordial nature of all phenomena.

The meaning is as follows: their union according to the instruction is "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*); by means of that, one attains the bliss of the Mahāmudrā, which is characterized by luminosity (*prabhāsvara*). Thus is the intended sense.
Being fully satisfied, Vajragarbha said; for what purpose did he say this? He spoke it because the commitment (*samaya*) and restraint (*saṃvara*) of that unsurpassed yoga had not yet been stated.
For that purpose, he gave the summary beginning with "living beings" (*prāṇinaḥ*).
This is its explanation: "single-mindedness" and so forth.
Single-mindedness is the attainment of the luminosity of the mind. To explain how that itself constitutes the taking of life, he says: "the vital breath," and so forth.
Since the mind is the life-force, its non-arising alone is its destruction;

[thinking] "I shall deliver the world," etc., is false from the perspective of ultimate reality because the world of sentient beings is not perceived. This is the chapter named *Sandhyābhāṣa*. Then all the Yoginīs said this to the Blessed One: "What, then, are those objects? What are the sense-faculties? What is the base? Which are the aggregates? And who, O Blessed One, are they? The Blessed One replied: "The six objects..."
Regarding these elements: what is their smell, taste, and likewise their touch, and what is their intrinsic nature?
Form, sound, as well as the nature of the dharma-element, and the six sense faculties—
these six are considered the objects.
The eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and likewise the mind—
these six sense faculties are joined with the vajras of delusion and the other [afflictions].
O Great Compassionate One, through the object and the subject, there are the twelve bases (āyatanas), as well as the five aggregates (skandhas) beginning with form and ending with consciousness.
The intended meaning is as follows:
"women" refers to the *vajra*-women; their "semen" is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). Since that is obtained through the cultivation of the non-dual path, it is therefore "not given.
One's own consort (*svābhā*), such as Sundarī or Nairātmyā and so forth—how could she be another's wife? Because her form is supremely excellent.
"Of these" refers to the objects and so forth; "endowed with Mohavajrā and the others" refers to these six, the eye and the rest, as will be explained.
The objects are those beginning with form and ending with mental formations; the subjects are the eye and so forth, up to mental formations; and consciousness is mentioned in between them.

Third: The *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā* states that the sense faculties, their objects, and the consciousnesses of the sense faculties are declared to be the eighteen elements for the awakening of the yoginīs.
The intrinsic nature is unarisen from the beginning; it is neither real nor false.
All things are like the moon reflected in water—thus do the yoginīs know them according to their will.
For example, depending upon the fire-drill wood, the base-wood, and the exertion of a person’s hands, fire is produced;
yet this fire does not abide in the fire-drill wood, nor in the base-wood, nor in the exertion of a person’s hands.
When thoroughly investigated in every way, that fire does not exist even in a single respect; it is neither real nor unreal.
O yoginīs, contemplate all phenomena in this manner. 37.
Then all the Vajra-Ḍākinīs, headed by Nairātmyābhyoginī, taking the five nectars and the samaya-substances, worship the Blessed One Vajrasattva;
they arouse passion through the *kunduru* yoga and drink the essence of the vajra-amrita. 38.
"Of the yoginīs" means of the beginner yoginīs; "for the sake of awakening" means for the purpose of instruction. || 35 ||
What is their intrinsic nature? It is "originally unarisen," meaning that from the very beginning their nature is non-arising.
How do they appear, and so forth? [The answer is:
"neither true nor false. Just as they appear, because they are unreal (*alīka*), they are neither true nor false.
"Like the moon in water," and so forth; because that which has one nature appears otherwise, "knowing" means "you should know. "By desire" means "governed by desire. || 36 ||

The fire-drill wood (*kāṇḍa*), the upper friction-stick (*uttarāraṇī*), and the lower friction-stick (*mathanīya*); the human effort and activity [involved]—these are "accidental" (*akasmāt*) in the sense that, even though they exist, [the fire] is not perceived [until the rubbing occurs].
It is not real because it lacks a nature that is either unitary or manifold.
"It is not false," because it appears as such;
"attend to it," thus one should hold it in the mind. || 37 ||
He causes [them] to drink, he causes [them] to drink the vajra-amṛta, the essence of bodhicitta. || 38 ||
Then, in the Vajra Tantra, when the Blessed One was satisfied, he displayed his empowerment:
"O, O Vajra-Ḍākinīs! I shall speak of the reality that has been kept secret by me and is venerated by all the Buddhas; through the power of the Vajra-worship, listen as you desire. (39)
Then all the goddesses, filled with enthusiasm, placed their right knees upon the ground and, bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, listened to what the Blessed One had said.

The Blessed One said: "One should consume food and drink as they are obtained; one should not avoid women who are approachable or unapproachable; one should not perform ritual bathing or purification; and one should not avoid sexual intercourse. || 41 ||
One should not rely upon meditative absorption (dhyāna), nor upon the senses; one should neither abandon sleep nor attempt to suppress the senses. ||42||
One should enjoy all that is to be consumed and all women with a fearless mind; one should practice the five colors [of the maṇḍala]. ||43||

"When she is pleased" means when she is satisfied by the practice characterized by the utter absence of conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), through which Vajrasattva becomes empowered; the sense is that he "shows," meaning he reveals, empowerment.
"Reality" (*tattva*) is so called because it is the cause for attaining reality. "Vajra-worship" is so called because of its firmness.
With desire and with respect. || 39 ||
The speech of the Blessed One is the word of the Blessed One. || 40 ||
In the *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*: "One should not cultivate affection for friends, nor should one practice hatred toward those who hate;
one should not pay homage to these gods made of wood, stone, or clay.
For a yogin must always abide in the form of the deity. [One should likewise treat] the Domba, Caṇḍāla, leather-worker, butcher, and others who are difficult to touch..."
One should touch the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others as if they were one's own body. || 45 ||
The five nectars, molasses, wine, poison, neem, that which is born of a woman, and the sour, sweet, and astringent tastes, as well as the bitter, salty, and pungent; || 46 ||
One should consume the foul-smelling and fragrant substances—water and blood—with the *bodhicitta*;
there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be consumed by the mind of non-dual gnosis.
Having obtained the self-arisen flower, one should place it within the vessel of the lotus.
But the observer of the vow should drink phlegm and snot mixed together. 48.
Having obtained a multi-colored loincloth and ornaments made of clay shards, as well as flowers from a cemetery, one should bind the excellent hair on the head. 49.
"By the thought of awakening" (bodhicittena) means by the thought that has attained awakening; or alternatively, the thought of the non-arising of all phenomena is the thought of awakening.
He says the same thing with the words "by the mind of non-dual gnosis" (advayajñānacetaseti). || 47 ||
The abode of pretas is the cremation ground;
"mūrdhaja" means hair. || 49 ||
In the Vajra Tantra, the chapter titled "Sandhyābhāṣā" (Esoteric Language): Then Vajragarbha said: "The sense faculties, indeed numbering six, are unrefined;
the Blessed One has taught that the purification of all objects [is achieved through them]. (50)
The Blessed One said: Delusion-vajrī resides in the eyes, Hatred-vajrī in the two ears, Envy-vajrī is known to be in the nose, and Attachment-vajrī in the mouth. || 51 ||
Īrṣyāvajrā is for touch, and Nairātmyayoginī is for the mind;
O Mahāsattva, with these [mantras] one performs the armor-rite for the purification of the sense faculties. ||52||

Vajragarbha said: "O Blessed One, please explain with certainty what is called 'twilight language' (sandhyābhāṣa)—the great pledge (mahāsamaya) of the yoginīs, which is not breached by the śrāvakas and others. (53)
Smiling with the eyes, embracing, and likewise the pair-by-pair union—even by means of the fourfold tantra—it is not expressed in literal words; this is the symbolic language (sandhyābhāṣa).

"Indriyāṇi," and so forth. Previously purified in the form of deities: "of all objects" means of the entire mandala of the knowable (*jñeya*). Mohavajrī is Vajrā; Dveṣavajrī is Nairātmyā; Mātsaryavajrī is Guptagaurī; Rāgavajrī is Vāriyoginī; Īrṣyāvajrī is Vajraḍākinī. (50–52)

"Sandhi" means intention; the meaning is that speech is primarily concerned with intention, not primarily with the literal syllables. "Great convention" (mahāsamaya) refers to a secret sign that is neither disclosed nor characterized. || 53 ||
By the words "hasita" and so forth, he declares its extreme secrecy;
"of the four" refers to Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, and Yogottara; "not spoken" means it was not told. || 54 ||

The Blessed One said: "O Vajragarbha, I shall explain the intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣa*) and the great language; listen with a one-pointed mind to the detailed exposition of the conventions of the pledge (*samaya*). (55)
Madana is considered to be wine, bala is meat, and malayaja is the meeting; gati is the planet, śava is food, and her ornament is nudity. || 56 ||
Āgati is said to be the swing (preṅkhaṇa); kṛpīṭa is considered the hand-drum (ḍamaruka). Abhavya is known as the small drum (dunduru), while bhavya is considered the kāliñjara. ||57||
The drum without touch is proclaimed; the skull is the lotus vessel;
the food to be known is that which provides satisfaction; and the fuel is the *mālatī* flower. (58)
Feces is said to be the "fourfold equal" (catuḥsama), urine is known as musk; the self-arisen (svayambhū) is to be understood as the "fourfold equal," and semen is considered camphor. (59)
Mahāmāṃsa is said to be *sālija*, the union of the two organs is *kunduru*;
*vajra* is known as *bolaka*, and *padma* is considered to be *kakkolaka*. (60)
The family is known to be fivefold, divided according to the distinction of castes; thus, through the intentional language (sandhyābhāṣā), there are the Buddhas and the five Kaulikas.
"Kula," and so forth; it is fivefold, of five types. The Buddhas will explain that in the language of intentional terminology (*sandhyābhāṣā*); they shall be the five Kaulikas. || 61 ||

In the *Vajratantro*, [the chapter titled] "The Sandhyābhāṣa": "The *ḍombī* is known as belonging to the Vajra family; likewise, the *naṭī* belongs to the Padma family. The *caṇḍālī* belongs to the Ratna family, and the *dvijā* is considered to belong to the Tathāgata family. (62)
The washerwoman and the woman of the artisan caste—these mudrās grant excellent accomplishment. Having worshipped them, the practitioner of the vow should drink their semen, which is the vajra. 63.
"O Vajragarbha, Great Being, whatever I have spoken to you—all that should be respectfully grasped as the most wonderful intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣa*). (64)"

Whoever has been consecrated here in this Hevajra [tantra] and does not speak in the sandhyābhāṣā (intentional language), for him there arises a violation of the samaya; of this there is no doubt. (65)
If he does not explain the intentional terminology (*sandhyābhāṣā*), even one who is enlightened may die from calamities, thieves, planetary afflictions, fever, poison, and the like. (66)
"Ḍombī," and so forth; "kulī" means family (kula), as it is known in the *Yoginītantras*. Why are these [goddesses] called families? Because they bestow excellent accomplishment (*susiddhi*).
"Vajra" refers to the cause for attaining vajra-gnosis; "having worshipped" means by means of the union of the lotus and the vajra. (62–63)
"O Vajragarbha," and so forth; "O Mahāsattva" refers to one who observes the commitments (samaya). || 64 ||
Betrayal of the samaya is the violation of the samaya. || 65 ||
These are the two types of diseases; their "upadrava" refers to the affliction or suffering caused by them. || 66 ||

[The third chapter: *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*. If one who knows their own samaya does not speak these words after having obtained [this teaching], then the yoginīs born of the four seats (*pīṭha*) will cause agitation. (67) *Samayavidrohana*: ka, gha; *saṃśayat*: ga. *Iti upadravacaureśca*: ka, gha; *iti upadravacoreśca*: ga; this portion "iti upadrava" does not exist [in some versions]. *Bhāṣayet*: kha, ga. *Samayaviddohanam*: ka. *Itayo*: ka. [End of] the third [chapter]. *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*. If one who knows their own samaya does not speak these words after having obtained [this teaching], then the yoginīs born of the four seats (*pīṭha*) will cause agitation. (67)
The third chapter, titled "The Esoteric Language of the Introduction to All Tantras of Hevajra."
"Of those who know their own samaya" means: having attained agitation, that is, hatred, [toward] the Hevajra yogins. (67)

He is the source of all tantras and the illuminator of the intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣa*). Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Intentional Language," in the second section of the *Yogaratnamālā*, a commentary on the *Hevajra* composed by the venerable Kṛṣṇācārya.

[The section on] the regulation of life—ka; and—ka. There is no [other work]; this is the fourth chapter, titled "The Summary Meaning of the Seals of All Tantras of Hevajra. Then all the ḍākinīs, headed by Vajragarbha, having fallen into doubt and fallen into despondency, spoke thus to the Blessed One, Vajrasattva: "May the Blessed One dispel our doubt! (1)
Regarding that which was taught in the Caryāpaṭala—song and dance that bestow accomplishment—I have a doubt concerning them: what is song, and what is dance? (2)

Regarding that which was taught concerning the sealing with hatred and the other [passions] following the consecration by the deities, a doubt arises in me: what is to be sealed, and by whom is the sealing performed? (3)
Regarding the seed-syllable of Nairātmyā and the others that was proclaimed in the Mantra-paṭala, a confusion has arisen within me: which is the seed, and for whom is it the seed-syllable? (4)
May the Blessed Ones explain the purification of those channels consisting of thirty-two, which are proclaimed in the *Kulapaṭala*; an error has occurred in my [understanding].
"Then," and so forth. "Led by Vajragarbha" means having Vajragarbha as their precursor.
"Doubt" means uncertainty. || 1 ||
Why is there doubt? Because common song and drama are of the nature of opposites. || 2 ||
"By the consecration of the deity" refers to the Chapter on the Consecration of the Deity; for it is stated there: "Being consecrated upon the head, one becomes the Lord of one's own family.
"Mudrā" means sealing. || 3 ||
"What is the seed?"—of what is that the seed, and why? The meaning is: "How did this delusion and lack of full knowledge regarding the deity arise? (4-5)

To all the Vajra-Ḍākinīs—ga. "Nāsti" (is not present) in the manuscripts *ka* and *gha*. "Dormanasprāptā"—*ṅa*, *ca*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*. Then, "bhaga0"—*ka*; "bhagavan"—*ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*. "Apanayantu"—*kha*, *gha*. "Paṭalam"—*kha*. "Siddhitam"—*gha*. "Sandeha"—*ka*, *gha*; "sandehe"—*ga*. "Devatāsekato"—*ka*, *kha*, *gha*; "yaśca"—*ka*, *gha*. "0mudranam"—*ga*; "0mudranām"—*gha*. "Nāsti"—*kha*. "Sandeha"—*ka*, *gha*. "Mudrām"—*ka*, *ga*, *gha*, *jha*; "mudram"—*cha*, *ja*. "Mantradvāre ca"—*ka*, *kha*, *gha*; "mantre dhāre ca"—*ga*. "Nairātmādevī tu"—*ka*, *gha*; "nairātmāṃ devīśca"—*kha*; "nairātmādevaśca"—*ga*. "Bhrānta"—*ka*, *ga*; "bhrāntam"—*gha*. "Kulapaṭalam"—*ga*. "0ṣoḍaśātmakāḥ"—*ka*, *gha*. "Teṣām"—*ga*.
