"Kathayante"—*ga*. "Prākṛta vā gītanāṭyayoḥ"—*ka*. "Devābhiṣeka0"—*gha*. "Mūrddhayām"—*ka*, *gha*; "mudrayamiti"—*gha*. [End of] Fourth [Chapter]. The Blessed One said: "Residing at Kollaira is the *bola*; at Mummuṇi is the *kakkola*. O thick one, the *kiviḍara* is being blown; compassion is practiced, not *rolā*. (6)

There, excellent food is eaten and strong liquor is drunk; O friend, on Mount Kāliñjara, the Dunduru drum is beaten there. Four-fold sandalwood, camphor, and musk are applied; there, the finest incense and Śāliñja rice are consumed. || 7 ||
Kollagiri is a specific sacred seat (pīṭha).
Mummuṇi is a field (kṣetra); the term "Bolakakkolet" indicates the meeting of the yogin and yoginī characterized by it, even though they are situated far apart.
"Ghaṇa" means continuously; "ki piṭaṃ" refers to a hand-drum (ḍamaruka).
"Compassion" means that due to mutual affection born of compassion, no harshness or clamor is produced. || 6 ||
To the question "Why is that not done?", he says:
"With force," and so forth. "Firmly" means as intensely as possible. "O Hales" is an address to the yoginīs.
"Kāliñjaras" refers to those who observe the *samaya* vows; "Dunduras" refers to those who do not observe the *samaya*.
The fourfold commitments (*samaya*) are taken up; there, at that gathering, they are consumed with intensity, as in the phrase "eat [it] thoroughly.
The pure one is the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*), and the impure one is the beginner (*ādikarmika*); both of these are not known [by others].
The syllable *ai* is placed upon the *aṅgacaḍāvī*.
Therein, the word *jeti* means that the *śarāva* vessel is also to be inserted; this is the sense. By this much, there are four *gāthās*, each consisting of four quarters.
At the end of each of the four verses, the refrain should be sung.
He states that very point: "O Malaya-born one," and so forth, at Kollagiri.

The ego (*ahaṅkāra*) situated on the head is *bola*; *kollayire*—*kha*, *jha*; *kollagiraṃ*—*kollagiriḥ*—*ka*; *kakkolo*—*ka*. *Kipiṭṭi*—*ka*, *gha*; *kibiḍa*—*kha*; *kībiḍa*—*ga*; *kiviṭa*—*bho0*. *Kia*—*jha*, *bho0*. *Tahiṃ*—*bho0*. *Bala*—*ka*, *gha*. *Khajjai*—*bho0*. *Gāḍe*—*jha*; *gāḍem*—*bho0*. *Pijiai*—*ka*; *pijjii ai*—*bho0*; *pijjaai*—*paṇeai*—*ka*, *gha*. [This phrase] does not exist in the manuscripts *ka* and *gha*. *Causama*—*ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*. *Kasturi*—*ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *cha*, *jha*; *kacchuri*—*ṅa*; *kācchuri*—*bho0*. [The word] "does not exist" (*nāsti*)—*ka*, *gha*. *Iai*—*ka*, *gha*. *Mālatī*—*ka*, *gha*. *Śāri*—*ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*. *Naru*—*ka*, *gha*. From affection (*vātsalyāt*)—*ka*. The letter "na" is absent—*ka*. "As it happens, he drinks"—*bho0*. They conclude with "causama"—*bho0*. *Tarhi*—*ka*. *Āśuddha*—*ka*. *Śarāya*—*ka*. *Brūvakaṃ*—*ka*, *gha*. In the *Vajratantre*, [the chapter titled] "The Meaning of the Pith of Mudrās": One does not know the pure or impure in the swinging cradle (*preṅkhaṇa*), the shield (*kheṭa*), or the dance (*karante*). There, the arrow (*sarāva*) is offered upon the body of the one who has no water (*niraṃsuara*). On Mount Malaya, the *kunduru* is prepared; at that time, the drum (*ḍiṇḍima*) is struck. (8)
The dance is performed in the form of Śrī Heruka through the yoga of undistracted mindfulness, with a mind of passion and a consciousness of uninterrupted practice. ||9||
The meditation is on *mummuṇi* at the navel; the syllable *aṃ* is the *kakkola*. From the union of these two, the *ghana*—the uninterrupted *anāhata* sound—surges forth as the *bāja*.

"Compassion" (*karuṇā*) means that it is neither performed nor not performed by the yogin. "In the *rolā*" refers to the external sexual union (*suratamudrā*). Therein, "force" (*bala*) means that the nature of the self (*ātmabhāva*) is consumed—that is, rendered non-perceptible—and "madana is drunk" means that the drink of great bliss born of yoga (*yogaja-mahāsukha-pāna*) is consumed.
The wind is Kāliñjara;
it is introduced into the interior by the merchant.
The dundubhas are the afflictions, such as passion and the rest.
The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) consists of four equal parts:

musk is feeling (*vedanā*), ambergris is perception (*saṃjñāna*), camphor is consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the act of cleansing with *lāiai* is the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). The self (*ātman*) is the vibration of egoity (*ahaṃkāra*) within all these.
"Therein" (*tahi*) means that in that yoga, [the self] is consumed, which is to say, rendered devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvīkriyate*). || 7 ||
"Pekhaṇakheḍa" refers to the coming (*preṅkhaṇa*) of the fluid of *bodhicitta* from great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and its going (*kheṭa*) again.
The meaning is that "pure and impure" are not known as existence and non-existence.
Therefore, due to their similarity to a *niraṃśuka* (a fine silken cloth), the drops of semen are called *niraṃśukāḥ*.
The word *aṅga* means that [the practice] is ascended by means of the channels (*nāḍī*) of each limb.
In that yoga, the meaning is that entry is made into the "all-dharmas-selflessness" (sarvadharmanairātmya), which is like a vessel for sale.
*Malayaja* refers to the confluence of the channels.
The *ḍiṇḍima* is the "non-apprehension of all things" (*sarvānupalambha*) samādhi. It is not to be avoided; rather, it is made one's own. 8.
Regarding "the dance" and so forth: the nature of Heruka is the form of Heruka.
How is it by means of that?
Through the yoga of unimpaired mindfulness, there is firm meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
He says that very thing: "cultivation," and so forth. || 9 ||
Fourth: By Vajradharma and the Buddhas, by the Yoginīs and the Mothers, this supreme [reality] is sung and danced through these two—song and dance. 10.
By this very [mantra], there is protection for the community as well as protection for oneself;
by this very [mantra], one gains mastery in the world, and likewise, the recitation of the mantra is performed by this very [mantra]. (11)
Where [the deity] is sung of with devotion and where he is danced for with devotion,
placing the Lord of the Gaṇas at the forefront, there one should observe the sense of smell.
One should perceive garlic as the first scent, then the vulture-scent,
then camphor, then sandalwood, and thereafter the locus of the Gītā.
The cry of a swan or the song of a bee may be heard as a remnant of music; furthermore, one should observe even the sound of a jackal in the outer garden. (14)
Sealing, the mark of the *liṅga*, and the family (*kula*) are identified by the insignia (*aṅka*).
One whose family is disordered through the yoga of contemplation attains neither accomplishment nor the status of a practitioner. (15)
"By the Vajra-dharmas" means by way of the form of Padmanarteśvara; "by the Buddha" means by way of the form of Vairocana.
"By the Mothers" means by the Blessed Ladies such as Nairātmyā and others.
"By these two" refers to those possessing the aforementioned characteristics; "supreme," and so forth. 10.
"Protection of the gaṇa" means protection of the gaṇacakra; "subjugation" (vaśam) means being brought under control; by this very [formula], the recitation of the mantra is accomplished.
"Smell" (ghrāṇam) means fragrance. || 11–12 ||
The substratum of song is the *yoginīs*; its characteristic mark is the sign. "Sound" refers to the noise;

the substratum of the song of the swan and the bee is heard from the remainder [of the passage]. The jackal (*gomāyu*) is the *śṛṅgāla*. In the outer garden—and by the word "also," even in the sky—by this much, the questions regarding song and dance have been answered. || 14 ||
To provide a response to the second [question], he says "sealing" (*mudraṇa*) and so forth; "sealing," "embracing" (*liṅgana*), and "limb" (*aṅga*) are synonyms.

By that sealing, one is characterized or recognized. To the question "What would result from this?", he says: "The meditation on the individual families and so forth... In the *Vajratantre*, in the chapter titled "The Summary Meaning of Sealing," it is said: "Nairātmyā by means of the Hatred-seal (*dveṣamudrā*), and Vajrā by means of the Delusion-seal (*mohamudrā*)."
One should seal Gaurī with the Piśuna-mudrā, and Vārī with the Rāga-mudrā. || 16 ||
One should worship Ḍākinī with the mudrā of envy, Pukkasī from the mudrā of hatred, Śavarī with the mudrā of delusion, and Caṇḍālī with the mudrā of malice. ||17||
One should worship Ḍombī with the mudrā of passion (rāga), Gaurī again with hatred (dveṣa), Caurī with the mudrā of delusion (moha), and Vetālī with the mudrā of malice (piśuna). || 18 ||
One should know the sealing by one's own desire: Ghasmarī with the seal of passion (rāga), Bhūcarī with the seal of delusion (moha), and Khecarī with the seal of passion. ||19||
The first is Āle, Nairātmyā; the second is Vajrāle;
the third is Āle; and the fourth is Gaurī, the Water Yoginī. ||20||
When there is yoga through meditative cultivation, if it is [otherwise] sealed, there is neither accomplishment nor a practitioner, due to the violation of the pledge (samaya).
Therefore, the intended meaning is that one must exert effort in the thorough knowledge of the *kula*. || 15 ||
"Selflessness," and so forth: hatred is Akṣobhya, delusion is Vairocana, malicious speech is Ratnasambhava, and passion is Amitābha. || 16 ||
Envy is Amoghasiddhi.
Regarding "Pukkasī," and so forth: Pukkasī, Śavarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī [are associated] with hatred, delusion, envy, and passion. 17.
Furthermore, one should know that "Gaurī" refers to the female gatekeeper; Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, and Ghasmarī correspond respectively to hatred, delusion, envy, and passion.
Bhūcarī is associated with delusion, Khecarī with passion, and Icchā with devotion. || 19 ||
To provide the third response, he says "āleḥ" and so forth: "āleḥ ādiḥ" means the letter *a*; "nairātme" means the seed-syllable of Nairātmyā. || 20 ||
The fourth is the Vajrapañjikā-Yogaratnamālā; the fifth is considered to be Vajraḍākī; the sixth is Pukkasī; the seventh is Śavarī; and the eighth is remembered as Caṇḍālī. || 21 ||
The ninth is Ḍombinī, and Gaurī again is the tenth;
Caurī is known as the eleventh, and Vetālī is considered the twelfth. || 22 ||
Ghasmarī is the thirteenth, Bhūcarī the fourteenth, and Khecarī the fifteenth; these are the own-seeds (svabījaka) of the Yoginīs.
Regarding the channels described in the Chapter on the Family as being of sixteenfold nature:
it is held that every two channels correspond respectively to one Yoginī. (24)
Lalanā, Rasanā, and Avadhūtī are considered to be the Yoginīs of Nairātmyā;
one should diligently abandon all the remaining [channels], because the sixteenth digit does not exist there. (25)

Because it does not perform purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), the *bodhicitta* becomes the moon consisting of fifteen digits; its form is *ālī*, which is great bliss, and the *yoginīs* are its rays. (26)
There are thirty-two, two channels each, with one Yoginī in each;
"successively" means in due order. || 24 ||
The three channels beginning with *lalanā* and the Yoginī Nairātmā constitute exactly fifteen Yoginīs.
This is what is meant: Vajragarbha said in the *Vajratantre*, in the chapter titled "The Summary Meaning of Sealing": "Why indeed should camphor not be abandoned? It arises from all the Yoginīs;
it is the nature of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), imperishable, full, and moving through space. (27)
Vajragarbha said: "By what means should the bodhicitta be generated? (28)
By means of the maṇḍala circle and so forth, and through the process of self-consecration, one should generate the bodhicitta, which consists of both the ultimate and the conventional aspects. (29)
[She is] Caṇḍikā Māradārikā of the house, known as the Khecarī Yoginī.
[An objection: "But there are thirty-two nāḍīs; by half of that, the *āli* consists of sixteen kalās. Whence, then, are there fifteen yoginīs?
To this, he says: "All," and so forth.
One should abandon everything else;
the meaning is that this [other] is not the true nature of the Yoginī.
Why? He says: "the sixteenth," and so forth; because she has no parts (*kalā*), she is "partless" (*akalā*).

For instance, in the bright fortnight, there are exactly fifteen lunar digits according to the sequence of the lunar days (*tithi*). While the sixteenth digit performs a causal function (*arthakriyā*) for the sake of indicating the increase through light and so forth, it is the cause of waning; therefore, one should diligently abandon it.
To the question "What is that?", he says: "The bodhicitta," and so forth. (25–26)
"Camphor," and so forth; "what? is used in the sense of deliberation (*vitarka*).
"It is not to be abandoned" means it is not to be relinquished; "arising from all the yoginīs" means arising from all the channels (*nāḍī*);
"having the nature of innate bliss" means being the cause of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).
It is imperishable because it arises again and again; it is full because it abides in all bodies;
and it is called "sky-goer" (khaga) because it moves in the sky, which is the womb (yoni). 27.
"As you have said" means that this [practice] must not be abandoned.
"The mandala circle and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," it is meant elsewhere through the cultivation of union (*sayogabhāvanā*).
This is the instruction on the stages of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*), which is the cultivation of the stage of completion (*niṣpannakramabhāvanā*). (28–29)
Fourth:
The Vajrapañjikā, the Yogaratnamālā. The concealed [nature] is like a kunda flower; the manifest has the form of bliss.
In the Sukhāvatī of the female *kakola*, it has the essential nature of the syllable *Evaṃ*.
Precisely because it protects happiness, it is called "Sukhāvatī," the support for Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Vajra-holders.
In this very way, saṃsāra is indeed nirvāṇa; it is said that apart from saṃsāra, there is no other nirvāṇa. // 32 //
Form, sound, and the rest are saṃsāra; feeling and the rest are saṃsāra; the sense faculties themselves are saṃsāra; and hatred, desire, and the rest are saṃsāra. // 33 //
These phenomena are indeed nirvāṇa, yet through delusion they take the form of saṃsāra;
for one who is undeluded, while wandering in saṃsāra, it becomes nirvāṇa through purity.
To the question "Where is it to be produced?", he says: "In the *kakola* of women," and so forth.
To the question "Why is it called Sukhāvatī?", he says: "Because of the protection (*rakṣaṇa*) of bliss (*sukha*).

[Objection: "Is it not the case that all this is merely a matter of mental resolve (*adhimokṣa*), and that this very cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is what we seek to escape from in our pursuit of liberation? [Response: For this very reason, he says "in this very way" and so forth;
the intended meaning is that apart from *saṃsāra*, nirvāṇa does not enter the range of experience (*pratīti*).
"These phenomena (dharmas), however, are by nature nirvana, yet through delusion they appear in the form of samsara";
thus,
they are called "dharmas" because they maintain their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa).
From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), nirvāṇa is the limit of existence (*bhūtakoṭi*) for all things by virtue of being the ultimate truth.

If these [phenomena] are indeed nirvāṇa, why is there saṃsāra? To this he says: "Due to delusion (*moha*), they have the form of saṃsāra. Delusion is ignorance (*ajñāna*), the non-realization of one's own true nature.
Therefore... [The chapter titled "The Summary of the Mudrā-Seal"].
Nirvṛti is indeed the bodhicitta, possessing the nature of both the manifest and the concealed;
she has a beautiful face and large eyes, adorned with beauty and youth.
She should be dark-complexioned, wise, and of noble birth, produced from the essence of sihnaka and camphor;
she must have been consecrated in Hevajra, possess beautiful hair, and be dear to the practitioner.
One should cause her to drink the *madana* (intoxicant) and then drink it oneself; thereafter, for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of both self and others, one should delight the *mudrā*.
Having placed the *bolaka* in the *kakkola*, the observer of the vow produces the *kunduru*;
the wise one should not abandon the camphor produced within that yoga.
Therefore, that nectar should not be grasped with the hand, nor with mother-of-pearl, nor with conch shells; it is to be taken with the tongue for the sake of strengthening Bala's power.
It becomes like nirvāṇa.
He asks, "How so? and replies: "Nirvṛti is indeed bodhicitta, which has the nature of both the manifest (vivṛti) and the concealed (saṃvṛti).
The manifest is great bliss (mahāsukha), while the concealed has the appearance of a jasmine flower and is characterized by the Saṃbhogakāya.
By this much of the discussion, the fact that camphor—which is characterized by great bliss—is not to be abandoned has been established, and its means [of realization] has also been established.
Now he speaks of the arising of the conventional [truth], beginning with "O fair-faced one" and so forth.
"Born from camphor and saffron" means she has been consecrated by the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*) and so forth.
The practitioner observing the vow acts for the sake of "edhanāya," which means for the sake of increase; by this much, it is established that one should not abandon camphor.
Camphor itself is Nairātmyā; bliss is the form of Nairātmyā, and its bliss is Mahāmudrā, who is situated in the navel-mandala. // 40 //
This Blessed Lady Prajñā, whose nature is the primordial vowel, is conceived by the Buddhas through the yoga of the utpannakrama. //41//
She is neither long nor short, neither square nor round; transcending taste, smell, and flavor, she brings about innate bliss.
In that [state] the yogin arises and enjoys its bliss;
together with her, there shall be accomplishment—Mahāmudrā, the bestower of happiness.
Form, sound, as well as smell, taste, and likewise touch, and the intrinsic nature of the dharma-element, are experienced through wisdom alone. // 44 //
She alone is the form of the innate (*sahaja*), the Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*), the divine Yoginī;
she alone is the mandala-circle, whose very nature is the five wisdoms.

Now, he describes another method for the production of camphor, which is of the nature of a manifestation, beginning with the words "camphor" and so forth. He asks, "Why is it 'selfless' (*nairātma*)? meaning it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). He answers this with the words "bliss" (*sukha*) and so forth;
because it is bliss, and that [bliss] has the form of selflessness, meaning it has the form of being devoid of intrinsic nature.
"Of him" means of Nairātmyā. What is the cause for attaining bliss? It is that "Great Seal" (Mahāmudrā), which is to say the supreme, internal seal.
To the question of where it resides, he says: "situated," etc., [meaning] in the navel-center, the *nirmāṇacakra*.
*Dhī* means wisdom (*prajñā*), because the action seal (*karmamudrā*) generates excellent knowledge.
"Not a bridge," and so forth, because it transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
"In that" means: "yogic state arises," and during the time of practice one experiences bliss; "by that" means for that reason. // 43 //

In the context of the stage of generation (*utpannakrama*), she alone is the *mudrā*, she alone is the *sahajā* (innate), because she is the cause for realizing that; she alone is the divine yoginī Nairātmyā, and she alone is the mandala-circle, because she is the nature of the assembly of all channels (*nāḍī*).

In the Vajra Tantra, the chapter titled "The Summary Meaning of Sealing": That very [nature] is the utterly pure dharmadhātu; she herself is I, whose form is the mirror-like gnosis (ādarśajñāna); she is that which brings about the gnosis of equality (samatājñāna);
she is the true discerning gnosis (sadbhūtapratyavekṣā), and she is indeed the gnosis of accomplishing activities (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna).
She herself is the yoginī of selflessness, whose essential nature is the dharmadhātu.
Maṇḍalādhipa Vajragarbha said: "The Blessed One previously taught the arising of the deities by way of the path of meditating on the wheel; now, please explain the *saṃvara* to me."
The Blessed One said: "The syllable *A*, situated within the body of the Yoginī, abides as the *saṃvara*;
just as it is externally, so too is that *saṃvara* revealed internally.
"She alone am I" means that she is not only the form of the Nairātmyā maṇḍala circle; "I too am she" refers to the Lord of the Maṇḍala being she herself, and so forth—thus [she is] Nairātmyā.
However, he states what its reality—that is, its essential nature—thus: "Vajragarbha spoke this as the fifth answer to the question. What did he say for the sake of the *saṃvara*?

Regarding the passage beginning with "in the middle of the body of the Yoginī": "the middle of the body" refers to the navel, which is the letter *a*, the first vowel; "situated" means it is always present. He states the meaning of *saṃvara* (the vow) with the words beginning with "just as," meaning that just as there is the meditation on Nairātmyā externally, so it is exactly the same internally;
the meaning is that it is not far from that.

The sense is that it is called "saṃvara" (restraint) because it is contained within the body. Thus, here, just as there is the maṇḍala of Nairātmyā, so too is the syllable *A* located at the navel; this is the *saṃvara* of Nairātmyā.
Likewise, the syllable *HŪṂ* is the vajra-abode, which is the means (*upāya*). The sense is that this is the *saṃvara* residing in the heart of Hevajra, who is the means.

The performance of duties (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna*) is that very [state] of the Yoginī of the Dharmadhātu, devoid of self (*nairātmya*): *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*. Of the Yoginī Nairātmā: *gha*. Of the Yoginīs Nairātmyā: *he0 paṃ0 mu0 va0*. The wheel (*cakra*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*): *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*. The wheel, the path of cultivation: *he0 paṃ0 mu0 va0*. The path—*cha*, *jha*. The arising of bliss (*sukhodaya*) in the stage of cultivation: *he0 paṃ0 mu0 va0*. The Blessed One (*bhagavān*): *kha*. All (*sarva*): *ka*, *gha*. The vow (*saṃvara*): *ga*. Not previously [mentioned]: *he0 paṃ0 mu0 va0*. Of the Yoginī: *ka*. Of the two Yoginīs: *gha*. The syllable *A*: *ka*, *ga*, *gha*. *he0 paṃ0 mu0 va0*.

He, Paṃ, Yo, Ra, Mā—this is the *saṃvara* established as Kha, Ga, Gha, and Saṃprakāśita; Ka, Gha, Hīna—O Bhagavān! [This is] the fourth: the bliss of *bola*, the *vajrapañjikā*, the *yogaratnamālā*, the *mahāmudrā*, the *vajrāyatana*, and the *upāya*.
By this secret union, the external duality is illustrated. || 50 ||
The three bodies (trikāya) are said to exist within the center of the body in the form of wheels; the five wisdoms of the three bodies are considered the wheel of great bliss. ||51||
The Dharma-body, Enjoyment-body, and Emanation-body, as well as Great Bliss—these three bodies are established in the navel, heart, throat, and head respectively. ||52||
Wherever the birth of all sentient beings without exception is proclaimed, there the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) exists; emanation is considered to be stable. //53//

He asks, "What would result from this? and replies with the words "the bliss of *bola*," and so forth. The meaning is that the bliss at the tip of the *bola* (penis) in the navel belongs to the *mahāmudrā*, because it is the cause for the accomplishment of the body of the *mahāmudrā*. Regarding the phrase "by this" and so forth: the secret union (*guhyasamāpatti*) is the internal union (*ādhyātmikasamāpatti*). To show what this is, he says: "The external pair is the sexual union (*surata*) of Nairātmyā and Heruka. (50)

"Tri-kāya," and so forth: the three bodies of the Buddhas are the *trikāya*. That which resides within the body of the practitioner of that yoga is described as the thorough knowledge of these three, which is the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*); this is the *svābhāvikakāya*. The meaning is that this body is the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*). The meaning is that the three bodies are taught in the form of the *saṃvara* [mandala] with the shape of the wheel of great bliss. || 51 ||
He states the names of the wheels: "Dharma," etc., and "Yoni," etc. "Yoni" refers to the region below the navel; "the three bodies" means they are accompanied by thorough knowledge. || 52 ||

He states the reasoning for the connection between the bodies and their locations with the words beginning "without remainder" (*aśeṣa*). Regarding the phrase "where it is sung," this means it is proclaimed that [the emanation] would exist there; thus, it is called an "emanation" (*nirmāṇa*). Furthermore, due to its similarity (*sādharmya*), even the emanations of the Buddhas remain as the emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) for as long as cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) lasts. Therefore, because it is stationary (*sthāvara*), and by virtue of this similarity to being stationary, the womb (*yoni*) itself is its location. || 53 ||

*Bolasaukhya* is not shown in manuscripts Ka, Ga, and Gha; it is indicated (*nirdeśita*) in manuscript Kha. *Parijñāna* is found in Kha, Ga, Gha, and Ṭa. *Cakraṃ mahatsukhaṃ*—in Ka and Ga it is *mahatsukhaṃ*; in Ga it is *yoginyāḥ*; in Kha it is *yoginī*; in Ga it is *yoginī*; in Cha and Jha it is *yoginyaḥ*. *Trayaḥ* is in Ka and Gha. *Yatotpattiḥ* is perceived (*pratīyate*) in Ka; in Kha and Ga it is *pratiyate*; in Cha it is *nimīyate*; in Ja it is *utpadyate*; in Jha it is *pramīyate*. *Nirvāṇa* is in Ka and Gha. *Sthaviraṃ* is in Ka; *sthavaraṃ* is in Kha and Gha. *Yataḥ* is in Ka and Gha. [In the commentary by Paṇḍita Munidatta: Regarding the two syllables (*a* and *hūṃ*), the bliss located at the tip of the *bola* is [the bliss] located in the body (*dehamadhyasthitam*). The reading enclosed in brackets in manuscript Gha is not appropriate, as the reading exists in manuscript Ka. *Nimmiti* is in Ka. [The Fourth: In the *Vajratantro*, the chapter titled "The Essential Meaning of the Mudrā" states: "By this, that which is produced is considered to be the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇika*)."
Dharma is the very nature of the mind; the Dharmakāya is said to be that which enjoys the Sambhoga[kāya], and it resides within the hearts of the six [Buddhas]. || 54 ||
The great bliss, having the nature of flavor, is situated at the crown of the head. ||55||

In the throat is the enjoyment wheel (*saṃbhogacakra*), and in the syllable *evaṃ* is the outflow (*niṣyanda*). In the enjoyment [wheel] is the human effort (*puruṣakāra*), from the dharma wheel is the maturation (*vipāka*), and in the bliss wheel is the purity (*vaimalya*). (56)
The fruit is said to be fourfold, distinguished by the outflow and the others; the Blessed Wisdom is the enjoyer of karma, impelled by the wind of karma. (57)
Therefore, he says: "That which arises is the dharma" means that all phenomena are mind-only; thus, it is the locus of the dharma-body, because it is the locus of the mind. || 54 ||

"Enjoyment" (*saṃbhoga*) means experiencing or partaking; "tasting" (*rasana*) occurs through the throat. Because of the similarity to enjoyment, the *saṃbhogakāya* exists there, consisting of the teaching of the secrets of the Dharma to the Bodhisattvas. "Great Bliss" (*mahāsukha*) refers to the fourth body, the *mahāsukhakāya*, which is situated on the head—that is, located at the crown. || 55 ||

Thus, demonstrating that there are four wheels—just as there is a restraint (*saṃvara*) of the bodies, so too there is [a result] of the fruits and the classes (*nikāya*)—he says "evam" and so forth. The syllable *evaṃ* is the wheel of the womb (*yonicakra*). To the question "What is there?", he says: the flow-result (*niṣyandaphala*) is in the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*); the ripening-result (*vipākaphala*) is in the wheel of enjoyment (*saṃbhogacakra*); the manly-effort-result (*puruṣakāraphala*) is in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*); and the purity-result (*vaimalyaphala*) is in the wheel of great bliss. || 56 ||

To the questions "How is the fruit of action experienced? and "Who is it that gives [it]?", he says: "The experiencer of action. It is wisdom (*prajñā*) alone, and not the self (*ātman*) or the like, that is the experiencer of the fruit of action; nor is it the wind of action (*karmamāruta*). And that [wind] is action itself, and nothing else, such as the self, the Lord (*īśvara*), or other such entities. (57)

They arise in the sky (kha), they are produced as ṭa, they are emanated in the sky (kha), and they are dissolved in ga. [The term] "emanator" refers to the emanation-body (kāyanairmāṇika). [The phrase] "it is remembered" is not found in this verse portion in the manuscripts Ka and Gha. Regarding the sequence: "the Dharma and the mind" (dharmaṃ citta) is found in Ka, Kha, Gha, He0, Paṃ0, Mu0, and Va0; "the Dharmadhātu" is in Ga; "and the Dharmakāya" is in Ka, Kha, Ga, Gha, He0, Paṃ0, Mu0, and Va0. "Of those having the form of taste" (rasarūpiṇām) is in Ga, Ṅa, Ja, He0, Paṃ0, Mu0, and Va0; "of those having form" (rūpiṇā) is in Cha and Jha. "But the wheel" (cakram tu) is in Kha; "and the Saṃbhogacakra" is in He0, Paṃ0, Mu0, and Va0. "Outflow" (niṣyanda) is in Ka and Gha; "perfected" (niṣpanna) is in Kha and Ga. "From the Dharmacakra" is in Gha. "And human effort" (puruṣakārañca) is in Ka, Ga, Gha, and Ja; "and human effort" (puruṣokāraṃ ca) is in Kha; "and the person" (puruṣaṃ ca) is in Cha and Jha. "All" (sarva) is in Ka. "Purity" (vaimalyaṃ) is in Ṅa; "and differentiated" (prabheditaṃ) is in Ga. "But karma" (karmantu) is in Ka, Kha, Ga, and Gha; "karma and wind" (karmāmāruta) is in Gha. "The tongue" (rasanāṃ) is in Ka; "karma-wind" (karmamāruto) is in Bhoṭa. "By the power of karma" (karmavaśaḥ) is in Bhoṭa. [End of the Fourth Chapter. *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*: "As it was done, so it is eaten; this is designated as 'outflow' (niṣyanda)."
Its maturation is the opposite of that; even from small action there is a great fruit.
It is the acquisition of human effort and purity through the purification of yoga. (58)
Sthāvarī is in the nirmāṇacakra because emanation is stable therein; and Sarvāstivāda is in the dharmacakra because it is the source of the discourse on the Dharma. ||59||
Because consciousness resides in the sambhogacakra at the throat, it is the *mahāsaṃghī*; and because great bliss (*mahāsukha*) resides in the *mahāsukhacakra*, it is the *mahāsukha*. (60)

To explain how the characteristics of the *niṣyanda* (outflow) and other types of karma are to be understood, he says "just as" (*yathā*) and so forth: Just as one’s own body of the Vajradhara, which effects the welfare of the world, is made [manifest] through the meditation on the *karmamudrā*—which is characterized by conceptual elaboration (*prapañca*)—and through the corresponding conduct of conceptual elaboration (*prapañcacaryā*) to be described hereafter, by means of the withdrawal, radiation, and so forth; in that same way, this [result] attained through enjoyment is called the *niṣyanda*.
For it is said, "The *niṣyanda* is similar to its cause. As for the *vipāka* (ripening), it is the opposite of that, being dissimilar to the [cause].
The characteristic of the *dharmamudrā* is as follows:

for while dwelling in the practice free from conceptual proliferation (*niḥprapañcacaryā*) through the illusion-like meditative absorption (*māyopama-samādhi*) within the *dharmamudrā*, one attains even from a very slight action a great fruit, namely the state of Vajradhara.

Furthermore, regarding the *mahāmudrā* and the *saṃbhoga[kāya]*, there is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*); for by means of the practice that is absolutely free from conceptual proliferation, the fruit to be accomplished is the personal achievement of the self.
Therefore, it is the fruit of human effort; because those of inferior vigor lack the capacity for it, it is "purity"— this is the yoga, the Mahāmudrā yoga.
Its purification is the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā immediately following the consecration (*sekānantaram*).

For indeed, for those of superior faculties whose intellects have been purified through meditation over incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeyakalpa*), the fruit—the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā—is independent of further meditation and resides in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*). || 58 ||

"Stāvarī," and so forth. Because of its connection with immobility (*sthāvaratva*), the entire class of *sthāvarī* resides in the wheel of emanation (*nirmāṇacakra*). It is called "Sarvāstivāda" because all doctrines (*sarvavāda*) exist within it. And why is that [the Sarvāstivāda] located precisely in the wheel of consciousness (*cittacakra*)? He says: "The origin of doctrines is the cause; the Dharma [arises] from the union with pure awareness (*saṃvit*). (59)

Because it is the consciousness of similar [beings], because of the greatness of perception, and because it is the assembly (*saṃgha*) of all phenomena, the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) is the Great Assembly (*mahāsāṃghī*);
for this very reason, it is said: "It is situated above the head of all."
Because of this—namely, because of that—there is the state of being a Mahāsāṃghika. || 60 ||
*śābditam*—kha;
*karmaṇyalpa*—kha, ga, cha, jha; *vaimalyayogaśābdikam*—kha; *vaimalyayogaśuddhiphalam*—ga, cha, jha.
This verse does not exist in the manuscripts Ka and Gha;
"cakra" is found in Ga, while "sarvāstivāda" is found in Ka, Kha, Gha, Ṅa, Ca, Cha, Ja, and Ṭa. This reading follows the manuscript Ga.
*Dharmovāda*—ka, ga, gha; *dharmovādasusaṃbhavaḥ*—kha. *Sukhacakre*—ka, gha; *mahāsukham*—ga;
*nāsti*—kha, ga;
*mahāsukhe*—kha.
stitā: - ka. gha;
karmāṇāṃ - gha;
tadanurūpatā - gha.
The practice free from conceptual proliferation—
how many eons? O Vajra Tantra, it is incalculable and immeasurable.
The chapter titled "The Meaning of the Sealing and the Aggregate" states: The body is called the *nikāya*; the belly is said to be the monastery (*vihāra*).
From one free from passion, the placenta arises in the womb as the blazing robe.
Likewise, the preceptress, the mother, salutation with palms joined at the head, the rules of training, worldly duties, the recitation of mantras, and I myself [are all included]. (62)
The syllable *a* is that of the womb-circle, and the syllable *ha* is that of great bliss;
the monk born [therefrom] is the resounding mantra, naked, with his head and beard shaven. (63)
Through these causal conditions, sentient beings are indeed Buddhas; of this there is no doubt.
The ten stages and the ten months are the sentient beings who are masters of the ten stages.

Then all the goddesses, headed by the Yoginī Nairātmyā— namely Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, Tārā, Bhṛkuṭī, Cundā, Parṇaśavarī, Ahomukhā, and others such as these, yoginīs as numerous as the atoms in Mount Sumeru— were struck with supreme wonder.
Now he states another type of vow, beginning with "the community" (*nikāya*), and so forth.
The "community" (*nikāya*) is the community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*); that vow is the body of the yogin, because it is the support for all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
The mother’s womb is the belly;
at the time of birth, one who is free from passion is "joined to the womb" because of the absence of passion, being radiant and unfading, while "uttering the mantra" means reciting the mantra.
"Naked" means with the waistband untied. || 61-63 ||
By these aforementioned [verses], it is said that they are "lords of the ten stages," meaning the stages prior to birth. || 64 ||
nikāya—ṅa, ca, cha, jha; jhaṭa—kha; nirmāṇa—kha;
mudāram—ṅa, ca; vītarāgam—ka, gha; vītarāgo—ga; rāgā—cha, ja; yonyo—kha, jha; yauno—ga, ja; yonyau—cha.
jjla—ka, ga, gha; jvale cīvare—kha; kāñjalī—ga; mastakāñjani—gha;
mantrajāpaṃ mahat—ka, gha; mantrajāpaṃ mahaṃ—kha.
The syllable *aṃ*—Ka, Gha;
the circle of Yoginīs—Kha; the Yoginī—Cha, Jha, Ha;
the syllable *haṃ*—Ka, Ga; the syllable *huṃ*—Kha; the syllable *hūṃ*—Gha.
The mantra *dhanan-mantraṃ*—*ka kha ga gha mantraṃ*—*cha ja jha he paṃ mu*.
Nagnaśirastuṇḍamuṇḍitaḥ—*ka kha ga gha*; *nagnaṃ ... muṇḍitaṃ*—*jha*; *sāmāgribhiḥ*—*gha ca*.
*sarvadevatyā*—ka, cha, ja; *athavā devabhyoḥ*—ga; *sarvadevatā*—gha; *nairātmā*—ga, caiva kha; *māmikā*—|
Pāṇḍarā—ka.
gha; Cuṇḍā—kha. ṭa; Patra—ka.
ga gha; Mahosukhā—ka. gha; Adhomukhā—kha. ga.
And likewise—the Yoginīs [said]:
"The brilliant one—ka; the unerring one—bho;
the fourth [syllable]—gha. Having heard these words from the *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*, they fainted, were terrified, and fell to the ground.
Seeing all those goddesses fallen to the ground, the Wielder of the Vajra praised them again in order to raise them up.
O Earth, Water, Wind, and Fire, you brothers, O Goddesses, listen; I shall speak very sweetly that which no one else knows. 67.
Having heard the words of the Blessed One, which were like a dream, they all regained their lives. || 68 ||
"Regarding this speech," that is, the word of the Blessed One, [it means] that sentient beings are indeed Buddhas. || 66 ||
"Earth, water," and so forth:
earth is the *nirmāṇa*-cakra, water is the *dharma*-cakra,
and wind is the *mahāsukha*-cakra.
The fire-god is the wheel of enjoyment;
"tuhye" means "you," who are Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍaravāsinī, and Tārā. O goddesses who have become worthy vessels, why do you not realize this?
O you whose nature is selflessness, you remain here as the witness; I do not speak a false word—why then are you unconscious?
If it is asked, "Why is this supreme secret being spoken? [the answer follows].
"I elaborate" means I expand upon the discourse of reality, the discourse of the ultimate truth, thinking that perhaps no one has understood it;
thus, out of supreme compassion, the sense is: "Since you are yourselves experts in the meaning and reality of this matter, why have you fallen into such astonishment?"
One explanation is as follows:
in the union of the lotus and the vajra, the initial cognition of solidity is the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*).
The water element is swift cognition; the fire element is movement and maturation;
the wind element is the production of semen.

O sisters, you are of the nature of one or another of these four; I declare to all beings that this very great bliss-wisdom (*mahāsukha-jñāna*) is *surata*, and that it alone is the form of the Vajra-holder (*vajradhara*). I proclaim this to sentient beings.
Why? Because no one knows this reality; and for that reason, they have become those who have attained life. || 67-68 ||
"terrified by meditation"—ka; "terrified"—gha; "fell down"—ka. gha; "shaking"—kha ga gha.
All those goddesses—*devatī* (ka, ga, gha; *devatī* cha; *devati* ja;
*devatīm* jha)—[the word] *santati* is not present in ka and gha.
Earth—ka. kha. ga. gha;
Wind—ka. kha. ga. gha;
Fire—ka. kha. ga. gha.
Listen—ka. gha; and the wind—ka. gha; the fifth—ja;
say—ka. gha; I shall tell—ga. ja.
That which is non-existent—ka. gha; that which is known by one who knows—ka. gha; that which is false—ka. gha; all those—ka. gha.
*bhāratī*—ka, gha; *pāṇḍuravāsinī*—gha (this reading is enclosed in brackets as it is found in the manuscript gha); this reading follows the manuscript ka.
Why do you not realize this? — O gods and men,
who stand as witnesses here.
Regarding "mudyata-ka," it is said: O, what is known as the earth element? Ka.
Apadhātuḥ—ka;
bhāginyaḥ—ka; gha;
surayaḥ—gha. In the Vajra-tantra, the Blessed One said: "Sentient beings are indeed Buddhas, but they are obscured by adventitious defilements."
By removing that [defilement], sentient beings are indeed Buddhas; of this there is no doubt. || 69 ||
The goddesses said: "So it is, Blessed One; this is true, not false. (70)
The Blessed One said: "Eat this poison! He who is inactive, free from delusion, and whose mind is fixed on the supreme reality—he alone shall be satisfied. (71)
Likewise, those who know the means to liberation in the *Hevajra* [tantras] are not seized by ignorance and the like, nor are they seized by the bonds of delusion and so forth. (72)
"They are indeed Buddhas," because they have the nature of the perfectly pure dharmadhātu;
as for "but rather" and so forth... [69]
"This is so," [this] is the acceptance that the words of the Yoginīs are not false. || 70 ||

If they are covered by impurities, how can there be liberation for them? To this he says: "ghumma," etc. When poison—that is, venom—is consumed, the world [is afflicted]; yet for one who is not insentient, who is ignorant of the true nature of poison, and who is free from delusion—meaning one whose mind is fixed on the reality of the destruction of poison through the thorough knowledge of the nature of poison—for such a person alone is sorrow utterly severed.
This is the illustration. || 71 ||
He states the application to the subject at hand with the words "In the same way," and so forth: *nirvṛti* is liberation;
those who have exerted effort in the *Hevajra* [tantra];
*kliṣṭājñāna* is ignorance (*avidyā*); and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), anger, greed, and so on are included.
Delusion is the clinging to these conventional phenomena as being true; they themselves are the bonds. 72.
In the *nicca* [section], [the letters] a, ka, kha, ga, gha, and ja are excluded—ka, kha, ga, gha;
*tatu maṇḍala*—cha; *tantumaṇa*—ja; *tatu maṇḍa*—jha.
She is the beginning (ā), she is the letter 'a' (a); she is cessation (nivṛtti) and the means (upāya);
those who have exerted themselves in virtuous deeds (sukṛtaśrama)—O you five-faced ones (he paṃ mu va)!
They grasp—ka, kha, ga; they are hidden—gha, ja; they are seized—cha, jha;
the bondage of delusion and so forth—ga; by means of bonds—ca, ṭa;
it was stated for the sake of establishing the meaning—gha.

Regarding the reading "ghuṇṇa" in the phrase "mṛṣetyabhyugamaḥ ka ghuṇṇa," the marginal note (pādaṭippaṇī) states that "gha" refers to one who is an expert in the reality of poisons (viṣatattvābhijña).

It breaks [the doubt]: "And where—in the *gha* recension—is the fourth? [The answer is: The *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*: "There is not a single sentient being who is not awakened, because of their own respective awakening."

Since those in the hells, among hungry ghosts, animals, and even the worms in filth never know happiness, the Buddha does not find it elsewhere; for the Fully Awakened One is indeed the mind itself—not the outcastes, the executioners, nor the gods, asuras, and humans. (73)
By their very nature, both gods and asuras are happy.
In some world-systems, the Buddha is manifested elsewhere. || 75 ||
Even those whose minds are intent on the purpose of killing achieve accomplishment by resorting to Hevajra; there is no doubt in this matter. (76)

Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "kiñcābuddha" (and who is not a Buddha), etc.: "from perfect awakening" (*saṃbodhāt*) means from direct realization (*saṃvedanāt*). "Of oneself" (*svasya*) means of the self; and "of one's own" (*svasya ca*) means of that which has the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), such is the meaning. The very perception of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the perception of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); that itself is awakening (*bodhi*), because of the scriptural statement: "That which is the *tathatā* of ordinary beings is the *tathatā* of the Omniscient One. Thus, all sentient beings are indeed Buddhas. Now, one might object: "Let those gods and others who possess unsurpassed experience of bliss be Buddhas; however, hell-beings and the like do not have such an experience of bliss. To this, he says: "In hell," etc. (verse 73).

"Constantly" means at all times. Now, from what [source] does their constant bliss arise? If it is asked whether the bliss produced by the collection of conditions (*sāmagrī*) arises from union and not from separation, he says: "By nature," meaning they are happy by their very essence (*prakṛti*). The meaning is that they are equal in terms of the category of bliss. Now, one might object: "The kind of bliss that belongs to gods and others does not exist for those in the hells and so forth. Let it not be so; for they do not know the bliss of either a god or an asura. Indeed, the Buddhas do not perceive the bliss of gods and asuras as being of the nature of bliss; rather, because it is impermanent and associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), they consider it to be suffering. Therefore, only Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*) is true bliss, and that is equal for all beings by virtue of being their natural state (*prakṛtirūpa*). (74)

"Not the Buddha," and so forth. He states another argument: "elsewhere. This means other than the bodhicitta characterized as previously described. For it is shown that "it is indeed the mind" refers to bodhicitta, and not anything else. || 75 ||

With the words beginning "Caṇḍāla," etc., [the author] demonstrates the greatness of the Tantra. [The ignorant ones] do not know this purpose, which is indeed the act of slaying (*māraṇa*), because it is the cause for the arising of the ultimate goal. They do not know the animals, nor the impure worms and such. They do not know the god and the asura; they are brought under control, whether by the asura or otherwise. It is obtained elsewhere, not here. The bamboo-workers and others, those whose minds are intent on the purpose of slaying Māra and so forth—by means of the path of Hevajra, they are accomplished in the final goal. In the Vajra-tantra: "Enveloped by ignorance, the fools do not know this state. Those deluded ones wander through the six realms within the prison of existence. (77) *Note: The reading "gṛhītaḥ" follows the Tibetan version.* **Sanskrit Text:** *caṇḍāletyādinā tantrasya māhātmyaṃ darśayati | māraṇamevārthaṃ arthotpattihetunāsti | tiryañca amedhyakīṭakādyān na jānanti | devasya ca surasya ca vaśyāpy asurasya vā labhyate | anyatra nānuveṇukārādyā mārādyamāraṇārthārthacittakāḥ | hevajramārgasya siddhānte | ajñānatathateti gṛhītastu bhoṭānusārī pāṭhaḥ | vajratantre ajñānenāvṛtā bālā imāṃ gatim ajānakāḥ | saṃsaranti ca te mūḍhāḥ ṣaḍgatau bhavacārake || 77 ||* **English Translation:** By the verse beginning with "Caṇḍāla," the author shows the majesty of the Tantra. The very purpose is slaying, which serves as the cause for the arising of the ultimate goal. They do not recognize the animals, nor the worms dwelling in filth. They do not understand the god or the asura; they are brought under subjection, whether by the asura or otherwise. This is attained elsewhere, and not [in other systems]. The bamboo-workers and others, whose minds are fixed on the purpose of slaying Māra and his like, [find success] through the path of Hevajra in the final realization. In the *Vajra-tantra*: "Obscured by ignorance, the foolish do not know this destination. Those deluded ones continue to transmigrate through the six realms within the prison of cyclic existence. (77) *Note: The reading "ajñānatathatā" is adopted according to the Tibetan translation.*
Having attained Hevajra, O Vajragarbha, they purify the sense objects; they shall obtain the unsurpassed means. (78)

Vajragarbha said: O Great Compassionate One, it is taught that Pṛthivī is Pukkasī; how then is there the sealing by Akṣobhya? Since delusion (*moha*) is solidity and the body is considered Vairocana, O Lord, the sealing of Pukkasī by the seal of delusion is appropriate. (79)
The Blessed One said: "Apart from the body, the mind has no other play; therefore, Vairocana, one should seal the body with the mind. (80)

Because of that meaning, it is the livelihood. Regarding "Hevajra": *he* refers to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and *vajra* refers to the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*). Having relied upon these, one brings them face-to-face through the internal sequence. || 76 ||
"Imām" refers to the reasoning stated in the *Hevajra*. "Bhavacāraka" means a prison. With this much, the answer to the question regarding the vows (*saṃvara*) is concluded. (77)

Now, there may arise in someone a misconception regarding the sealing (*mudraṇa*); therefore, the following responses are given, beginning with "Earth," etc. This verse of inquiry belongs to Vajragarbha. Solidity is Earth; that [solidity] and the body of delusion (*moha*)—both of these are Vairocana. Therefore, sealing by that alone is appropriate, not by another: such is the meaning of the question. Regarding the passage beginning with "Therefore," etc.: since it is thus, Pukkasī has the nature of the body; one should seal her with the mind alone, which is Akṣobhya. (79)

[The following variants are noted: *nāsti*—ka. gha; *ye*—ka. gha; *mahāmaha*—kha. ga, *mahāmahā*—cha. jha; *kakkhaṭatvaṃ-moha*—kha. gha; *kāyā*—kha; *nāsti*—kha; *prabhoḥ*—kha. cha. jha; *vṛto*—gha; *gatimajātataḥ*—ka. ga, *gatimajānataḥ*—gha; *mūḍhātmā*—ka. gha, *mūḍhaḥ*—ga; *upāye*—ka. gha; *mahāmahaṃ*—ka. gha, *mahāmahī*—ja; *viśodhyati*—kha; *ye*—ka. kha. ga. gha; *kakkhaṭattaṃ*—gha; *pūjyate*—cha, *pūjyanta*—ja, *pūjyan*—jha (this reading follows the manuscript *kha*); this half-verse portion is absent in manuscripts *ka*, *ga*, and *gha*; *rahitaṃ*—ga; *vairocanaṃ*—ka. kha. ga. gha; *mudrayat*—kha. ga. gha; *tenārthaḥ jīvikāṃ*—ka (this reading follows the Tibetan manuscript); *āgamye*—ka; *imāni*—ka; *praśno'syottaraṃ*—ka; *saṃvara* is absent—gha; *kakkhāṭatvaṃ*—in the reading of Mahodaya Phero; *kāyasva vā*—ka. **Vajragarbha said:** The water element is known as Śavarī, and Akṣobhya has the nature of fluidity. O Lord, the sealing of Śavarī by the seal of Akṣobhya is appropriate. (81) [Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā, Chapter Four] Vajragarbha said: The water element is known as Śavarī, and Akṣobhya has the nature of fluidity. O Lord, the sealing of Śavarī by the seal of Akṣobhya is appropriate. (81)
The Blessed One said: Apart from the mind, no other stability of the body is perceived. Therefore, the mind should become delusion; one should seal the mind with delusion. (82)
Vajragarbha said: Tejas is known as Caṇḍālī; how is there sealing by means of Ratna? It is fitting for Caṇḍālī to be sealed by the seal of passion (rāga), and not by any other seal. ||83||

The Blessed One said: Since passion (rāga) is known as that which is colored (rakta), and the colored one is Ratnasaṃbhava, then because fire has the nature of being colored, one should seal passion with the Piśuna [mudrā]. 84.
Vajragarbha said: "O Lord, because the ḍombinī is the Amogha wind, having the form of wind, her sealing with the Amogha-mudrā is appropriate. (85)
"From non-existence comes Śavarī," and so forth. Therefore, the mind itself is delusion (moha) and Vairocana. || 81 ||
"Tejaścaṇḍālī," and so forth. "By the mudrā of passion" means by the mudrā of Amitābha. || 83 ||
"Blood" refers to the female menses; [it is] Ratnasambhava. "By the malicious one" means by Ratnasambhava. (84)
"Ḍombī," and so forth; "the form of wind" means the nature of wind. || 85 ||

Akṣobhya—ka, kha, ga, gha. Liquid form—ka, kha, ga, gha. By means of form—ga; Akṣobhya—gha. By means of the mudrā—ka. Is worshipped—cha, jha; are worshipped—ja. O Lord—ka, gha. Of the sky—ka, gha. Another state—ka. Nāstika. One should seal—ga. There is none—ga. Tejacaṇḍālinī—ka, ga, gha. Ka—gha. Ratneśa—ka, gha; Ratnaiḥ—kha; Ratnasya—ga. Mudraṇa—ka, kha. Caṇḍālyo—cha, jha. Rāga—ka, kha, ga, gha. Rakta—kha, gha. There is none—ga. Sambhavam—ka, kha, gha; Sambhavām—ga. Raktasvarūpa—ka, ga, gha; Raktasvabhāve—kha. Piśuna—ka, gha. There is none—kha. Yathā—ka; Tasmāt—ga; there is none—gha. Vāyuramogham—ka, kha, ga, gha. Vāyurūpakam—ka, kha, ga, gha. Ḍombinī Amogha—ka, ga, gha. Is offered as oblation—ka. O Lord—ka. Āpadhātuḥ—ka, gha. In the *Vajratantro*, in the chapter titled "The Summary Meaning of Sealing," the Blessed One said: "Having abandoned passion (*rāga*), there can be no arising elsewhere than from envy (*īrṣyā*)."
Therefore, the wise man should seal the Ḍombinī with the seal of passion. || 86 ||
Since form is hardness, Vairocana is considered the consort of Gaurī;
according to the very same principle previously stated, she should be sealed by Citteśa alone. (87)
By that same method, one should likewise [seal] Caurī and Vetālī, and by that same logic, Ghasmarī; thus is the sealing performed without error. (88)
While the deity Hevajra, the holder of the vajra, remained established in meditative absorption, Nairātmyā there asked about the great bali for the sake of sentient beings. (89)
Seated in the form of the syllable *Evaṃ*, Vajrasattva should offer the bali for the protection of the life-force of sentient beings from obstacles and obstructing spirits. (90)
O Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Yakṣa, Bhūta, Vahni, Vāyu, Rakṣas, Candra, Sūrya, Mātṛ, Pitṛ, and the eight serpents of the netherworld—svāhā!
|| 91 || Having abandoned passion, etc.—it would not be, it would not come to pass. || 86 ||
"Form," and so forth; "by the previously mentioned" means by the one liberated from Pukkasī; this is the reply. || 87 ||
"Caurī," and so forth;
likewise, "and Ghasmarī" refers to what was stated regarding the questions concerning Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī.
The meaning is that this is the non-perverted sealing (*aviparītamudraṇa*). || 88 ||
"Thus," and so forth, are the words of the compiler.
"Seated" means having entered the meditative absorption of Nairātmyā.
"Vajrasattva" refers to Hevajra; "should instruct" means he teaches. (90)
"Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Yakṣa"—this is the address to the guardians of the directions.

"Bhūta, Vahni, Vāyu, and Rākṣasa"—[these are the names of the goddesses] Ḍombinī, [Cāmuṇḍā], [Rūpiṇī], and [Lampaṭā]. *Note: Variants indicate that the reading "Ḍombinī" is found in manuscripts *ka*, *gha*, and *kha*; the term "rūpa" is found in manuscripts *ka*, *ga*, and *gha*.*
Hardness—ka, kha, ga, gha. Gaurī is joined with Citteśa alone—kha, ga, ṅa; joined—kha, gha.
Devī—ka, gha; 0dhāriṇaḥ—ka, gha; 0dhāriṇe—kha; 0dhāriṇā—ga; Vajradhāriṇī—cha;
Nairātmyo—ka; Nairātmā—kha.
For the sake of all purposes—ka. gha; for the sake of sentient beings—ka. kha. ga. gha. cha, sattva—ja; for the sake of protection—ga.
vighnāṃ—ka. gha; vighnā—ga | oṃ indra—ka. khaṃ. ga. gha | yama—ka. kha. ga. gha | yakṣa—kha. ga |
*bhūta*—ka. kha. ga. gha. *he paṃ muva*. *he0 paṃ yo0 ra0 mā0*.
*rakṣaka*, *rākṣa*—kha. ga. gha. *candra*—ka. kha. ga. gha.

vāpya—ka. gha, vapya—kha;
0pātāla—ka. gha; aṭṭhayasya—ka, addhasarpa—kha, sarpa—bho0.

0rakhyeti—ka; 0rakheti—gha. [Fourth: *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*: "Oṃ! Enjoy this offering (bali), smell it, O Phulla! Burn incense, eat the meat, drink the wine! Accomplish all tasks, be patient, remove obstacles, and grant success! 92.
Oṃ, the syllable A is the gateway to all phenomena because they are primordially unarisen.
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. || 93 ||

If, by means of this offering, yogins perform worship to all beings for the sake of auspiciousness, then there will be untroubled happiness for them, and the gods and the well-being of the world will be pleased. (94)

Subjugation, sorcery, the destruction of enemy armies, eradication, killing, and attraction—as well as peace, happiness, and nourishment—shall come to pass; he who offers this eternal oblation here to the host of spirits shall obtain these results. (95)
Of the lords of the intermediate directions: "Candra" means the Moon;
"Sūrya" means the Sun;
"Mātā" means the Earth.
*Bappa* means father (*pitā*). *Aṭṭha* means eight nāgas. *Svāhā* is the word *svāhā*, used for the purpose of pleasing. || 91 ||
"Edam" means "this," referring to this offering (bali). "Bhuñje" means "eat.
"Jighe" means "smell."
He asks, "What is that? and says: "Phulladhūpa" refers to flowers and incense.
"Māṃsaviṅghaya" means: O Māṃsī, increase this [offering].
"Ambha kārja sarva sādhehi" means: accomplish all our tasks.
O patient one, burst forth from that [wound] on the limb! 92.
Thus, he speaks of the benefit resulting from the offering of the bali: "for the auspicious" means for the welfare of oneself and others;
"unclouded" means stainless mind;
"the prosperity of the world" refers to those from whom the excellent well-being (*bhūti*) or success of the world proceeds. || 94 ||
"Subjugation," and so forth.
"It would be" means it is accomplished; "constantly" means eternally. || 95 ||

Vajragarbha said: In the Vajra-tantra, the chapter titled "The Summary Meaning of Sealing": "By which seal is Khecarī sealed, and by whose seal is Bhūcarī? How is the sealing to be performed? O Lord, why was this not known by me previously? (96)
The Blessed One said: "The three secrets are within the center of the wheel, distinguished by body, speech, and mind;
the lower, upper, and middle positions are established within the center of the wheel. (97)
Bhūcarī is the body-mudrā, downward-facing, and the embodiment of the Body-Vajra;
Khecarī is the passion-mudrā, upward-facing, and the embodiment of the Speech-Vajra. || 98 ||
Cittavajrī and Nairātmyā are the mind; the mind has the form of Nairātmyā.
The mind is the middle state; therefore, Nairātmyā is born from the middle. 99.
They say there are six types of families; one should explain them in detail.
They are also said to be threefold and fivefold; listen, O Yoginī! (100)

Akṣobhya, Vairocana, Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, and Vajrasattva; hatred, delusion, malice, passion, envy, and bliss—these indeed should be meditated upon in their respective order of purification. 101.
Vajragarbha said, asking about "the sky-farer" and so forth. 96.
Regarding "the three secrets":
how are they the three secrets?
By way of the divisions of body, speech, and mind.
How then [is it] "from the middle of the wheel"? He says: "Below," and so forth.
The connection is according to the sequence. || 97 ||
Since he is the Body-Vajra, he should therefore be sealed with the Body-Vajra. || 98 ||
"Cittavajrī," and so forth; "born in the middle" means born in the central position. 99.
The families are of six kinds; by this purification—that is, by the purification of the six families—they are to be cultivated, meaning they are to be meditated upon.
Fourth: Having set aside that which is called Vajrasattva, there is subsequently a fivefold family;
thereafter, it proceeds to a threefold state by means of delusion, passion, and hatred. (102)
But the single family is the Lord of Mind, whose form is Akṣobhya-Dveṣa;
this is the power of Dveṣavajra, and the family is considered to be fivefold within the six. (103)
The fourth chapter, titled "The Summary Meaning of the Seals of All Tantras of Hevajra."
"Having abandoned" means having relinquished; "thereafter, the threefoldness" refers to the form of the fivefold compendium. || 102 ||
One family consists of six pentads. || 103 ||

This alone is the entire *Sarvatantra*, as it is the essence of all the *Hevajratantras*; and since it is the summarized meaning (*piṇḍārtha*) of the sealing (*mudraṇa*), the chapter that elucidates it is described accordingly.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Summary Meaning of the Seals," in the second kalpa of the *Hevajrapañjikā*, composed by the venerable Kṛṣṇācārya as part of the *Yogaratnamālā*.
The fifth chapter, the Arising of Hevajra. Now, the Vajra-holder, the Great King, Hevajra, the Lord who bestows all, whose nature is the essence of all forms, shall fully reveal the mandala. 1.

Seated in Sukhāvatī, possessing the nature of all forms, the Lord of the Maṇḍala is the Hero produced from the seed-syllable of Cittavajra, having sixteen arms, eight faces, and wearing a garland of skulls. (2)
The goddess Nairātmyā herself asks the god, who has four legs, who is terrifying, whose neck is embraced by Nairātmyā, and who bears the five mudrās: ||3||
This wheel of yours, surrounded by fifteen [deities], has been described by you;
O Lord, what is your maṇḍala like? Previously, it was not known by me. (4)
Having kissed Nairātmyā and placed the vajra in her skull-cup, and having massaged her breasts, he should reveal the maṇḍala. ||5||
The face is the mouth; the leg is the collection of shanks and feet; "terrible" means fear-inspiring;
"heroic" because of the possession of unsurpassed valor;
the neck is the throat.
He is called a god (deva) because he plays (divyati) with the powers of mastery (vaśitā) and so forth. || 3 ||
Because it has not been stated. || 4 ||
That which protects happiness (*kaṃ sukhaṃ*) is *kapāla*; thus, it is the lotus (*kamala*). || 5 ||
Two verses.
Two verses.
Yours, yours.

The fifth [chapter], on the collection of shanks and feet: The *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā* states: "The wheel, as previously described, adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, possessing four gates, and decorated with vajra-lines. (6)
Together with you, O fair-faced one, by virtue of the nature of innate bliss. ||7||
There, in the center of that square, I am present; with great passion and affection, I have eight faces and four feet, trampling upon the four Māras, and am terrifying even to fear itself. || 8 ||
He bears a universal vajra upon his head and is black in color and terrifying. ||9||
Adorned with sixteen arms,
wearing a necklace made of a garland of severed heads, standing upon the sun and engaged in the *tāṇḍava* dance,
one should emanate the syllable *HŪṂ* from the mouth, his body smeared with ashes.
Having entered into the union of passion, he was joined with Nairātmyā.
Regarding the phrase "the wheel," one brings forth the foundation mandala as before; the meaning is that it is exactly as previously described. || 6 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "here," etc.: the meaning is that one should meditate upon this *vidyā*—Nairātmyā—as embracing [the deity] who is the *adhibhūta* Vajrasattva, whose characteristics will be described according to the sequence of the fivefold realization (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*) starting with "I" (*aham*). Passion for the welfare of the world is "great passion" (*mahārāga*).
Attachment to that is *prīti*;
for this reason, he says: "By virtue of having innate bliss as its intrinsic nature (*sahajānandasvabhāvataḥ*)," for this is indeed the very nature of the Blessed One. || 7 ||
"Even of fear" means even of that which is terrifying. || 8 ||
"Muṇḍeti" means [she] wears a garland of fresh heads;
"sūryastham" means [he] stands upon the solar disc, trampling the four Māras;
"tāṇḍaveti" means accompanied by the tāṇḍava dance in the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka); the meaning is that he performs that [dance]. || 9 ||

Previously, from her own mouth, Nairātmyā taught the Cakra-vidyā; in place of the word "śabda," the reading is "ataṃtra. It is not presided over by an external deity, but is embraced [by the consort]. [The Fifth: The Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā, the Hevajrābhyudaya chapter of the Vajra-tantra, which has attained waveless bliss, describes him whose nature is waveless:
his right [hand] is like a kunda flower. (11)

The primary face is deep black, while the right and left faces are red and most terrifying; the face on the crown has twenty-four eyes and the like. As for the remaining faces, they emerged while you and I were playing in the beautiful city of old: Gaurī in the eastern direction at the eastern gate, and Vikarālī, who is like a bumblebee in color. 12.
Filled with intense delight, she was perfectly situated. || 13 ||
Furthermore, through the process of churning with the churning-stick, Caurikā emerged again;
having emerged, she became the female gatekeeper at the southern gate. (14)
Through the union of *bola* and *kakkola*, Vetālī emerged once more;
having emerged, she sat at the western gate as the destroyer of Māra. (15)
During the great union, Ghasmarī emerged;
having emerged, she sat at the northern gate, possessing a terrifying form.
"Bhṛṅgā" means those resembling bees.
From this point onward, the text is for the most part disordered;
therefore, it must be understood through the oral instruction of a guru.

We, however, shall explain [the text] according to the order of the recitation (pāṭhakrama) and not according to the order of the logical connection (sambandhakrama), because the latter requires a great deal to be said, and because the means for attaining the Blessed One are easily accessible even through that [former order]. || 12 ||
"By you and by me," and so forth;
"play" means through the play of sexual union (*suratakrīḍā*); "with those full of passion" means with the enjoyments of passion (*ratisaṃbhoga*);
"emerged" means through the transformation of the *bodhicitta*.

"In the direction of Indra" means in the eastern quarter; having accomplished the welfare of the world with clouds of radiance, she stands at the eastern gate in the dramatic gesture of the *tāṇḍava* dance. || 13 ||
And "theft" is likewise [produced] by the transformation of one's own seed-syllable; thus it is for both. || 14 ||

There is no [door] on the south; having emerged from the delightful *Ramya*, she stands stationed at the door. There is no *Vetālī*; having emerged and seated herself, she of terrible form emerges [again]. [Fifth: From the friction and union of the two, the Vajrinī, together with her consort (*vidyā*), emerges as if melted by great passion.
Then the goddesses [appear] with various offerings of song. (19)
Arise, O Bharāḍa, essence of compassion! Protect me, O Pukkasi!
Abandon me to the union of great bliss; abandon me to the concentration on emptiness. 20.
The friction and movement of the two vajras, which are selfless (*nairātma*), is fire (*pāvaka*); its corner is the southeast (*āgneya*).
"In the direction of the Rākṣasa" means in the southwest (*nairṛtya*).
"Māruta" means wind; the meaning is the northwest corner (*vāyavya*).
Here too, there is a distinct yoga based on instruction. || 18 ||
Then, regarding "the Vajra-holder," and so forth:
after the words "by you and by me," it should be understood that [he] should meditate on [himself] as having entered the state of melting together with the consort Nairātmyā.
Then, following another rule of discipline, the goddesses— Pukkasī, Śavarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī—
having arrived from their respective directions, sat upon their own seats;
they urge and impel [the practitioner], having arisen from the sequential meditative absorption (*kramasamādhi*).
"By various songs" means by means of individual musical offerings. || 19 ||
Therein, Pukkasi first exhorts him: "Uttha bharāḍo" means "Arise, O Blessed One!
"Karuṇamaṇḍa" means "O you whose mind consists of compassion. "Pukkasī mahum" means "Pukkasi, me," and "paritrāhi" means "protect me, O Great Bliss," and so forth.

Yoga is for the sake of great bliss; O Vajra-form, arise from that fluid [of passion] and desire me! Abandon, cast away the "void-concentration" (śūnyasamādhi), which is a concentration on a melted state devoid of form. || 20 ||

[The fifth: In the *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*, elephants, horses, donkeys, oxen, camels, humans, and deer—along with those born from eggs—are to be known as the bipeds and so forth, according to their sequence. || 24 ||

Earth, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Fire, the Moon, and the Sun are in the eight right skull-cups; Antaka and Dhanada are in the left skull-cups, characterized by compassion, wonder, and peace, and endowed with the sentiments of dance and music. (25–26)

Through the sentiments of the erotic, the heroic, the loathsome, the furious, the comic, and the terrifying, and with the syllables *aṃ*, *hūṃ*, and *bhyāṃ*, the Great Vajrin arises from a liquid form,
spreading his feet across the earth and threatening the gods and asuras.
One should create these [goddesses] by means of the seed-syllables gaṃ, caṃ, vaṃ, ghaṃ, paṃ, śaṃ, laṃ, and ḍaṃ;
and their presiding lords by means of the seed-syllables ra and ti, which are blue and terrifying with flames, together with hūṃ and aṃ.

"elephant, horse," and so forth;

"How has it arisen? and so forth.

in the right hand of Caurī is a fire-pot, and in her left hand a boar. In the right hand of Vetālī is a tortoise, and in her left a lotus-vessel.

Fifth: *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā* Gaurī and the others are considered to have two arms; they stand in the dance posture with one leg half-bent (*ardhaparyaṅka*), possess three eyes, have hair standing on end, and are adorned with the five mudrās. Gaurī is black in color, Caurī resembles the sun, Vetālī has the luster of molten gold, and Ghasmarī is like an emerald. Pukkasī has the hue of sapphire, Śavarī the radiance of a moonstone, Caṇḍālī is dark blue like the sky, and Ḍombī is considered to be the color of karcūra. Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, Rudra, Vaivasvata, Nairṛti, Vemacitrin, and Vināyaka are the seats for Gaurī and the others. Having adorned the *bolaka* and worshipped the Blessed One with devotion, Nairātmyā asks for the mantra with firm embraces and kisses. [The mantra] which brings women under control, likewise the threatening of the wicked, and the mantra which causes the subjugation of the *nāgas*, beginning with "black-colored" and so forth. [It is] the crushing of gods and asuras. Upendra is Viṣṇu; Vaivasvata is Yama; Vittanāyaka is Kuvera; Nairṛti is the lord of the *rākṣasas*; Vemacitrin is the lord of the asuras; and *viṣṭara* means a seat. By this much, the two meditations—the Ādiyoga and the Maṇḍalarājāgra—have been explained.

The third [chapter], *Karmarājāgrī*, is to be understood according to other tantras as the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of one who has recited the vidyā. In the context of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), [the disciple] asks for the mantra of the Bhagavatī. Regarding what its specific characteristics are, he says: "Of women," and so forth; this is easy to understand. [Notes: 0nāṭyastha—ka, gha; 0paryaṅkā—ga.
