In the Vajra-tantra, I shall now speak of this; listen, O Goddess, for this was not taught by me elsewhere among the Buddhas or Bodhisattvas. This is the chapter on the Arising of Hevajra, which bestows happiness. O Goddess, regarding that which actually occurred concerning this mantra and what was performed by Vajrasattva, I am extremely afraid; however, out of deference to you, it is being told. Having drawn the mandala, which is terrifying with its garland of flames, one should summon Tilottamā in order to confer the initiation upon Vajragarbha. By means of ten thousand recitations, performed clearly with a long and beautiful sound, and subsequently joined with the yoga of the Eight-Faced One, all women are summoned. (43) Through a hundred thousand recitations, the yogi, whose self is yoga, performs all rites by means of the *He*-syllable Vajra-yoga, with a mind free from doubt. (44) [The mantra] is adorned with the half-moon and the bindu, and has tawny hair standing erect. (45) To the one with twenty-four eyes, then sixteen arms, whose body is like a black cloud, who wears many garlands of skulls, whose mind is exceedingly cruel, and who has fangs like a crescent moon. (46) "That I... and so forth is the speech of the Blessed One. (40) "Yoga" refers to the yoga possessing the characteristics already described.
"Everything" refers to the fourfold ritual action, beginning with pacification (śānti). "Of the Vedas," and so forth; the first syllable is the *praṇava*.

[The fifth: "His very nature is adorned. *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*: "Kill! Kill! Make [them] kill! Make [them] kill! Roar! Roar! Threaten! Threaten! Dry up! Dry up the seven oceans! Bind! Bind the eight Nāgas! Seize! Seize the enemies! Ha hā hi hī huhū he hai ho hau haṃ haḥ phaṭ svāhā! Then, being pleased, that Goddess asks about the beautiful maṇḍala through the union of the churner and the churned, with firm embraces and kisses. (48) There, the Teacher, the possessor of great wisdom, himself draws the maṇḍala; his mind joyful and composed through the union of the vajra and the lotus. (49) It has one enclosure, four gates, and is provided with four archways, filled with various rays of light, and adorned with vajra-lines. (50) One should then draw it endowed with five lines and eight vases.
Alternatively, with powders made of the five jewels, or with rice-grains and the like, or even with bricks from cremation grounds and likewise with charcoal from cremation grounds. (51)
The mantra ends with the syllable *ha*, adorned with twelve [vowels], followed at the end by *phaṭ* and *svāhā*.
One should ask for the mandala; it is the Blessed One’s mandala to be drawn. (47–48)

In that context, when he is satisfied, the Teacher—the Great Knower, the Master—should speak; this is the ellipsis. He himself should draw the mandala; at the outset, he should not have it drawn by another, such as a painter or the like. || 49 ||

One should depict eight vases; "eight" refers to the goddesses. As for the question of with what colored powders one should draw the mandala—including the *vijaya-kalaśa* and the *sārvakarmika-kalaśa*—it says: "with the finest [powders] consisting of the five jewels."
With middling materials such as rice and the like, or with inferior materials such as bricks from cremation grounds and the like. || 51 ||

In the *Hevajratantra*, in the chapter on the Arising of Hevajra, it says: "In the center of that, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus with its filaments; and upon the pericarp, one should draw Naraka, white in color and three-segmented. (52)
One should also draw a Śarabha in the northeast, a mendicant (bhikṣu) in the southeast corner, a wheel in the southwest, and a thunderbolt (kuliśa) in the northwest.
Likewise, one should draw a knife at the eastern gate and a fire-pot at the southern; one should draw a tortoise at the western and likewise a serpent at the northern.
The eight symbols are proclaimed according to the distinction of the colors of the goddesses; in the center, one should draw a white skull-cup marked with a double-vajra.
Then one should present the victory-pitcher (vijayakalaśa), which has young sprouts at its opening, is well-wrapped in cloth, contains five gems within, is divine, and is filled with *śāli* rice.
What is the use of much talk? It should be performed exactly as the mandala ritual is described in the Tattvasaṃgraha. || 57 ||
"In its center" means in the middle of the mandala; "naraka" refers to the guardian of hell (Narakapāla). || 52 ||
The śarabha, the lion, the uraga, and the serpent. || 53–54 ||

"Of the goddesses," and so forth: just as are the emblems of the goddesses, so are their emblems to be drawn; one should draw a skull-cup situated in the center, presided over by a double-vajra (viśvavajra). || 55 ||
"One should give the victory-vase (vijayakalaśa) and so forth as before"; by this it is meant that one should place the vases of the goddesses in their respective positions. || 56 ||

*trikhaṇḍikam*—ga; *varṇaṃ trikhaṇḍitam*—gha; *khaṇḍitam*—ṭa; *īśāne ca*—ka. gha; *īśāne likhet*—kha. ga; *pi* is not present—ka. kha. ga. gha; *bhikṣur agneyakoṇakam*—ka. gha; *bhikṣur agneya*—kha; *bhikṣur anyai*—ga; *likhet*—ka. ga. gha; *ca* is not present—ka. ga. gha; *vāyuve*—ka; *vāyavye*—gha; *kartri*—ka. gha; *kartti*—kha. jha; *katṛ*—ga; *kartti*—cha; *kṛpītam*—ka. kha. gha; *kṛpitā*—ga; *paścimeṣu likhet*—ka. ga. gha; *kūrmam uragam uttaram*—ka. gha; *tanmadhye*—ka. gha; *śukrakaroṭakaś ca*—ka; *karoṭāñ ca*—ga; *kalaśaḥ*—ka. gha; *saṃketitaḥ koṣṭhake ca*—[implied]; *suvastreṇa*—gha; *tattvena saṅgrahaḥ*—ka; *tattvasya saṅgrahaḥ*—kha; *saṅgrahe*—ga; *kartavyaḥ*—ka. gha; *karotakam*—gha; *devatīnām*—gha; *tattvam pañcamaḥ*—gha; *vajrapañjikā yogaratnamālā*; *maṇḍale ca praveṣṭavyāḥ*—ra; *vidyāś cāṣṭau mahāsukhāḥ*. Twelve years old, twice eight [sixteen], adorned with necklaces and anklets. (58)

The mother, the sister, the daughter, the sister’s daughter, the wife of the maternal uncle, the mother’s sister, the husband’s sister, and likewise the father’s sister—these eight are proclaimed as the Vidyās. (59)
The yogi should honor these [deities] with firm embraces and kisses; he should consume camphor there, and by that, the maṇḍala is sprinkled.
The yogi should cause them to drink [the juice]; he will quickly attain accomplishment. In that case, madana should be drunk, and one should eat the fruit of the *balaśālija* plant.
Having stripped her naked, he should kiss her vulva again and again; and by them, his *bola* is stimulated, while he sings and dances most excellently.

"In the mandalas," and so forth; "should be made to enter" means they should be caused to enter. "Twice eight years" means sixteen years; thus it is said that there are eight types of *vidyās*. || 58 ||

Asking "Who are they?", he says: "The mother," and so forth. These women are not related by worldly ties. "The mother" is the teacher’s beloved; she alone is the disciple’s mother. "The sister" is her friend. "The daughter" is the teacher’s female disciple. "The niece" is his female disciple. "The wife of my maternal uncle" is the beloved of the mother’s dear friend. "The mother’s sister" is the teacher’s friend. "The sister-in-law" is the beloved of the disciple. "The father’s sister" is the teacher’s sister. Of these and others, the "Yogin" is the teacher. (59–60)

In the mandalas—[the word] *ca* is not found in Ka and Ga; they are to be entered—Ka. Two sixteen-year-old [girls], the Bhāganeyikās—Ka, Kha, Gha; Bhāganeyakās—Ga, Ṭa; Māmakasya—Ka, Ga, Gha; of the mother—Ka, Kha, Ga; of the sister-in-law—Gha; of the mother-in-law—He0 Paṃ Mu Va; the Vidyās—Ka, Ga, Gha; the Vidhās—Ṅa, Ca, Cha, Ja, Jha, Ṭa; the Yogin—Ga; one should drink there—Ga; the sprinkling of the mandala—Ka, Ga, Gha; the sprinkling of the mandala:—Kha; one should cook—Kha; and in Madana—Ga; possessing strength and power—Ka; rice—Gha; of them—Ka, Gha; it is sucked—Ka, Kha, Ga; they are sucked—Gha; one should cause to increase—Ṭa; they dance and sing—or—Ka, Gha; *param* is not present—Ka, Ga, Gha; the sister—Gha; "of the sister-in-law"—Ka, Gha. In the Vajra-tantra, play is performed there through the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*. [The Hevajrābhyudaya chapter: one should cause the disciple to enter there. 63.
Afterwards, during the second watch, having covered the eyes of the disciple there with a cloth, the mandala is shown; then the consecration is bestowed there at midnight in a secluded house.

Just as the empowerments have been described, categorized according to the distinctions of the master and so forth, so too should the praise and worship, as previously explained, be inferred by well-trained disciples.
And there he should teach the reality (tattva) beginning with the Virama and ending with the Parama; that which has been hidden in all tantras is here revealed to the very end.
There, that goddess asked him regarding the practice of Vajra-worship: "O God, O Great Lord, tell me at once what its nature is. (67)
As it has been stated, such as "praise and worship" and so forth in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and other works, [the phrase] "and so on" is to be inferred (*unneya*). || 65 ||

"Viramādi" means that which is both *virama* (the cessation) and the "beginning" (*ādi*). "Paramāntaka" means the ultimate end; the meaning is that this is the reality (*tattva*) of the third consecration, because the reality characterized as the innate (*sahaja*) has been taught in all tantras. To the question, "What is the distinction here?", he says: "It is concealed," and so forth. This consecration of wisdom (*prajñā-abhiṣeka*), whose characteristics will be described below, must be kept secret in all tantras. If so, what was previously revealed? [The answer is: "The end and the end," and so forth; the meaning is that the Master’s consecration and the Secret consecration were revealed, because this consecration of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna-abhiṣeka*) was not revealed before. || 66 ||

For this reason, he asks: "Therein," because all other consecrations—such as the water, crown, and so forth—are of an identical nature compared to the consecration of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), there is a distinction [to be made] regarding the application of the *vajra*-worship among the four consecrations; therefore, he asks about that: "What is that moment like? Here, by the word "moment" (*kṣaṇa*), the attainment of the essential nature of the moment is expressed; these are the words of the compiler (*saṃgītikāra*). (67)

"Neither nine nor nine selves"—thus it is devoid of the grasped and the grasper. Thus ends the seventh chapter, the "Chapter on the Hevajra Feast," in the illustrious *Hevajra Tantra*, titled "Of Great Fortune. Therein, the Yoginīs ask: "What, then, is Mahāmudrā like?"
O bestower of happiness, please speak in the form of conventional appearances. ||1||
The Blessed One said: "Neither too tall nor too short, neither black nor pale, with a form like a lotus petal, her breath is fragrant. (5.2)
And his sweat shall be fragrant, possessing a luster equal to musk;
in an instant, he shall act like a lotus, emitting the scent of the lotus and the blue water-lily. || 3 ||
The wise man should perceive her fragrance as that of camphor and *sihlaka*, or like the scent of a blue lotus, or a fragrance resembling black agallochum. ||4||
Steadfast and indeed unshakable, speaking pleasantly and charming,
with beautiful hair and a waist marked by three folds— such a woman is considered a Padminī by common folk.
And having attained that, there shall be the accomplishment whose nature is innate bliss. ||5||

Regarding the passage beginning with "Therein" (*tatra*), *mahāmudrā* has already been explained previously. Now, for the practitioner of the elaborate conduct (*prapañcacaryā*), with what [consort] is the accomplishment of *mahāmudrā* attained?
To this, he says: "By means of the conventional" (*saṃvṛtyā*) refers to worldly discourse; "conduct" (*ācāra*) refers to pleasant speech and so forth;

Mṛganābhi is musk; "of equal luster" means having an identical appearance; "indīvara" is the blue lotus; "in a moment" (kṣaṇāt) means at some time; "one should practice" (ācaret) means one should carry [it]. || 3 ||

[Chapter] Eight: *Hevajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā* Then the Yoginī Nairātmyā said: "Blessed One, what kind of vow (*praṇidhāna*) should be made?

The Blessed One replied: "May I be born into a noble family, free from madness, observant of the commitments (*samayī*), a teacher of Hevajra, compassionate, and devoted to the Guru, in birth after birth. (6)
With hands ringing the vajra and bell, reciting the profound Dharma,
may I become one who partakes of the semen of women in birth after birth.
Then that goddess, being thus satisfied, spoke these words:
"By what means indeed are beings who are difficult to subdue and difficult to tame brought to spiritual discipline? (8)

Regarding "Yogācāra," it is the view that this entire universe is mind-only (*cittamātra*); that when an object does not exist, the appearance of an object arises through delusion, just as in a dream. Regarding "Madhyamaka," it is the non-arising of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanutpāda*).
"Every system of mantra" (*sarvamantranaya*) refers to the fivefold division consisting of Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, Yogottara, and Anuttarayoga.
What is intended here is the totality of the various types beginning with the Vaibhāṣika, not a totality of substances, because [substances] are infinite.
"One should grasp" means one should practice.
"Respect for this tantra means reverence. || 9-10 ||

The Ninth Chapter on the Extraction of Mantras. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the encapsulation (*saṃpuṭa*) and the extraction (*udghāta*);
by the mere knowledge of which, the practitioner shall attain accomplishment.

O Goddess, the great jewel possesses a body enveloped in garlands of flames;

Regarding "a needle": having visualized—that is, meditated upon—a blazing vajra-needle, fiery in form and glowing, as the fire-syllable *repha* (the letter *ra*), which is the consumer of oblations. || 5 ||

It is a secret because it is not within the sphere of experience of beings who lack the potential; it is the supreme accomplishment of one's desired goal without effort; it is non-conceptual, meaning it is free from doubt. || 7 ||

"Great jewel" refers to the *cintāmaṇi* jewel. What is that jewel? He says: "Body" is one's own body; "flame," O Goddess, is the flame of great bliss (*mahāsukha*); "garland" refers to the channels (*nāḍī*) whose nature consists of the fifteen yoginīs. By these, it is "filled," meaning established in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

If it were unperforated—that is, unpierced—it would remain merely worldly and unknown; just as a gem that is unperforated is unfit for all types of jewelry, so too, being unknown, it is not capable of attaining Buddhahood.
To the question "What does it do when it is pierced? he says: "It bestows radiance," which means it accomplishes one's desired aims. (8)
In the same way, the jewel of cyclic existence—which consists of the five qualities of sensual pleasure—is like the *vajra-pañjikā* or the *yogaratnamālā*.

"Regarding 'the extraction of the mantra':
this is the verse of the Goddess's question. (14)

The arms are remembered as [the syllables] *ka*, *cha*, *ja*; emptiness (*śūnyatā*)—*kha*, *gha*, *ṅa*, *ca*, *ṭa*; the five Buddhas—*ka*; the faces of the five Buddhas—*ga*; the *ḍombinī*—*ka*, *ga*; the four truths—*ga*; the extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*)—*ka*, *ga*; the extraction of the mantra (*mantra uddhāraṇaṃ*)—*cha*, *ja*; as many as—*ga*; by the mothers and so forth—*ka*. In the *Vajra-tantra*, the Chapter on the Extraction of Mantras: The Blessed One, the Great Vajrin, whose body is the essence of the vajra, said:
"Listen, O Goddess of great fortune; I shall tell you the mantra. (15)
First, having placed Vairocana and the fourth of the sibilants (ḥ),
one should join [the mantra] ending in *svāhā*— this being the divine and beautiful Pukkāsī, white in color and conjoined with the Void (Śūnya).
By this recitation of one hundred thousand times, one shall always paralyze the world.
Having first placed the Lord of the Letters (A), followed by Khecarī,
and then having joined it with "svāhā" at the end, one may bring even the Buddhas under one's control.

Having given the first letter of the Vedas, followed by the second letter of the first [Veda], one should join it with the void (śūnya) ending in svāhā; this will cause even the Buddhas to be driven away.
Having first placed Vairocana, [one places] the third of the second, joined with *ra* and adorned with water (*va*), [followed by] the void (*śūnya*) conjoined at the end with *svāhā*;
this causes all humans to feel hatred. || 19 ||
"The Blessed One said" refers to the words of the compiler; "Listen, O Goddess," and so forth, are the words of the Blessed One. || 15 ||
Vairocana is the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ). The fourth of the sibilants (*ūṣman*) is the letter *ha*. Pukkasī is the letter *ū*.
The anusvāra is empty; "ending with svāhā" means that the word svāhā is at the end. || 16 ||
The Lord of the Vowels is the syllable OṂ; Khecarī is the syllable AṂ. || 17 ||
The second [letter] of the first [group] is the syllable *kha*; the third of the second [group] is the syllable *ja*; and for "vārī," it is the syllable *i*. (18–19)
In the Vajra Tantra, [the chapter on the extraction of mantras]: the fourth of the third [group], beginning with *oṃ*, adorned by Caurī;
the fourth of the semivowels (*antasthā*), joined with the Picu-vajra. (26)
The fourth of the sibilants (ūṣman), adorned by Pukkasī, conjoined with the Void (the letter *ha*), and tripled;
the second of the fifth [varga] (*pa*);
and the first of the third [varga] (*ta*): this is the heart-mantra of Hevajra, ending with *svāhā*. (27)

The fourth [syllable] of the fifth [group], joined with the blazing fire of Virocana and the others, is the mantra. Having first placed the Lord of Letters (A), followed by the third of the fifth [group], that [syllable] is conjoined with Śūnyā and Ḍākinī, ending with Svāhā; this is the Abhicāruka [mantra]. (20) *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā* states: "Having first given the Lord of Letters, [one takes] the third of the fifth.
It is conjoined with Śūnyā and Ḍākinī, ending in Svāhā, for the purpose of malevolent rites (*abhicāruka*). (20)
Furthermore, having bestowed [the mantra] with the eldest of the castes (varṇajyeṣṭha) and resembling the color of the syllable *hūṃ*,
one should immediately summon Rambhā and others, ending with Tilottamā, by means of the word *svāhā*.
First, having uttered the syllable *moha*, one should employ the sound *ghu*;
then, having again appended *svāhā* at the end, one may slay gods and humans. || 22 ||
The first [syllable] of the first [group], however, is conjoined with Vajraḍākinī;
having placed Vairocana at the beginning, the second [syllable] of the semivowels [is added]. (23)
Again, the first [of the labials] conjoined with Vajraḍākinī;
the third of the semivowels conjoined with Vajraḍākinī. (24)
Again, one should join with that very same [syllable], and thereupon place the syllable *hrīḥ*, adorned by Caurī;
then one should perform it again, ending with *svāhā*.
This is the mantra of Kurukullā. || 25 ||
The Lord of Colors is the syllable Oṃ;
the third of the fifth [vowel group] is the syllable Ba, and Ḍākinī is the syllable U. || 20 ||
The syllable Oṃ is the eldest by caste. || 21 ||
The first [syllable] of the first [group] is the letter *ka*.
Vajraḍākinī is the short vowel *u*, and the second of the semivowels (*antastha*) is *ra*. || 23 ||
The third [syllable] of that very [word] is the letter *la*, and *caurī* is the letter *e*. || 25 ||
The syllable preceded by Oṃ, the third of the fourth [group], adorned by Caurī, and the fourth of the semivowels (antasthā) joined with the Picu-vajra. 26.

The fourth of the sibilants (ūṣman), adorned by Pukkasī, conjoined with the Void (the nasal bindu), and tripled; the second of the fifth [varga], and the first of the third [varga], ending with svāhā—this is the heart-mantra of Hevajra. (27)
The fourth [vowel] of the fifth [group], joined with the blazing fire of Virocana and the others, conjoined with the first of the semivowels (antasthā), and adorned by Ghasmarī. (28)

The fourth of the sibilants (ūṣman), adorned with Vajraḍākinī, conjoined with the Void (śūnya) and tripled; the second of the fifth [varga] and the first of the third [varga], ending with svāhā—this is the mantra of the Four-Armed One. ||29||
Of the first [maṇḍala] beginning with Vairocana and of the third, the first is adorned by Gaurī within; the first is embellished by Gaurī within. || 30 ||
The third of the fourth [group] is the letter *da*.
The fourth of the semivowels (*antasthā*) is the letter *va*. || 26 ||
The fourth of the *ūṣman* [sibilants] is the syllable *ha*; *Pukkasī* is the sixth vowel;
the second of the fifth [class of consonants] is the syllable *pha*. || 27 ||
The fourth letter of the fifth [varga] is the syllable *bha*. The first of the semivowels (*antasthā*) is the syllable *ya*. || 28 ||
The first [syllable] of the third [group], with the internal Gaurī (i). || 30 ||

Adorned by Caurī—[variant: Gaurī]—adorned by Ga. Cha. Ja. Joined—Ka. Ga. And the *uṣman*s—Ka; but the *uṣman*s—Kha; the *uṣman*s—Ṅa. Ca. Ṭa. Adorned by Pukkasī—Ka. Ga. Cha. Ja; adorned by that Pukkasī—Kha. Jha. Overcome by emptiness—Ka. Ga. Joined with *jvala*—Ka. Ga. The fourth—Ga. It does not exist—Ka. Ga. Of the final dentals—Ka. Ga. Adorned—Ka. Ga. Adorned—Ga. Caurī—Ga. Residing in Gaurī—Ka; Caurī—Ga. Ninth. *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*: Having doubled [the sequence], the third of the fifth, the third of the second, adorned by fire.
Combined with three *hūṃ* syllables, the second of the fifth [vowel] and the first of the third [consonant], ending with *svāhā*, is the mantra of the six-armed one. || 31 ||
The first [syllable] of the fourth [group], Vairocana and so forth, joined with fire (ra) and adorned by Vetālī;
the third of the semi-vowels (antasthā), adorned by Ghasmarī;
the first of the first [group], joined with the first of the semi-vowels and adorned by Vajrā. || 32 ||
The syllable *kṣa*, adorned by Caurī;
the first of the fifth [varga],
adorned by Vajraḍākinī, which is the fourth of the sibilants (*ūṣman*).
The mantra for the two-armed [form] consists of the syllable ŚŪṂ, followed by three repetitions of ĀKRAṄTA, and ends with PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. || 33 ||

The mantra for agitating the city consists of the first [letter] of *nairātmyā*, the first of the first [varga], the first of the second, the first of the third, the first of the fourth, the first of the fifth, the first of the semivowels (*antasthā*), and the first of the sibilants (*ūṣman*), followed by Vairocana and ending with *svāhā*. It should be recited one hundred thousand times. (34)
The third of the fifth [vowel] is *ba*; the third of the second [vowel] is *ja*; and *vahni* is the letter *ra*. || 31 ||

The first of the fourth [vowel] is *ta*; *Hutāśana* is *ra*; *Vetālī* is *e*; the third of the semivowels (*antaḥsthāna*) is *la*; the first of the first [consonants] is *ka*; the first of the semivowels is *ya*; and *Vajrā* is *ā*. || 32 ||
And *caurī* is here; the first [syllable] of the fifth [letter] is *pa*.

Nairātmā consists of: *a*, the first of the first [group] (*ka*), the first of the second (*ca*), the first of the third (*ṭa*), the first of the fourth (*ta*), the first of the fifth (*pa*), the first of the semivowels (*antaḥsthāna*) (*ya*), and the first of the sibilants (*ūṣman*) (*śa*). || 34 ||

*Nāstika*, doubled—*ga*. *Nāsti*—*kha*. *Nāsti*—*ga*. *Vetālī-bhūṣitam*—*ka kha ga*. Of the semi-vowels (*antasthānām*)—*ka*; five semi-vowels—*ga*. The third—*ka kha*. Adorned (*vibhūṣitam*). The first—*ka kha*. *Nāstika*, joined together—*ga*. Adorned with a vajra (*vajrī-bhūṣitam*)—*ka*; adorned with a vajra (*vajrā-vibhūṣitām*)—*ga*. Adorned—*ka. ga*. Adorned—*ga*. *Nairātmā*—*ga*. This portion of the text does not exist in manuscript *ka*. The first of the sixth—*ga*. The first—*ka*. "Of the sibilants" (*ūṣmāṇām*) does not exist—*ka*; the first of the sibilants—*ṅa. ca. ṭa*. And the first—*kha. ga*. The mantra for agitating the city (*purakṣobha-mantra*)—*ka*; the mantra for agitating the city (*purakṣobhya-mantra*)—*ga*. *Vaḥ*—*ka*. In the *Vajratantre*...
The Chapter on the Extraction of Mantras: The fourth [vowel] preceded by Oṃ, adorned with Caurī, and the fourth of the semivowels joined with Picu-vajra. (26)

The fourth of the sibilants (ūṣman), adorned by Pukkasī, conjoined with the Void (the nasal bindu), and tripled; then the second of the fifth [varga], and the first of the third [varga], ending with svāhā—this is the heart-mantra of Hevajra. (27)
Vairocana and so forth are joined with the blazing fire; the fourth of the fifth [vowels] is joined with the first of the semivowels and adorned by Ghasmarī. || 28 ||

The fourth of the *ūṣman* letters, adorned by Vajraḍākinī and conjoined with the Void (*śūnya*), tripled; the second of the fifth [vowel] and the first of the third [consonant], ending with *svāhā*: this is the mantra of the Four-Armed One. (29)
Of the first and the third [mandalas], beginning with Vairocana, the first is adorned within by Gaurī;
the first is embellished within by Gaurī. || 30 ||
The third of the fourth [group] is the letter *da*;
the fourth of the semivowels (*antasthā*) is the letter *va*. || 26 ||
The fourth of the *ūṣman* letters is the syllable *ha*; Pukkasī is the sixth vowel.
The second of the fifth [group] is the syllable *pha*. (27)
The fourth letter of the fifth [group] is the syllable *bha*;
the first of the semivowels (*antasthā*) is the syllable *ya*. || 28 ||
The first [syllable] of the third [group], which is the internal Gaurī. || 30 ||

Adorned with Caurī—Ga; adorned with Gaurī—Cha, Ja; the fourth from the semivowels (antasthā)—Ka; the fourth—Ga; joined with Vajra—Ka, Ga; and the sibilants (uṣman)—Ka, Kha, Ṅa, Ca, Ṭa; the fourth—Ga; adorned with Pukkasī—Ka, Ga, Cha, Ja; adorned by Pukkasī—Kha, Jha; overcome by Śūnyatā—Ka, Ga; joined with Jvala—Ka, Ga; the fourth—Ga; does not exist—Ka, Ga; of the semivowels—Ka, Ga; adorned—Ka, Ga; adorned—Ga; Caurī—Ga; seated upon Gaurī—Ka, Ca; Caurī—Ga. [Chapter Nine] *Vajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā*: Having doubled [the fifth], the third of the fifth; the third of the second, adorned with Fire.
Joined with three *hūṃ* syllables, the second of the fifth [letter] and the first of the third [letter], ending with *svāhā*, is the mantra of the six-armed one. || 31 ||
The first [syllable] of the fourth [group], Vairocana and so forth, joined with fire (ra) and adorned by Vetālī;
the third of the semi-vowels (antasthā), adorned by Ghasmarī;
the first of the first [group], joined with the first of the semi-vowels and adorned by Vajrā. || 32 ||
The syllable *kṣa*, adorned by Caurī;
the first of the fifth [class],
adorned by Vajraḍākinī, which is the fourth of the sibilants (*ūṣman*).
The mantra of the two-armed [form] consists of the syllable ŚŪṂ, followed by three repetitions of ĀKRAṂTA, and ends with PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. || 33 ||
The first [mantra] of the first [deity] is *nairātmyā*; the first of the second; the first of the third; and the first of the fourth, beginning with Vairocana and ending with *svāhā*. || 34 ||
The third letter of the fifth [varga] is *ba*; the third letter of the second [varga] is *ja*. || 31 ||
The first [syllable] of the fourth [meter] is *taḥ*; *vetālī* is *ai*, *la*, *la*; the first [syllable] of the first [meter] is *ka*, *ya*; *vajrā* is *ā*. (32)
And *caurī* is here; the first *pa* belongs to the fifth [note]. || 33 ||

Nairātmā is *a*. The first letter of the first [varga] is *ka*; the first of the second is *ca*; the first of the third is *ṭa*; the first of the fourth is *ta*; the first of the fifth is *pa*; and the first is *śa*. || 34 ||
In the Vajra Tantra:

"The second of the semivowels (*antasthā*) twice, namely the syllable *kṣa*; again in the middle, the second of the semivowels; three *hūṃ* syllables interspersed with the syllable *phaṭ* belonging to Vairocana and the others, ending in *svāhā*. (35)
Following that, Vairocana and the others [are placed], ending with the vajra and the syllable HŪṂ.

Following Vairocana and the others, there is the letter *a*, which is the first of the *ūṣman* letters, the third of the semivowels (*antasthā*), and the fourth of the consonants (*dharmāṇām*). Subsequently, because it is unarisen from the beginning, there is *vajrā*. Thus: *oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
The Chapter on the Extraction of Mantras.
The second of the semi-vowels is *ra*, and the *vajras* are *ā*.
Thus ends the chapter on the extraction of mantras from the second kalpa in the *Hevajrapañjikā*, the *Yogaratnamālā* composed by Kṛṣṇapāda.
Now, therefore, the tenth chapter, titled "The Recitation," concerning Vajrasattva, the single vow of all phenomena;
having kissed Nairātmyā, he reveals the subject of recitation. (1)
With crystal one performs recitation for subjugation, and with red sandalwood for the same; likewise, with boneless [materials] one performs it for causing dissension.
With a dagger, one performs malevolent magic; with a horse-hoof, expulsion; with a human bone, attraction;
with elephant bones, the bringing of rain; and with buffalo bones, killing. (3)

For the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*), one should drink milk; for subjugation (*vaśya*), one may act according to one's own will. For killing (*māraṇa*), one should use *sihnaka* (ambergris), and for attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), one should use the four [substances] equally. ||4||
For causing enmity, *śālija* is prescribed; for expulsion (*uccāṭana*), musk (*kastūrikā*) is said [to be used].
Alternatively, one should employ the syllables beginning with *anta*, *śva*, *na*, *ga*, and likewise *ha*.
The tenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Recitation."
Then he said, and so forth;
that is the Akṣasūtra concerning that subject. || 1 ||
And [the same applies] to Mahiṣa; thus [ends section] 3.
He states the distinction regarding the timing for each ritual action: || 4 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter, on Recitation, in the second kalpa of the *Vajrapañjikā*, the *Yogaratnamālā* composed by Kṛṣṇapāda.

The eleventh chapter, titled "The Meaning of the Innate": Embracing Hevajra firmly and pressing his lower lip, Nairātmyā asks there concerning the family-form (*kularūpaka*) of embodied beings with her teeth. (1)
"Having established the *liṅga* in the *bhaga*, so says the Lord of the Wheel (*cakranāyaka*).
I shall describe the own family (*svakula*) of embodied beings; listen, O Prajñāpāramitā! (2)
If at the base of the ring finger of either a woman or a man there should be a nine-pronged vajra, it belongs to the supreme Akṣobhya family. (3)
Vairocana’s [symbol] shall be the wheel, Amitābha’s the lotus,
Ratnasaṃbhava’s the great jewel, and that of the Karma-kula the sword.
For whichever yogi is Kṛṣṇa, Akṣobhya is his deity; for whichever yogi is Mahāgaura, he has the Kuladevatā as his deity. //5//
For the yogi who is Mahāśyāma is the deity, and for the yogi who is Mahāpiṅga, Ratneśa is the family deity.
"Deeply," and so forth; "he said" refers to what is about to be stated. (1–2)
"Akṣobhya family" means that it is his family. || 3 ||
The yogi who is red and white belongs to the family deity Amitābha;
indeed, the yogi who is white and pale belongs to the Vajrasattva family. ||7||
Living beings should not be held in contempt nor should they be harmed by those who have reached the further shore of yoga;
for they belong to the family of the Tathāgatas, having relied upon a conventional form.
The characteristics of women are exactly like those of men; their families likewise exist according to their concealment, conduct, and appearance. (9)
There, the Great Vajrin, delighted by the kissing of the bhaga and liṅga, awakened Nairātmyā; listen, O Goddess, to the method of worship.

In a garden, in a secluded place, or within one's own private chambers, the knower of yoga should always worship the Mahāmudrā after having her naked; likewise, he should perform kissing, embracing, and the touching of the vulva. (11)
The phallus of Naranāsā was a vessel for the honey of her lower lip. ||12||
The "family of beings" refers to the Vajrasattva family. || 7 ||
"Of them" refers to women; "those" refers to the Tathāgatas. || 9 ||
"Bodhayāmāsa" means he addressed him. || 10 ||
In the Vajra-tantra, one who possesses *bola* always performs the activity with the limbs of passion;
likewise, with the elbows of the limbs of play, and with well-stretched-out hands, [one acts] for the sake of the innate (*sahaja*). (13)
The wielder of the vajra should desire [union] again and again, and gaze upward from below;
he attains vast accomplishment and becomes equal to all Buddhas. || 14 ||
And especially therein, camphor is drunk; one should also consume madana and bala there for the sake of camphor.
The eleventh chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Meaning of the Innate."

*Madana* is that which arises from great bliss (*mahāsukha*); "limb" (*aṅga*) refers to the nail-marks made with the hands for that purpose; "action" (*karman*) refers to the movement of two fingers and so forth; "possessing *bola*" (*bolavān*) means having a rigid *bola*. By the passage beginning with "on the swing" (*dolāya*), he explains the nature, characteristics, instructions, and performance of the four consecrations (*sekas*): "the swing" (*daulā*) is like a swing, referring to the *aupariṣṭaka* [consecration].
Here, the woman is the agent—she should gradually swing her hips from front to back.

Seated upon the buttocks, it is designated as the *dolā* (swing) posture. Regarding the phrase beginning with *kūrpara* (elbow): here, the man is the agent; having placed [the woman’s] right knee level [with his chest], he should join it with his left arm. This is the upward extension (*ūrdhvakaraṇa*), performed while both stand facing each other. Regarding the phrase beginning with *suprasārita* (well-stretched): these are proclaimed as the *uttāraṇā* (crossing/raising) postures, having the form of a swan’s wings.

With two well-stretched feet, it is the *suprasārita*. By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), he indicates the *sūcī* (needle) posture: where one stands with the feet turned upward and downward like a staff.
With the side slightly bent and the *trika* (the junction of the neck, back, and thighs) somewhat contracted, this is known as *sūcīkaraṇa*. ||11-13||
—The *Hevajrapañjikā Yogaratnamālā* is for the sake of camphor, for the purpose of increasing camphor. || 15 ||
Because it illuminates that specific performance of the innate meaning (*sahaja-artha*), the chapter is thus named.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter on the Innate Meaning in the second section of the *Hevajra-pañjikā*, the *Yogaratnamālā*, composed by Kṛṣṇapāda.
The second chapter of the *Mahāmāyā-kalpa*, the Great Tantra King of the Great Vajra. Now, therefore, the Vajra-holder spoke of the four empowerments:
"Take up the great bell, O you who are established in the Vajra. (5)
O Vajrācārya, this very day, perform the initiation of the disciple. || 1 ||
Just as the sons of enlightenment were sprinkled by the Buddhas of the past,
so have you been sprinkled by me with the secret consecration through the stream of the mind.

"Take it, take it, O Great Being! This knowledge is the giver of delight, the giver of accomplishment, the goddess who is the form of the universe, beautiful to the mind, supremely subtle, stainless, bestowing liberation, and peaceful; having taken it, perform the worship. || 3 ||
The diamond-matrix is like space;
you yourself are its father.
The mantra for the empowerment of the vajra-lotus:
Oṃ padma sukhādhāra mahārāga sukhaṃ dada caturānandasvabhāva viśva hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ, perform my task! ||5||

"Thus," and so forth, are the verses for the offering of the wisdom consort (*prajñārpaṇa*) according to the instruction for the four empowerments (*abhiṣeka*). "Established in the Vajra" means established in the state of a Vajradhara. "Awakening" (*bodhi*) is wisdom (*prajñā*); its "sons" are the Bodhisattvas. (1–2)
Rati is delight; it is the abode of the bodhicitta. || 3 ||

"This" refers to that which is extremely subtle; because it is not an object of perception, it is the Vajra Tathāgatas. Their "maṇḍa" is the essence; it is like space because it is without appearance, and it is stainless because of the destruction of the afflictions.
Oṃ vajra vajrapañjikā yogaratnamālā mahādveṣa caturānandadāyaka khagarbha ekamukha rasara nātha hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ, accomplish my purpose!
The syllable Oṃ at the head, the syllable Hūṃ at the heart, and the syllable Ā in the pericarp. ||6||
The second chapter of the *Māyākalpa*, the Great King of Tantras.
It bestows liberation because it transcends cyclic existence;
it is your father because it is to be personally realized by each individual;
and it is the empowerment of the vajra and lotus by which one is empowered.
Having composed this commentary on the *Hevajra* within the *Yogaratnamālā*, a garland of jewels of yoga, may all people, by whatever merit has been accumulated thereby, become free from afflictions.
The *Śrīvajrapañjikā-yogaratnamālā* is completed.
This work is the composition of the learned master, the venerable Śrī Kāṇḍapāda.
Following the royal genealogy beginning with Parameśvara as before,
this manuscript was written on the [specific] day of the month of Bhādrapada by Kāśī-Gayākara for the illustrious Govindapāladeva.
